The next evening, Fiona replied. She agreed to meet Emma for twenty minutes in a café near the river. Emma could not record the conversation. She could not use Fiona's name in her article without permission.

Fiona added one sentence: Bring dates, not theories.

Emma arrived early and ordered tea. Fiona came in exactly on time. She carried a large bag.

“I remember your old article about Claire Morrison,” Fiona said.

“I remember it too,” Emma replied. “I wrote something I could not prove. I'm sorry.”

Fiona sat down. “Then listen carefully. I worked on some of the trust's accounts. Other people could also use the system. I did not approve every payment.”

Emma asked how the scholarship money was recorded.

“There were three steps,” Fiona explained. “First, the trust offered a scholarship. Second, someone asked the bank to send the money. Third, the bank confirmed the payment.”

Fiona drew three boxes on a paper napkin.

“My daughter says I draw diagrams for everything,” she said. “Even when I explain how to cook an egg.”

Emma smiled. Fiona seemed more relaxed now.

“Can the numbers be different?” Emma asked.

“Yes. A student may receive an offer before the money is sent. But there should be records to explain what happened.”

Emma showed Fiona an email from Calum. She covered his address and other private information.

“The trust wrote this on 19 November 2010,” Emma said. “It says his payment was being processed.”

“Then look for the instruction to the bank,” Fiona replied. “And check if the bank confirmed the payment.”

“Do you remember this payment?”

“No. I remember the system, not every payment.”

“Do you have copies of the records?”

“I didn't say that.”

Emma stopped asking about copies. She wanted Fiona to trust her.

“What if an old record was changed later?” Emma asked.

“There should be a history of changes. It should show who made the change and when. Sometimes people correct honest mistakes.”

When Fiona stood up to leave, she gave Emma one last piece of advice.

“Check the original record for 19 November 2010.”

“Why that day?”

“Because you can check it.”

Emma arrived early. She ordered tea and put her notebook away until Fiona appeared. Outside, people crossed the bridge with their coats pulled tightly around them.

Fiona arrived on time, carrying a canvas bag.

“I remember your article about Claire Morrison,” she said.

“So do I,” Emma replied. “I published something I couldn't prove. I'm trying to do better.”

Fiona looked at her for a moment. “Then listen. I worked on some entries for the trust. I wasn't the only person who could change the accounts, and I didn't approve every payment.”

Emma asked how scholarships were recorded. Fiona explained that there were three separate stages. First, the trust approved an award. Next, someone instructed the bank to send money. Finally, the bank confirmed the transfer.

She drew three boxes on a paper napkin and joined them with lines.

“My daughter says I turn everything into a diagram,” Fiona said. “Even boiling an egg.”

Emma smiled. It was the first personal thing Fiona had said.

Emma showed her the date on Calum's email, covering his private details. The trust had written on 19 November 2010 that his payment was being processed.

“Find the payment instruction from that week,” Fiona said. “Then see whether the bank confirmed it.”

“Do you remember that payment?”

“I remember how the system worked. I won't claim to remember a document I haven't seen.”

“Did you keep copies?”

“I didn't say that.”

Emma did not press her. Instead, she asked how to check whether a later summary had been changed.

“You'd need the original entry and the history of changes,” Fiona said. “Who changed it, when, and why. A correction isn't necessarily dishonest. But there should be a record.”

At the door, Fiona gave Emma one last piece of advice: check the original entry for 19 November 2010 before publishing anything.

“Why that date?” Emma asked.

“Because it's one you can test.”

Fiona's reply arrived the following evening. She would meet for twenty minutes, without recording, and nothing could be attributed to her without explicit agreement. "Bring dates, not theories," the message concluded.

Emma arrived early at a quiet café near the river and chose a table from which Fiona could leave without having to pass behind her. She ordered tea, then closed her notebook. She wanted to be ready to listen rather than conduct an interrogation. Through the window she watched people crossing the bridge, their coats lifting in the wind. She had travelled north in search of answers, but she had begun to suspect that the most useful thing she could do was slow down.

Fiona arrived exactly on time, a canvas bag over one shoulder.

"I remember your article," she said before sitting down.

Emma did not defend it. "I published a claim I couldn't verify. I'm trying not to repeat that."

"Then listen carefully. I handled entries for the trust. I wasn't the only person with access, and I didn't authorise every payment."

"When I was younger," Emma said, "I thought a source who refused to answer was hiding something. I wrote as though that were a fact."

"And now?" Fiona asked.

"Now I know it might mean I haven't earned an answer."

Fiona did not smile, but she remained in her chair. Emma opened her notebook. Fiona explained that an award approval, a payment instruction and a bank confirmation were three separate records. Comparing a brochure's promised maximum with an annual report's paid total could be misleading. But a legitimate discrepancy ought to have an explanation in the records.

Fiona drew three small boxes on a paper napkin, joining them with quick, firm lines.

"My daughter used to say I couldn't explain how to boil an egg without making a flowchart," she said. She seemed surprised to have mentioned her daughter at all.

Emma looked at the boxes: approval, instruction, confirmation. A delayed transfer could be corrected later, Fiona explained, but each stage left a different kind of trace. Fiona folded the napkin and slipped it into her bag. Emma made no move to photograph it.

Emma showed Fiona the dates from Calum's emails, hiding his personal details.

"The trust wrote that the payment was being processed on the nineteenth of November 2010," Emma said.

Fiona studied the date. "Then find the payment instruction from that week. And check whether there's a bank confirmation."

"Do you remember the entry?"

"I remember the system. I won't certify a record I haven't seen."

"Did you keep copies?"

Fiona folded her hands on the table. "I didn't say that."

Emma was tempted to ask whether Fiona had ever seen Claire in the office, or whether Malcolm Vale had ordered someone to alter a record. Neither question followed from what Fiona had actually said. Emma glanced at the clock and decided to use her remaining minutes on a narrower point.

"If the later summary disagrees with the original," she asked, "how would I tell whether it was a correction or something more serious?"

"You'd need the amendment history," Fiona said. "Who changed the entry, when they changed it, and what document supported the change. An amendment isn't automatically dishonest. But it shouldn't be invisible."

Emma let the question rest. Fiona had agreed to discuss a process, not to become an anonymous source for a predetermined accusation.

At the door Fiona paused. "Check the original ledger entry for that date before you publish anything. A later summary isn't the same document."

"Why that date?"

"Because you can test it."

Emma walked back to her hotel. The river was dark and the air was cold. She thought about Fiona's words.

In her room, Emma opened Calum's email again. It said the payment was being processed. It did not say the college had received the money. These were two different things.

Emma wrote to Calum. She asked him to give his old college permission to check its records. The college needed his written agreement because the information was private.

Emma also checked the college's rules. Some old records might no longer exist. If the college found no payment, she would need to ask why.

Next, Emma wrote to the trust. She asked how it offered scholarships, sent money and checked payments. She did not mention Fiona.

Malcolm Vale was still the chairman. His photograph was on the trust's website. Emma looked at it for a moment. She did not know if he had approved Calum's payment.

Sarah called that evening.

“Did you find anything?”

“A date. I need to check it.”

“Good. And the letter?”

“I still don't know who sent it.”

Emma then read her old article about Claire. In 2011, she had written that Claire might have left her family because she wanted to be alone. Emma could not find proof of this in her old notes. She felt ashamed. She saved the article. One day she would need to correct it.

She took a clean page and wrote two headings: What I know and What I don't know.

She knew the dates of the emails. She knew what the trust had published. But she did not know where all the money had gone. She did not know who had changed any records. And she did not know who had sent the strange letter.

A message arrived from Calum. His college had received his permission form. The college had not checked the old payments yet.

Then Fiona sent another email.

Check the original account entry for 19 November 2010. If it is different from the later report, ask who changed it. I can't talk tonight.

Emma read the email twice. Fiona had not said that Malcolm stole money. She had not said anything about Claire. But now Emma knew what to look for.

She wrote in her notebook: 19 November 2010. Original record. Who changed it? When?

“Sometimes that's better.”

She divided a page into two columns. In the first she listed facts: dates on documents, the people she had contacted, and the trust's published information. In the second she listed questions: where the money had gone, who had changed any records, and who had sent the letter.

Calum then emailed to say the college had received his permission form. It had not yet searched the records.

A second message arrived from Fiona.

Check the original ledger entry dated 19 November 2010. If it is different from the later summary, ask who changed it. I can't discuss this tonight.

Emma read the message twice. Fiona had not accused Malcolm of stealing money. She had not mentioned Claire. But she had pointed towards something that could be checked.

Emma wrote one final line in her notebook: 19 November 2010. Original entry. Who changed it, and when?

units.title: The Date
units.transcript:
The walk back to the hotel took longer than Emma expected. She stopped beside the river and looked at the grey water, trying to remember the first time she had heard Claire Morrison's name. In 2011, a disappearance had seemed like a story with a single hidden answer. Now the investigation was made of ordinary details: a form, a date, a person who had signed something, a payment that might or might not have reached its destination.

Back at her hotel, Emma reopened Calum's documents. The trust's message said payment was being processed. It did not say that the college had received it. She had understood the difference intellectually; now it seemed central.

She asked Calum to authorise the college to check its archived finance records. She checked the college's published procedure for historical finance enquiries. It required written authorisation from the former student, and it warned that older records might have been archived or lawfully destroyed. Emma could not make the absence of a document mean more than it did. If the college had no record, she would need to know whether that was unusual before drawing any conclusion.

She drafted a separate request to the foundation for its scholarship conditions and the process by which payments were approved, instructed and confirmed. She did not disclose Fiona's name.

Malcolm Vale remained chairman according to the website. His photograph appeared beside a statement about integrity. Emma closed the page. A chairman's title was not evidence that he had personally authorised any particular transaction.

Sarah rang after nine.

"Any revelation?"

"A date I can check. That's better."

"And the letter?"

"Still private. I don't know who sent it."

After the call, she reread her original article about Claire. There was a paragraph she had once considered powerful: a description of the young woman's silence, followed by the suggestion that she had deliberately cut herself off from her family. Emma remembered the editor's approving nod. She had not remembered the absence of any source for that inference.

She saved the article beside her new notes, not to punish herself but to keep the mistake visible. The fact that she regretted it now did nothing to correct the public record.

Emma made two columns in her notes: verified and unverified. The dates on the correspondence went in the first. The destination of the payments and the identity of whoever had made decisions went in the second. That column was longer.

A message from Calum confirmed that the college had acknowledged his consent form. It had not yet checked the old records. Emma resisted treating the acknowledgement as confirmation of his account.

Another email appeared, this time from Fiona.

Check the original ledger entry dated 19 November 2010. If it differs from the later summary, ask who amended the record. I cannot discuss it further tonight.

Emma read the words twice. Fiona had not alleged theft. She had not named Malcolm or Claire. She had given Emma a testable lead.

Emma wrote one last line in her notebook: 19 November 2010. Original entry. Who changed what—and when?

units.title: The Unanswered Question
units.transcript:
Emma wanted to read the old police records about Claire Morrison. She imagined a room full of files and an officer who could help her. But getting the records was not easy. She spent three days finding out which documents she could see.

Finally, she received part of a police report from 2011. Some names were covered, and two pages were not included. Emma knew this was only part of the investigation.

The report said that Claire's family contacted the police on 22 September. It also mentioned a possible sighting of Claire on the road to Inverness. Next to this information, Emma saw a name and a note: D. Reid — follow-up pending.

She could not find a report about what Reid did next. But that did not mean he had done nothing. Perhaps the information was in another document.

Emma checked the report number in her old notebook. She had written two numbers in the wrong order in 2011. She corrected the mistake. Then she called the records office. An employee explained that different types of police records were kept in different places. Emma asked for more information.

She found Daniel Reid's name in her old notes. He had spoken to journalists when Claire disappeared. Reid was now retired from the police. He worked for a charity that helped people travel to appointments. Emma called his office and left a message.

Her colleague Sarah phoned later.

"Did you find the police report?" Sarah asked.

"Only part of it. They didn't give me two pages."

"Be careful. Don't tell people the pages are missing. They may simply be private."

"I know. I haven't written the story yet."

"That's good news!" Sarah joked.

Emma smiled. "I'm going to speak to Daniel Reid."

"Then listen carefully to what he says," Sarah replied.

Emma went back to the old newspaper archive. She found a photograph of a police officer speaking to reporters outside the station. The caption named Daniel Reid, but it did not say whether he had investigated the sighting. She printed the picture and placed it beside the report. In 2011 she had kept the photograph because it looked good on the page. Now she was interested in the words underneath it. She called the newspaper's picture desk to check the date. The employee could confirm when the photograph was taken, but not what Reid knew. Emma added that answer to her notes.

units.title: The Unanswered Question
units.transcript:
Emma had imagined police archives as rooms full of old files, where a helpful officer could find almost anything. The reality was much slower. It took her three days to discover which records she could request and which were restricted.

At last she received part of an incident log from 2011. Several names had been removed, and two pages had been withheld. It was not the complete police file, so she reminded herself not to treat it as one.

The entry for 22 September described a report from Claire Morrison's family. Another line mentioned a possible sighting on the road to Inverness. Beside it were the words D. Reid — follow-up pending. There was no completed report in the pages Emma had received.

That was interesting, but it proved very little. Perhaps Reid had never written a report. Perhaps it existed somewhere else. Emma checked the reference number against her old notebook and noticed that she had copied two digits in the wrong order fifteen years earlier. She corrected the mistake and wrote down the date.

Later, an administrator explained that witness statements and basic incident logs were kept in different systems. The two withheld pages might not be missing at all. Emma submitted a more specific request for the follow-up reference.

She searched her old notes and found Daniel Reid's name on a list of officers who had spoken to reporters. She thought she remembered a tall man outside the police station, but she could not be certain. Reid was now retired and worked for a charity that organised transport for local people. Emma called the charity office and left a message.

Sarah rang that afternoon.

"You've found the old log?" she asked.

"Only part of it. Two pages are withheld."

"Then don't call them 'missing pages'. You know what readers will imagine."

"I haven't written a headline yet."

"That's a first. Shall I tell the whole newsroom?"

Emma laughed. Then she looked again at Reid's name. "I'm going to ask him what happened."

"Good," Sarah said. "Just let him answer before you decide what his answer means."

Emma went back to the old newspaper archive. She found a photograph of a police officer speaking to reporters outside the station. The caption named Daniel Reid, but it did not say whether he had investigated the sighting. She printed the picture and placed it beside the report. In 2011 she had kept the photograph because it looked good on the page. Now she was interested in the words underneath it. She called the newspaper's picture desk to check the date. The employee could confirm when the photograph was taken, but not what Reid knew. Emma added that answer to her notes.

units.title: The Unanswered Question
units.transcript:
The police archive was not the sort of place Emma had imagined when she was twenty-one. She had pictured shelves of brown folders and an officer willing to search them for a persuasive journalist. Instead she had spent three days establishing which records could be requested, which were restricted and which might no longer exist in their original form.

The document she eventually received was a partial copy of a 2011 incident log, released with names and contact details removed. It was not the complete investigation file. Emma wrote that distinction at the top of her notebook before she read a word of it.

The entry for 22 September recorded a report from the Morrison family. A later line referred to a possible sighting on the road towards Inverness. Beside it was a short notation: D. Reid — follow-up pending. No completed follow-up appeared in the extract.

Emma checked the page numbers. Two pages were missing, both explicitly withheld. The absence of a visible report could mean the officer had never filed one, or simply that the report was elsewhere. She had no right to choose the more dramatic explanation.

Before calling, Emma compared the reference printed at the top of the extract with the one in her old notebook. She had copied the latter from a press briefing, and two digits were reversed. It was a minor mistake, but it altered the route by which she could request the original material. She corrected the entry and dated the correction. Fifteen years earlier, she would have erased the mistake and hoped nobody noticed. Now she wanted a record of how her understanding had changed.

A second document arrived from the archive that afternoon: a short explanation of the retention policy. It did not identify Reid or Claire, but it made clear that administrative extracts and witness statements were held in different systems. Emma highlighted the passage. The missing pages might not be missing from the investigation at all. They might simply belong to a category she had not been authorised to see.

She telephoned the records office. The administrator explained that the extract could not establish what action had been taken after the notation. Emma asked whether she could submit a narrower request for the follow-up reference number. She could, the administrator said, although the response might still be restricted.

Then Emma searched her own 2011 notes. Daniel Reid's name appeared once, in a list of officers who had spoken to reporters outside the police station. She remembered a tall man who had answered questions cautiously and then walked away when a camera crew arrived. That memory might have belonged to a different day; she had never written a description beside the name.

She found a current professional listing for Daniel Reid, now retired from policing and working with a community transport charity. The public contact number led to an office rather than a private address. Emma left a message saying she was reviewing her own reporting about the Morrison case and wanted to clarify a historical record. She did not mention the letter.

Sarah rang before Reid returned the call. Emma described the notation and the missing pages.

"You've got the old log?" Sarah asked.

"An extract. Two pages are withheld."

"So don't write 'missing pages' in the headline. You know how people will read that."

"I haven't written a headline."

"A miracle. I might put it in the staff newsletter."

Emma laughed, then glanced at the notation beside Reid's name. "It says his follow-up was pending. I'm going to ask him what happened."

"Good. Ask him. And Emma?"

"Yes?"

"Let him answer before you decide whether you believe him."

The joke faded, leaving Emma with the old headline open on her screen. Sarah knew precisely where to press.

The police archive was not the sort of place Emma had imagined when she was twenty-one. She had pictured shelves of brown folders and an officer willing to search them for a persuasive journalist. Instead she had spent three days establishing which records could be requested, which were restricted and which might no longer exist in their original form.

The document she eventually received was a partial copy of a 2011 incident log, released with names and contact details removed. It was not the complete investigation file. Emma wrote that distinction at the top of her notebook before she read a word of it.

The entry for 22 September recorded a report from the Morrison family. A later line referred to a possible sighting on the road towards Inverness. Beside it was a short notation: *D. Reid — follow-up pending.* No completed follow-up appeared in the extract.

Emma checked the page numbers. Two pages were missing, both explicitly withheld. The absence of a visible report could mean the officer had never filed one, or simply that the report was elsewhere. She had no right to choose the more dramatic explanation.

Before calling, Emma compared the reference printed at the top of the extract with the one in her old notebook. She had copied the latter from a press briefing, and two digits were reversed. It was a minor mistake, but it altered the route by which she could request the original material. She corrected the entry and dated the correction. Fifteen years earlier, she would have erased the mistake and hoped nobody noticed. Now she wanted a record of how her understanding had changed.

A second document arrived from the archive that afternoon: a short explanation of the retention policy. It did not identify Reid or Claire, but it made clear that administrative extracts and witness statements were held in different systems. Emma highlighted the passage. The missing pages might not be missing from the investigation at all. They might simply belong to a category she had not been authorised to see.

She telephoned the records office. The administrator explained that the extract could not establish what action had been taken after the notation. Emma asked whether she could submit a narrower request for the follow-up reference number. She could, the administrator said, although the response might still be restricted.

Then Emma searched her own 2011 notes. Daniel Reid's name appeared once, in a list of officers who had spoken to reporters outside the police station. She remembered a tall man who had answered questions cautiously and then walked away when a camera crew arrived. That memory might have belonged to a different day; she had never written a description beside the name.

She found a current professional listing for Daniel Reid, now retired from policing and working with a community transport charity. The public contact number led to an office rather than a private address. Emma left a message saying she was reviewing her own reporting about the Morrison case and wanted to clarify a historical record. She did not mention the letter.

Sarah rang before Reid returned the call. Emma described the notation and the missing pages.

"You've got the old log?" Sarah asked.

"An extract. Two pages are withheld."

"So don't write 'missing pages' in the headline. You know how people will read that."

"I haven't written a headline."

"A miracle. I might put it in the staff newsletter."

Emma laughed, then glanced at the notation beside Reid's name. "It says his follow-up was pending. I'm going to ask him what happened."

"Good. Ask him. And Emma?"

"Yes?"

"Let him answer before you decide whether you believe him."

The joke faded, leaving Emma with the old headline open on her screen. Sarah knew precisely where to press.

units.transcript:
Daniel Reid called Emma the next morning. He agreed to meet her at the charity office. He did not want to discuss private information on the phone.

Emma arrived early. Volunteers were helping older people arrange journeys to hospital. It was a friendly place. Emma wondered what Reid was like now, fifteen years after Claire disappeared.

Reid arrived with some notes. "I wrote these after your call," he said. "They are only my memories. They are not police documents."

Emma showed him the report.

"Were you asked to check the possible sighting of Claire?" she asked.

"Yes."

"Did you speak to anyone?"

Reid was quiet for a moment. Then he answered.

"I spoke to someone. But I did not write everything I learned in my report."

"Why not?"

"I thought someone might be in danger if I wrote it down. I believed I could make that decision myself. I was wrong."

Emma looked at him. "Are you saying Claire was alive?"

"No. I'm saying I kept important information out of a missing-person investigation. I don't want to speak about another person's private life."

Emma had many questions. Had Reid helped Claire leave? Did he know where she went? But he had not said these things. She asked a different question.

"Did your decision change the investigation?"

"Perhaps. I can't be sure."

"Did you tell your manager?"

"Not then. I have now asked for advice about correcting the record."

Reid looked at Emma. "You wrote stories about Claire's family in 2011."

"Yes," she said quietly. "I published claims I could not prove."

"Then you know why I don't want people to guess what happened."

Emma asked whether they could meet again. Reid said he would think about it.

During a break in the conversation, Emma looked at Reid's hands. He was turning his empty cup without drinking. She wondered whether he was nervous or simply uncomfortable with an old story. She could not know. She returned to her prepared questions instead of asking him why he looked worried. She wanted him to describe what he had done, not what she imagined he had felt. When he paused, she waited. The silence lasted longer than she expected. A car passed outside, and Reid looked towards the window before answering. Emma wrote down his words without adding an explanation of her own.

units.title: The Road North
units.transcript:
Reid returned Emma's call the next morning. He agreed to meet her at the charity office but said he could not discuss private information over the telephone.

Emma arrived early. A volunteer was preparing envelopes for elderly passengers who needed lifts to hospital appointments. The place felt ordinary and welcoming. She wondered how much a person's work today could tell her about a decision they had made fifteen years ago.

Reid brought a folder of handwritten notes. "I wrote these after you contacted me," he explained. "They're my memories, not official records."

Emma showed him the incident-log extract. "Were you asked to investigate the possible sighting?"

"Yes. I was asked to make an enquiry."

"Did you follow it up?"

He looked towards the window. Two volunteers were loading chairs into a van.

"I spoke to someone," he said. "But I didn't include everything I learned in my report."

Emma waited before asking why.

"I believed someone could be put in danger if I recorded the detail," Reid said. "I also thought I had the right to make that decision alone. I was wrong about that."

"Does that mean Claire was alive?"

"It means I left out information that mattered to a missing-person investigation. I won't make public claims about another person's life."

Emma wanted to ask whether he had driven Claire north or helped her disappear. Instead, she asked what his decision had meant for the investigation.

"It may have affected it," he replied. "I can't tell you how much."

"Did your supervisor know?"

"Not at the time. I've since asked for advice about correcting the record."

He paused. "You wrote about the family back then."

"I did. And I made mistakes."

"Then you understand why I don't want a simple story built around this."

Emma did not ask for forgiveness. She asked whether he might speak to her again after taking advice. Reid said he would think about it.

Emma glanced at Reid’s hands as he turned his empty cup. She wondered whether he was nervous or simply uncomfortable, but she could not know. Rather than interpret his expression, she checked that she had recorded his answers accurately. Outside, a car passed the charity office. Reid waited until it had gone before standing to leave.

units.title: The Road North
units.transcript:
Daniel Reid returned her call the next morning. He sounded older than Emma remembered, if she remembered him correctly at all. He said he would answer questions about procedure but would not discuss protected personal information over the telephone. They agreed to meet in a public room at the charity office.

Emma had reached the charity office early. In the waiting area, a volunteer was sorting envelopes for elderly passengers who needed lifts to medical appointments. The ordinary work going on around her made the old case feel strangely intrusive. Whatever Reid had done in 2011, he had also spent the years since helping people get to places they could not reach alone. Neither fact cancelled the other.

She opened her notebook to a page headed Questions I can ask without naming a source. Beneath it she had written: what was the assignment, what action followed, what record should exist, and who was responsible for recording it? She deliberately left out the question she most wanted answered: where had Claire gone?

Reid arrived with a folder containing his own handwritten chronology. He placed it on the table but kept one hand over the cover.

"I don't have police records," he said. "These are notes I made for myself after you contacted me. Memories, not evidence."

Emma thanked him for the distinction. She showed him the redacted incident-log extract.

"I recognise the notation," he said. "But I can't tell you what was in the withheld pages."

"Were you assigned to the possible sighting?"

"I was asked to make an enquiry."

"Did you?"

He did not answer immediately. Outside the window, two volunteers were loading folding chairs into a van. Emma heard each chair strike the next with a hollow metallic sound.

"I spoke to someone," Reid said at last. "And I did not put everything I learned into the follow-up note."

Emma kept her pen still. "Why?"

"Because I believed a person might be in danger if I did. I also believed I could decide that for myself. I was wrong about the second part."

"Are you saying Claire was alive?"

"I'm saying I withheld a relevant detail in a missing-person enquiry. I won't turn that into a public statement about another person's life without understanding what the consequences would be."

Emma glanced at the redacted log. Reid's initials were still there, beside an enquiry that appeared unfinished. He had offered a reason, not an official record. She turned the page in her notebook and wrote a question for the newsroom's legal adviser: What duty did an officer have to record this?

Emma felt the pressure of a hundred questions. Had he driven Claire north? Had he spoken to her? Was he protecting someone who had asked for help, or someone who had done harm? She chose the one question he might actually answer.

"Did your decision affect the investigation?"

"It may have. I can't measure that now."

"Did you tell your supervisor?"

"Not then."

"Have you told anyone since?"

"I've sought advice about how to correct the record. I'm not asking you to keep my conduct secret. I'm asking you not to confuse my conduct with proof of where Claire is today."

Emma wrote his words as closely as she could. He watched her do it.

"You published things about the family," he said.

"I did."

"Then you know why I don't trust an easy story."

She did not ask him to forgive her. She asked whether he would agree to a further interview once he had taken advice. He said he would consider it.

units.title: What Silence Cost
units.transcript:
At her hotel, Emma read her notes. Reid had admitted one important thing: he had left information out of the police report. But he had not told her what the information was.

She phoned Sarah and explained the meeting. Sarah asked if Emma could use Reid's name in an article. Emma said Reid had agreed that she could report what he admitted, but he wanted to check that she had written his words correctly.

Emma sent Reid a short summary. She also asked the police records office for more information.

Then she received an email from Calum, a student who had received a scholarship from the foundation. His college had found an old payment record. The money arrived later than promised, and the amount was smaller than the amount in his award letter. The college was still checking its other records. Emma asked Calum for permission to get an official copy.

She thought about the two discoveries. There was a problem with a scholarship payment. There was also a problem with an old police report. The police record came from 2011; Calum's scholarship correspondence began in 2010. But Emma did not know if they were connected to each other.

That evening she walked beside the river. She remembered the Morrison family and the stories she had written when Claire disappeared. She wanted to find the truth this time without hurting people again.

Her phone made a sound. Reid had sent a message.

Your summary is correct. I am ready to explain my actions to the right people. I do not know where Claire Morrison is now.

Emma read the last sentence twice. Reid did not know where Claire was now. But did he know where she had been in 2011? She still needed to ask him.

She saved the message and returned to her hotel. Her next plan was to speak to James Morrison, Claire's brother. She knew he might not want to talk to her.

units.title: What Silence Cost
units.transcript:
Back at the hotel, Emma read her notes from the meeting. Reid had admitted that he had kept something out of the record. He had not explained exactly what it was. She could report the first point, but she could not invent the second.

She called Sarah and read the important lines aloud. Sarah asked whether Reid had agreed to be named. Emma explained that he would allow her to report his acknowledgement of an incomplete follow-up, provided she gave him the chance to correct factual errors. He would not be allowed to control the article.

Emma sent Reid a written summary and asked him to check it. She also submitted her request for the missing reference number.

Then an email arrived from Calum, one of the former scholarship students. His college had found an old account entry. A payment had arrived, but later than promised and for less than the amount in his award letter. The college had not yet checked whether there had been later adjustments. Emma asked Calum for permission to request an official copy.

She placed the two discoveries side by side: a delayed scholarship payment and an incomplete police note. The police record came from 2011; the scholarship correspondence began in 2010. Both involved people connected to Claire's disappearance. That did not prove they were part of the same plan.

At dusk Emma walked beside the river. She thought about the Morrison family waiting for news, and about the harm caused when reporters treated guesses as facts. Protecting a person's privacy mattered. So did telling the truth. Sometimes those duties were difficult to separate.

Her phone vibrated. Reid had replied.

Your summary is accurate. I am willing to explain my actions to the appropriate authorities. I do not know where Claire Morrison is now.

Emma read the final sentence again. Reid had said nothing about whether he knew where Claire had been in 2011.

She saved the message. Tomorrow she would try to speak to James Morrison, Claire's brother. After the articles Emma had written fifteen years earlier, he had every reason not to trust her.

Back at the hotel, Emma read her notes from the meeting. Reid had admitted that he had kept something out of the record. He had not explained exactly what it was. She could report the first point, but she could not invent the second.

She called Sarah and read the important lines aloud. Sarah asked whether Reid had agreed to be named. Emma explained that he would allow her to report his acknowledgement of an incomplete follow-up, provided she gave him the chance to correct factual errors. He would not be allowed to control the article.

Emma sent Reid a written summary and asked him to check it. She also submitted her request for the missing reference number.

Then an email arrived from Calum, one of the former scholarship students. His college had found an old account entry. A payment had arrived, but later than promised and for less than the amount in his award letter. The college had not yet checked whether there had been later adjustments. Emma asked Calum for permission to request an official copy.

She placed the two discoveries side by side: a delayed scholarship payment and an incomplete police note. The police record came from 2011; the scholarship correspondence began in 2010. Both involved people connected to Claire's disappearance. That did not prove they were part of the same plan.

At dusk Emma walked beside the river. She thought about the Morrison family waiting for news, and about the harm caused when reporters treated guesses as facts. Protecting a person's privacy mattered. So did telling the truth. Sometimes those duties were difficult to separate.

Her phone vibrated. Reid had replied.

*Your summary is accurate. I am willing to explain my actions to the appropriate authorities. I do not know where Claire Morrison is now.*

Emma read the final sentence again. Reid had said nothing about whether he knew where Claire had been in 2011.

She saved the message. Tomorrow she would try to speak to James Morrison, Claire's brother. After the articles Emma had written fifteen years earlier, he had every reason not to trust her.

units.title: What Silence Cost
units.transcript:
Back at the hotel, Emma replayed the meeting from her notes. Reid had admitted withholding information; he had not said what it was. That distinction frustrated her, but it was the only responsible account of the conversation.

She called Sarah and read the crucial sentences aloud. Sarah asked whether Reid had consented to attribution. Emma said he had agreed that she could report his acknowledgement of an incomplete follow-up, subject to giving him a chance to check the wording for factual accuracy. She would not give him editorial control.

"You have something," Sarah said. "Not enough to publish the whole story, but something that deserves careful checking."

Emma sent Reid a short written summary of what she understood him to have said. She asked him to identify factual inaccuracies, not to rewrite the questions. Then she submitted the narrower records request.

An email arrived from Calum. The college had found an archived account entry corresponding to the scholarship period. It showed a payment, but not on the date he had been told to expect it, and not for the full amount stated in his original award letter. The college had not yet confirmed whether later adjustments existed. Emma asked permission to obtain a certified extract before drawing conclusions.

For a moment she considered the two lines of enquiry together: a delayed scholarship payment and a police officer's incomplete note. They concerned the same trust and the same town, across 2010 and 2011. That was not enough to make them one conspiracy. She drew a line between them on her page and wrote possible connection — unproven.

At dusk she walked to the river. She thought about the family who had waited for answers in 2011, about the people whose names had appeared in articles they had never wanted written, and about the difference between protecting someone's privacy and deciding on their behalf what the public should know.

Her phone vibrated. Reid had replied to her summary.

Your account of what I said is accurate. I am prepared to explain my conduct to the appropriate authorities. I cannot tell you Claire Morrison's current whereabouts. I do not know them.

Emma read the last sentence twice. It did not answer whether he had known where Claire was in 2011. She would ask that another day, when the record was clearer.

For now, she saved the message, dated it and returned to her hotel. The next person she needed to speak to was James Morrison. If anyone had earned the right to distrust her questions, it was Claire's brother.

units.title: At the Door
units.transcript:
Emma called James Morrison before visiting him. James was Claire's brother. He agreed to a short visit, but he did not promise to answer her questions.

On the train, Emma read her old newspaper article. In 2011, she had suggested that Claire disappeared because of a family argument. She had never found good evidence for that story. She felt ashamed.

James opened the door only a little.

“I know who you are,” he said.

“I wrote something about your sister that I could not prove,” Emma replied. “I'm sorry.”

“You made people think she left because she was angry with us.”

“I was wrong.”

James looked tired. Emma remembered his face from photographs taken after Claire disappeared. He looked older now. His anger was still clear.

“I don't want another story about my family,” he said.

“I won't use your words without asking you first.”

“That's what reporters always say.”

Emma stepped back. “Then I'll leave. You have my number if you change your mind.”

She was almost at the gate when James called her back.

“Five minutes. In the kitchen. No recording.”

A child's drawing was on the fridge. Emma saw it but did not ask about it. James had a family and a life outside Claire's story.

“What do you want?” he asked.

“I want to correct my article. And I want to understand what happened.”

“You want to find Claire.”

“I don't know if she's alive,” Emma said. “And finding someone doesn't mean I should tell everyone where she lives.”

James looked at her for a long time.

“That's a better answer than the one you gave fifteen years ago.”

James filled the kettle and asked whether Emma wanted tea. She said yes, although she had already had two cups on the train. The ordinary question made the room feel less like an interview. Emma put her recorder back into her bag where James could see it. She opened her notebook only after he sat down.

units.title: At the Door
units.transcript:
Emma had called James Morrison before travelling to see him. He had agreed to a short visit, although he warned her that he might refuse to answer her questions. She spent the journey reading the article she had published in 2011. It was worse than she remembered: the suggestion that Claire had vanished after a family argument was presented almost as a fact.

James opened the front door without stepping aside.

“I know who you are,” he said.

“I wrote an article about Claire that I couldn't support with evidence. I'm sorry.”

“You made it sound as though she'd abandoned us after an argument.”

“I did. And I was wrong.”

James looked older than in the photographs Emma remembered. His anger, however, seemed untouched by the years.

“The last reporter who promised not to quote me put my words in a Sunday paper,” he said.

“I won't record you. I won't publish anything you say without your agreement.”

“You expect me to believe that?”

“No. I'm asking you to decide for yourself.”

Emma stepped away from the door. She had almost reached the gate when he called her back.

“Five minutes. In the kitchen.”

The kitchen was bright and ordinary. A child's drawing hung on the fridge, and the kettle stood beside the sink. Emma noticed both details but decided they were not hers to describe in an article.

“What exactly do you want?” he asked.

“To correct the record. And to find out what happened before Claire disappeared.”

“You want to track her down.”

“I don't know whether she's alive. And if I found her, that wouldn't automatically give me the right to publish her address.”

James studied her.

“That's a better answer than you gave fifteen years ago.”

James filled the kettle and asked whether Emma wanted tea. She said yes, although she had already had two cups on the train. The ordinary question made the room feel less like an interview. Emma put her recorder back into her bag where James could see it. She opened her notebook only after he sat down. Through the window she could see a bicycle resting against the garden wall. It was a quiet home, and she understood why James did not want his family drawn back into a public investigation. She wrote the date at the top of the page, then left the rest blank.

units.title: At the Door
units.transcript:
Emma had considered sending a letter instead of arriving in person. In the end she had telephoned first and asked whether James would speak to her. He had not agreed to an interview, but he had said she could come by for five minutes if she was prepared to hear the answer no. On the journey she had read her original article twice, forcing herself to look at every unsupported implication rather than only the sentences she could defend.

She had brought a notebook and no camera. The absence of a camera did not make her visit harmless; James would still have to decide whether speaking to her was worth the risk of seeing his family's grief turned into another story.

James Morrison answered the door without opening it fully. From somewhere behind him came the sound of a kettle clicking off. Emma recognised him from an old photograph, although the years had changed the shape of his face. He was no longer the exhausted young man who had stood outside his parents' house asking reporters to leave them alone. He looked tired in a quieter, more permanent way.

"I know who you are," he said.

Emma had rehearsed an introduction on the train. She abandoned it. "I wrote an article about Claire that I couldn't properly support. I'm sorry."

"You said she had left because of an argument."

"I suggested it. I should not have."

"The headline didn't suggest anything."

He was right. Emma had brought a printout of the article, with the headline circled. She did not take it from her bag.

"I'm not asking you to forgive me," she said. "I'm trying to correct the record. I won't quote you unless you agree."

James looked past her towards the street. "The last time someone said that, I read my own words in a Sunday paper."

Emma stepped back from the doorway. "Then I can leave. If you want to talk later, you have my number."

She had reached the gate when he called her name.

"Five minutes. In the kitchen. No recording."

The kitchen was bright and ordinary, with a child's drawing held to the fridge by a magnet. James moved it aside to take down a telephone number written on a shopping list. Emma looked away. His family had not volunteered to become part of her investigation.

"What do you actually want?" he asked.

"To understand what was wrong with the story I published, and what I can establish about Claire's disappearance."

"You want to find her."

"I don't know if she's alive. And I don't believe finding an address would automatically give me the right to publish it."

James studied her for a long time. "That's a better answer than you gave fifteen years ago."

units.title: The Years Between
units.transcript:
James had agreed to give Emma five minutes. They were already in the kitchen. James introduced his mother, Nora, who stood beside the window. He stayed nearby, clearly unwilling to leave a journalist alone with the conversation.

Nora was looking at the garden, but Emma had the feeling that she was thinking about something far away.

“People came to ask questions after Claire disappeared,” Nora said. “Police officers. Journalists. People who knew her. I told them what I thought was important.”

“And now?” Emma asked.

Nora turned round. “Now I think I left something out.”

Emma took a small notebook from her bag. She did not open it yet.

“You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to,” she said. “But I'd like to know what you remember.”

Nora sat at the table. Her hands rested on a folded tea towel.

“It was the evening Claire went away,” she began. “I was walking home. The road was quiet. I saw her near a car.”

Emma waited.

“I knew it was Claire. I had known her for years. She was carrying a bag.”

“Did you see someone force her into the car?”

“No.” Nora answered quickly, then looked down. “That's not what I saw.”

“What did you see?”

“Claire opened the door herself. She got in. The car drove away.”

For a moment, Emma could hear only the clock above the sink.

“What did you tell the police?”

“I did say I'd seen her that evening. But I didn't explain it clearly. Later, everyone was talking about an accident, or someone taking her. I wasn't sure what my little story meant.”

“Did Claire look frightened?” Emma asked.

“I don't know. I wasn't close enough to see her face properly.”

“Then we can't say she wanted to leave.”

Nora looked relieved. “That's what I've been trying to explain to myself for fifteen years. Getting into a car is not the same as having a choice.”

Emma finally opened her notebook. She wrote down Nora's words carefully. She also wrote memory after fifteen years beneath them.

“Is there anything else you're certain about?” she asked.

“Only that I saw her get in,” Nora said. “I remember that because she opened the door before anyone came out to help her.”

Emma closed her notebook. This was important, but it did not solve the mystery. Claire might have planned to leave. She might have been scared. Both ideas were still possible.

Nora looked at her. “You won't write that she left happily, will you?”

“No,” Emma said. “I'll write what you saw. Nothing more.”

James had agreed to give Emma five minutes. They were already in the kitchen. James introduced his mother, Nora, who stood beside the window. He stayed nearby, clearly unwilling to leave a journalist alone with the conversation.

Nora was looking at the garden, but Emma had the feeling that she was thinking about something far away.

“People came to ask questions after Claire disappeared,” Nora said. “Police officers. Journalists. People who knew her. I told them what I thought was important.”

“And now?” Emma asked.

Nora turned round. “Now I think I left something out.”

Emma took a small notebook from her bag. She did not open it yet.

“You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to,” she said. “But I'd like to know what you remember.”

Nora sat at the table. Her hands rested on a folded tea towel.

“It was the evening Claire went away,” she began. “I was walking home. The road was quiet. I saw her near a car.”

Emma waited.

“I knew it was Claire. I had known her for years. She was carrying a bag.”

“Did you see someone force her into the car?”

“No.” Nora answered quickly, then looked down. “That's not what I saw.”

“What did you see?”

“Claire opened the door herself. She got in. The car drove away.”

For a moment, Emma could hear only the clock above the sink.

“What did you tell the police?”

“I did say I'd seen her that evening. But I didn't explain it clearly. Later, everyone was talking about an accident, or someone taking her. I wasn't sure what my little story meant.”

“Did Claire look frightened?” Emma asked.

“I don't know. I wasn't close enough to see her face properly.”

“Then we can't say she wanted to leave.”

Nora looked relieved. “That's what I've been trying to explain to myself for fifteen years. Getting into a car is not the same as having a choice.”

Emma finally opened her notebook. She wrote down Nora's words carefully. She also wrote *memory after fifteen years* beneath them.

“Is there anything else you're certain about?” she asked.

“Only that I saw her get in,” Nora said. “I remember that because she opened the door before anyone came out to help her.”

Emma closed her notebook. This was important, but it did not solve the mystery. Claire might have planned to leave. She might have been scared. Both ideas were still possible.

Nora looked at her. “You won't write that she left happily, will you?”

“No,” Emma said. “I'll write what you saw. Nothing more.”

“When Claire disappeared, everyone wanted a clear story,” Nora said at last. “An argument, an accident, a stranger in the night. Something with a beginning and an end.”

“What did you tell them?”

“That I had seen her on the evening she went missing. It was true. But it wasn't the whole truth.”

Emma took out her notebook without opening it. “What was missing?”

Nora pulled out a chair and sat down. “I was coming home along the road. It wasn't late, but the light was beginning to go. There was a car stopped near the turning. Claire was standing beside it with a bag.”

“Are you sure it was Claire?”

“Yes. I'd known her for years. I recognised her before I was close enough to speak.”

“Did you speak to her?”

“No. I hesitated. By the time I had decided whether to call out, she'd opened the passenger door and climbed inside. Then the car left.”

Emma waited before asking the question that mattered most. “Did anyone make her get in?”

“Not that I saw.” Nora frowned. “Please don't turn that into something it isn't.”

“What do you mean?”

“For years I've thought: if she opened the door herself, perhaps she wanted to go. But wanting to leave and feeling that you have no other choice can look exactly the same from the other side of a road.”

Emma finally opened her notebook.

“Could you see her face?”

“Not well enough to tell you whether she was frightened. And I didn't see what happened before I arrived.”

“Did you tell the police about the car?”

“I told them I had seen Claire that evening. I remember being asked several questions. But I don't know whether I described every detail, and I won't pretend I remember the exact words now.”

Emma made a note of that distinction. A witness's memory of an event was one thing; a witness's memory of a conversation about the event, fifteen years later, was another.

“Why speak about it now?” she asked.

“Because I keep hearing people speak about Claire as though they already know what happened. I stayed quiet because I wasn't certain. But my silence didn't make anyone more certain, did it?”

“No,” Emma said. “It didn't.”

Nora looked directly at her. “If you use this, don't make her sound carefree. Don't say she went willingly just because you didn't see someone force her.”

“I won't,” Emma replied. “I'll distinguish what you witnessed from what neither of us can know.”

units.transcript:
James had granted Emma five minutes, a narrow concession she had no right to mistake for forgiveness. Already in the kitchen, he introduced his mother, Nora, and remained nearby. She stood at the window, watching rain collect along the lower edge of the glass. Beyond it, the garden looked as though it had been allowed to grow on its own terms. Emma resisted the urge to interrupt. Years of reporting had taught her that a silence, properly left alone, could reveal more than a question asked too soon.

“When Claire went missing,” Nora said, “people were desperate for the event to mean something recognisable. A quarrel. An accident. A stranger. Anything that could be fitted into a story and put away.”

“And you saw something that didn't fit?”

“I saw something I didn't know how to interpret. There's a difference.”

Emma placed her notebook on the table, still closed.

“I told the police I'd seen Claire that evening. I've repeated that much to myself for fifteen years. It was true, as far as it went.” Nora turned from the window. “But I kept coming back to the part I hadn't explained properly.”

“Tell me only what you're sure you remember,” Emma said.

Nora sat opposite her. She folded a tea towel into a narrow rectangle and straightened its edges before speaking again.

“I was walking home. The light was going, but it wasn't dark. There was a car near the turning, stopped off the road. Claire stood beside it. She was carrying a bag. I recognised her straight away.”

“Did she notice you?”

“Not that I could tell. I almost called out. Then I thought perhaps I'd only be intruding.”

“What happened?”

“She opened the passenger door and got in. There was no struggle that I saw, no one holding her by the arm. The car pulled away before I'd made up my mind to speak.”

Emma felt an immediate temptation to arrange these details into an explanation. She recognised the temptation for what it was: the same impatience that had once allowed an insufficiently checked account to become a newspaper story.

“Did Claire appear to be leaving of her own accord?” she asked, then corrected herself. “No. That's unfairly put. What could you actually see?”

Nora gave a brief, tired smile. “That's the question I've been asking myself all these years. I could see her open a door. I couldn't see whether she was frightened. I couldn't see what had been said before I arrived. And I certainly couldn't see the choices she believed were available to her.”

Emma wrote the answer down almost word for word.

“Why didn't the account emerge clearly at the time?”

“I can't tell you precisely what I said in that interview. I remember telling the police I'd seen her. I remember answering questions. But if I claim I can reproduce the conversation after fifteen years, I'm doing exactly what I don't want you to do: making a memory sound more complete than it is.”

Emma underlined not a verbatim recollection. The distinction mattered. Nora's present account could provide a lead without establishing what had been recorded in 2011. Both the original statement and the new recollection would need scrutiny.

“For a long time,” Nora continued, “I thought the fact that she got in herself settled the question. Then I began wondering what 'herself' meant. People can take an action without making a free decision. Fear doesn't always look like resistance.”

“And that uncertainty kept you silent?”

“Partly. I was frightened of becoming another person who claimed to know Claire's mind. People spoke about her as if she were either helpless or selfish. I knew neither of those things.”

Emma watched Nora flatten the tea towel again. Silence had not preserved the truth intact; it had merely allowed other explanations to grow around the gap.

“If you write about this,” Nora said, “promise me you won't say she left happily. Or even willingly, without explaining what that word can and cannot establish.”

“I'll describe the action you witnessed,” Emma replied. “I won't pretend it tells us her reasons.”

Outside, the rain had eased. Emma had arrived hoping for a definitive answer and was leaving with something less comfortable: an observation that could change the investigation, provided she did not ask it to prove more than it could.

units.title: The Car by the Hall
units.transcript:
James looked at the clock on the kitchen wall. Emma's five minutes were nearly over.

“There's one more thing,” Nora said. She looked at James before speaking again. “I wasn't sure I should mention it.”

Emma kept her notebook open. “Only tell me what you remember.”

“The car was dark,” Nora said. “I think it was blue. It had a small dent near one of the back lights.”

“You noticed that from across the road?”

“There was a streetlamp. And I had seen that car before. I used to see it parked near the community hall.”

“Did you know who owned it?” Emma asked.

Nora shook her head. “No. But I remember a man standing beside it once. I knew his face from the foundation's meetings.”

James put his cup down. “Nora.”

“I said I wasn't certain.”

Emma looked at James, then back at Nora. “Who was the man?”

“Mr Reid. I don't know his first name. He worked with the trust sometimes. That's all I knew.”

Emma wrote Reid — car? and added a question mark. She did not know whether the car from the community hall was the same car Nora had seen on the evening Claire disappeared. A dark colour and a dent were not enough to prove it.

“Did you see Reid driving that evening?” she asked.

“No. I couldn't see the driver. I saw Claire get in, and then the car left.”

James moved towards the table. “People took one small detail and turned it into a whole story last time. You should remember that.”

“I do,” Emma said. “I'm not going to name anyone in a story because of one memory.”

“Then why write his name?”

“To check whether the car belonged to him. And whether he was involved with the trust in 2011.”

James studied her for a moment. “You can check records. You can't come back here and make Nora repeat this for your newspaper.”

Emma nodded. Nora opened a drawer and took out a small photograph. It showed several people outside the community hall. A dark car stood at the edge of the picture, but its number plate was not clear.

“It's from a summer event,” Nora said. “I don't know if it's the same car. I kept it because my sister is in the picture.”

Emma did not take it. She asked whether Nora could send a copy if she decided she wanted to. Nora agreed to think about it.

At the front door, James spoke quietly. “Claire was my sister. Don't turn another guess into an answer.”

Emma walked back into the rain with a name to check, a photograph she had not seen properly, and no proof of who had driven the car. She had learned something. She had not solved anything.

James glanced at the kitchen clock. The five minutes he had offered Emma were almost gone, and she was preparing to leave when Nora spoke again.

“There is another detail,” she said. “I didn't mention it because I can't be sure it matters.”

Emma remained seated. “What do you remember?”

“The car was dark blue, I think. There was a dent close to the rear light, on the left side. I could see it when the car moved under the streetlamp.”

Emma paused. “That's quite a specific detail after fifteen years.”

“It is. Which is exactly why I don't want you to treat it as proof. I may be remembering a different car. I saw one like it outside the community hall more than once.”

“Did you know who it belonged to?”

“No. But I once saw a man beside it after a meeting. His face was familiar because he sometimes attended events organised by the education trust.”

James set down his mug. “Nora, you don't have to go further.”

“I know.” She turned back to Emma. “I believe his name was Reid. I couldn't tell you his first name or what his job was.”

Emma wrote *Reid?* in her notebook, then underlined the question mark rather than the name.

“Was Reid in the car when Claire got in?”

“I never said that. I didn't see the driver's face. And I don't know whether the vehicle at the hall and the one on the road were the same.”

James leaned against the worktop. “This is how it started fifteen years ago. A small observation became a rumour, and somebody printed the rumour as if it were a fact.”

Emma recognised the accusation. Her old article had connected Claire's disappearance to a personal argument on the basis of a source she had not checked carefully enough.

“I won't publish Reid's name on this evidence,” she said. “But I can look for records from the trust, or photographs from that time.”

Nora opened a drawer and found an old photograph from a community event. There were people beside the hall and a dark vehicle near the edge of the frame. Its registration could not be read.

“My sister is in that photograph,” Nora explained. “That's why I kept it. The car may have nothing to do with Claire.”

Emma examined the image without taking it from Nora's hands. “Would you consider sending me a scan?”

“I'll think about it.”

James walked Emma to the front door. “You can investigate. Just don't make my mother part of another headline.”

Outside, Emma wrote down three separate points: Nora remembered a dent; she associated a similar car with the hall; and she associated a man called Reid with that other occasion. Joining the three points into one explanation would be tempting. But a possible link was not yet a verified chain.

She left with a lead to investigate, not a driver to accuse.

units.title: The Car by the Hall
units.transcript:
James's five-minute concession had already stretched beyond its promised limit. Emma was putting her notebook away when Nora interrupted the movement with a quiet request.

“There is something else, although I suspect it's the least reliable part.”

Emma stopped. “Then tell me the part you're confident about first.”

Nora described the vehicle as dark blue, with a shallow dent near its left rear light. She thought the streetlamp had caught the damaged metal as the car pulled away. Yet the precision of that image troubled her: she could picture the dent clearly without knowing whether it belonged to the car she had seen Claire enter.

“I'd noticed a similar car outside the community hall,” Nora explained. “More than once, I think. It may be that I'm carrying an image from one evening into another.”

Emma asked what connected the hall to the disappearance.

“Not what. Perhaps who. I once saw a man standing beside that other car after an event run by the education trust. I recognised him from the meetings.”

James's mug made a sharp sound against the table. “Mum, you don't owe her a name.”

Nora acknowledged him with a nod, then looked directly at Emma. “Reid. That is the surname I remember. I couldn't tell you what role he had, or even whether he owned the vehicle.”

Emma wrote the name followed by a question mark. Her first impulse was to ask whether Reid had helped Claire disappear. Instead she asked a narrower question: “Did you see him in the vehicle on the night Claire left?”

“No. I never saw the driver's face. I can't even establish that it was the same car.”

James folded his arms. “You know what a reporter can do with three things that nearly fit together.”

“Yes,” Emma said. She remembered the article she had written after Claire disappeared: a disputed personal account, insufficiently corroborated, had acquired the authority of print. She had learnt, too late, that cautious verbs in a paragraph did little to soften a damaging headline.

“I won't identify a driver on the strength of this conversation,” she said. “The name is a lead. The connection needs evidence.”

Nora searched a kitchen drawer and produced a photograph from a summer gathering. Her sister appeared among the people outside the hall. At the far edge of the image stood a dark car, cropped so tightly that its number plate was unreadable.

“That's why I've kept it,” Nora said, touching her sister's face in the picture. “Not because of the car. For all I know, it's entirely unrelated.”

Emma resisted the urge to photograph it immediately. She asked whether Nora might be willing to send a scan once she had considered the request. Nora made no promise beyond thinking about it.

At the door, James said, “Investigate whatever you need to. But don't give us another certainty that turns out to be somebody else's guess.”

In the rain, Emma separated what she had heard into three propositions: Nora recalled damage to a vehicle; she remembered a similar vehicle at the hall; and she associated a man called Reid with the latter occasion. None established ownership, presence on the night, or participation in Claire's departure.

She had obtained a possible route towards verification, not a conclusion. For once, that distinction felt more valuable than a headline.

units.title: The Missing Minutes
units.transcript:
Emma reached the hire car she had collected after her train journey. The rain was becoming heavier. She put her notebook on the passenger seat but did not start the engine. The conversation at James Morrison’s house was still in her mind.

Nora had seen Claire enter a car on the evening she disappeared. She also remembered a similar car near the community hall and a man called Reid. But she had not seen the driver. Emma could not treat those details as proof.

Her phone rang. It was Sarah, her editor.

“Are you coming back to Edinburgh tonight?” Sarah asked.

“Yes. But I need to check something first.”

“Is it about Claire Morrison?”

“It is. I have a name, but I can’t explain it properly yet.”

“Then don’t send me a story yet,” Sarah replied. “Send me what you can prove.”

Emma ended the call and opened her old notes on her laptop. She searched for Reid. There were several people with that name in the documents. One was mentioned in a list of volunteers for the Glenarraidh Education Trust. His first name was Daniel.

That was useful, but not enough. Emma did not know if Daniel Reid was Nora’s Mr Reid, or if he owned a dark car in 2011.

She wrote three questions in her notebook. Was Daniel Reid at the community hall? Did the trust have records showing what he did? Could anyone confirm the car?

Then Emma noticed a date beside his name. It was on a list from August 2011, only weeks before Claire disappeared. The document was an old programme for a local event, not a police record.

Emma took a photograph of the screen so she would remember where she had found the name. She did not publish anything. She sent Sarah a short message: I’m checking a possible witness connection. Nothing confirmed.

Emma also found an online list of the trust’s old meetings. It showed meetings during the summer of 2011, but she could not find entries for September. This did not mean the meetings had stopped. The website might not have all the records.

As she closed the laptop, another message appeared on her phone. It came from an unknown number.

You should ask why the trust stopped keeping its old meeting records.

Emma stared at the screen. There was no name and no explanation. Anyone could have sent it.

She saved the message. Then she looked back towards the Morrison house. Its windows were dark now.

She had two new questions: was the Daniel Reid she had interviewed the man Nora remembered, and who wanted her to ask about the records? Neither question had an answer yet.

units.title: The Missing Minutes
units.transcript:
Emma reached the hire car she had collected after the train journey. Rain struck the windscreen hard enough to blur the Morrison house behind her. She left the engine off and placed her notebook on the passenger seat.

Nora’s account had given her a direction, but not an accusation. She had seen Claire get into a car. She associated a similar vehicle with the community hall and remembered a man called Reid standing beside it on another occasion. She could not identify the driver on the evening Claire vanished.

Emma read her notes again, checking where observation ended and assumption began. She had crossed out a sentence that described Reid as the driver. She had never been entitled to write it.

Sarah called before Emma could leave.

“Are you driving back tonight?”

“In a little while. I’ve found a possible lead.”

“Something we can use?”

“Not in print. Not yet.”

“Good,” Sarah said. “I’d rather have a verified fact tomorrow than an interesting mistake tonight.”

After the call, Emma opened the scanned material from her 2011 reporting. Searching for Reid returned several results. One appeared in a programme for an August event organised by the Glenarraidh Education Trust. Under Community volunteers was the name Daniel Reid.

Emma studied the document. A name on a programme could establish that somebody had been listed, but not that he had attended the event, owned a particular car or helped Claire leave. It did not even establish that this Daniel Reid was the man Nora remembered.

She drafted a small list of checks: the hall’s old booking records, the trust’s volunteer registers, and any contemporary photograph with a readable number plate. She would also need to ask Nora, through James, whether the first name Daniel meant anything to her. She would not call Nora again without permission.

A second document caught her attention: a surviving index of the trust’s committee meetings. The entries ran regularly through the summer of 2011, then stopped before September. There might be an ordinary explanation. The file could be incomplete; older minutes might be held elsewhere.

Emma wrote gap in archive — reason unknown.

Her phone lit up with a message from a number she did not recognise.

Ask why the trust stopped keeping its old meeting records.

For a moment the words seemed almost too well timed. Someone apparently knew what she was examining. But the message contained no evidence that its sender had seen her screen, nor that the trust had actually stopped keeping records. It might have been based on public information or a guess.

Emma saved the message, including the time and number, and forwarded it to Sarah without attaching a theory.

Then she started the engine. As the wipers cleared the glass, the village road came into view. She had a name to verify, a break in an archive to investigate, and an anonymous message that could mean something—or nothing at all.

units.title: The Missing Minutes
units.transcript:
Emma reached the hire car she had collected after arriving by train, but did not turn the ignition. Rain moved across the windscreen in uneven sheets, erasing and restoring the Morrison house beyond it. She set her notebook beside her and reread Nora’s account before memory could smooth away its qualifications.

Claire had entered a vehicle without visible force. Nora had associated a similar dark car with the community hall and, on a separate occasion, a man she knew only as Reid. She had seen neither the driver’s face nor a registration number on the night in question. The chain of association was tempting precisely because it was so easy to mistake for a chain of evidence.

Emma put a line through the phrase Reid’s car in her notes. Even as shorthand, it attributed an ownership nobody had established.

Sarah rang while Emma was still working.

“You sound as if you’re writing the lead in your head,” her editor said.

“I’m trying not to.”

“Then tell me what you can verify, not what you suspect.”

“An eyewitness remembers Claire getting into a car. The rest needs checking.”

There was a pause. “That’s not a headline,” Sarah said. “Which is why it’s a reasonable place to start.”

After they hung up, Emma searched the digital scans she had kept from 2011. The surname Reid appeared repeatedly, attached to unrelated people and organisations. One entry stood out: an August programme for a Glenarraidh Education Trust event listed Daniel Reid among its community volunteers.

It was the kind of discovery that could mislead a reporter hungry for progress. The programme proved only that the name had been printed. It did not prove attendance, possession of a particular vehicle, or even that Daniel and Nora’s Mr Reid were the same person. Emma recorded the source, its date and those limitations together.

She made a verification plan rather than a paragraph for publication. Could the hall confirm bookings from that period? Had the trust retained its volunteer register? Was there a photograph whose registration plate could be read independently? And would James permit a single, carefully framed follow-up question to Nora?

While reviewing the trust’s digitised files, Emma came across an index to committee minutes. Entries appeared at regular intervals until late August 2011; none were visible for the weeks around Claire’s disappearance. An absence on a website was not evidence that meetings had ceased, still less that records had been deliberately destroyed. The original archive might simply be elsewhere.

She typed: online index incomplete after August; determine custody of originals.

A message arrived from an unfamiliar number.

Ask why the trust stopped keeping its old meeting records.

Its timing made her uncomfortable. The wording converted a question about an incomplete index into an assertion that record-keeping itself had stopped. Whoever had written it might possess useful knowledge, or might be trying to steer her towards a conclusion. Nothing in the message established access to her laptop or confirmed the claim.

She preserved the message with its timestamp and sent Sarah a factual account of its arrival. She would not reply before finding out whether there was anything to verify.

At last Emma started the engine. The wipers briefly revealed the empty road ahead. She had not advanced from uncertainty to certainty. She had narrowed the uncertainty into questions that evidence might answer—and identified one new attempt to shape the questions she asked.
