units.transcript:
Emma arrived at her flat in Edinburgh later than she had planned. Before going to bed, she sent Sarah a copy of the strange message. She also wrote down where she had found Daniel Reid’s name. She did not want to forget which details came from documents and which came from Nora’s memory.

In the morning, Sarah called her.

“The trust says it has records from 2011,” she said. “I spoke to someone in the office. They told me that the website does not show everything.”

“Who did you speak to?” Emma asked.

“A woman called Fiona Bell. She works with the trust’s accounts. She said there are paper files in storage. But she cannot say whether the September meeting papers are among them.”

Emma opened the trust’s website. The list of meeting dates stopped just before September 2011. That looked strange, but Fiona’s answer gave another possible explanation: the website might be incomplete.

“Can I call her?” Emma asked.

“She said you could send questions by email. She wants them in writing.”

Emma wrote a short message to Fiona. She asked three things: whether the trust had held meetings in September 2011, whether the minutes still existed, and who was responsible for keeping them. She did not mention the anonymous message.

After she sent the email, she looked again at the August programme. Daniel Reid’s name was printed under ‘volunteers’. There was no photograph and no job description. She searched an old newspaper website and found a short report about the community hall’s summer repairs. The report mentioned a local driver named Daniel Reid, who had helped move equipment.

Emma felt a moment of excitement. A driver. A hall. The same name.

But the report did not say what vehicle Daniel used. It did not place him at the hall on the evening Claire disappeared. Emma underlined those missing facts in her notebook.

Then her phone rang. The number was hidden.

A man spoke quietly. “Stop asking about the minutes. Ask who signed the payments.”

“Who is this?” Emma asked.

The line went dead.

Emma stared at her notes. Someone had now pointed her towards the trust’s financial records. She could not know whether the caller was helping her or trying to lead her away from the truth.

She saved the time of the call and told Sarah exactly what had been said. This time, she wanted a record of every step before she followed the next clue.

Before bed, Emma found another envelope at her door. It had arrived by courier. The letter was signed Claire. It said: ‘Stop asking about the scholarships. If you publish anything, you will only hurt people who have already suffered.’ Emma kept the envelope and its delivery label. She did not know who had written it. The first letter had asked her to investigate; this one wanted her to stop. She sent Sarah a copy and put the two letters in separate folders.

Fiona Bell was not Fiona Kerr, the former accountant Emma had met near Inverness. Bell worked with the trust's current records.

units.title: The Accounts
units.transcript:
By the time Emma returned to Edinburgh, she had stopped trying to make the pieces fit neatly together. Nora’s account belonged in one column of her notes; the August programme belonged in another. Both might matter. Neither identified the driver of the car Claire had entered.

The next morning Sarah rang with a small but useful development. She had contacted the Glenarraidh Education Trust and spoken to Fiona Bell, who worked with its financial records.

“Fiona says the online meeting index isn't a complete archive,” Sarah told her. “Some of the older paperwork was moved into storage. She couldn't confirm whether the September 2011 minutes survive.”

“Then we can't describe them as missing,” Emma said.

“Not yet. We can say they aren't available on the website.”

Fiona had agreed to receive written questions, although she had made no promise to answer them. Emma drafted an email asking whether meetings had taken place in September 2011, who had custody of the minutes and whether copies could be inspected. She kept the anonymous message out of it. She wanted Fiona's answer to be independent of the wording someone had sent to her phone.

While she waited, Emma searched newspaper archives for Daniel Reid. One short article about repairs to the community hall referred to a local driver of that name who had helped transport furniture in August 2011. She checked the article's date twice.

A driver connected with the hall was interesting. Yet the article gave no registration number, no description of a car and no indication that Reid had been present on the night Claire disappeared. Emma wrote the limits of the evidence beside the reference rather than in a separate notebook where she might overlook them later.

At eleven seventeen, her phone rang from a withheld number. She answered without introducing herself.

“Forget the minutes,” a man's voice said. “Find out who approved the payments.”

“Which payments?” Emma asked.

The caller hung up.

She immediately wrote down his exact words. She had no recording and could not be certain she would recognise the voice again. The second contact might have come from the same person who had sent the message, but nothing established that.

Emma told Sarah. Sarah's first suggestion was to ask Fiona about the payments as well.

“Not in the same email,” Emma replied. “If she's willing to answer the archive questions, we should see what she says without supplying someone else's accusation.”

Sarah agreed. They would keep the call separate, request publicly available financial statements and ask for the trust's record-retention policy. Emma closed her notebook with an uneasy sense that someone was setting the order of her investigation.

The question was whether that person knew something worth finding—or merely knew which words would make her look.

Before going to bed, Emma found a second envelope delivered by courier. The letter was signed Claire: ‘Stop asking about the scholarships. If you publish anything, you will only hurt people who have already suffered.’ It contradicted the first letter's request to investigate. Emma photographed the delivery label, kept both originals separately and sent Sarah a copy. A familiar signature could not establish authorship. Whoever had arranged this delivery had given her another document to check, not a reason to abandon the enquiry.

Fiona Bell's work with the current records was separate from Fiona Kerr's earlier accounting role. Emma would keep the two sources distinct.

units.title: The Accounts
units.transcript:
Emma had returned to Edinburgh with a familiar professional temptation: the urge to turn three incomplete fragments into a story that sounded inevitable. Nora had recalled a car, an old programme named a volunteer, and an online index appeared to fall silent at an inconvenient moment. Arranged in the right order, they suggested a conspiracy. Examined individually, they remained questions.

Sarah rang shortly after nine. She had made a preliminary enquiry at the Glenarraidh Education Trust and reached Fiona Bell, a member of the finance team.

“The index on their website isn't comprehensive,” Sarah reported. “Fiona says older files were transferred to physical storage. She wouldn't confirm whether the September 2011 minutes are there, or even whether she has personally seen them.”

Emma looked again at the anonymous message: You should ask why the trust stopped keeping its old meeting records. Its confident premise now seemed particularly suspect. An incomplete public index was not evidence that the organisation had stopped taking minutes. Nor was Fiona's account proof that the documents existed.

“Did she offer access?” Emma asked.

“Written questions only. And no guarantee of a response.”

Emma composed a measured email. Had the board met in September 2011? Who had been responsible for recording and retaining its decisions? Did any original minutes or copies remain available for inspection? She deliberately avoided repeating the anonymous allegation. If Fiona knew nothing of it, Emma preferred not to contaminate a potentially independent account.

Next came Daniel Reid. A search of contemporary newspaper archives yielded a brief item about refurbishment work at the community hall. It credited a local driver named Daniel Reid with transporting furniture in August 2011. The coincidence was worth recording, but the source did not identify a vehicle, establish attendance on the evening of Claire's disappearance, or demonstrate that this Daniel Reid was the man Nora remembered. Emma added those exclusions directly beneath the clipping.

At 11.17 a.m., a withheld number appeared on her phone. She answered and heard a male voice, low and controlled.

“You're wasting time on the minutes,” he said. “Look at who authorised the payments.”

“Which payments? And who am I speaking to?”

The connection ended.

Emma wrote down the exchange immediately, marking the phrasing as a recollection rather than a recording. The timing encouraged a connection with the earlier text message; the evidence did not. Nor did a reference to payments constitute an allegation she could responsibly publish. A genuine whistle-blower, an interested party with a grudge and someone deliberately trying to misdirect her might all have used the same instruction.

Sarah proposed adding a question about payments to Fiona's email. Emma declined. It had already been sent, and modifying the enquiry might make it impossible to tell what Fiona volunteered without prompting. Instead they agreed to seek the trust's published accounts, check what financial disclosures actually covered and make a separate request about approval procedures.

After the call, Emma reopened the file she had named Unverified. It was growing faster than the folder called Evidence.

She could live with that imbalance, provided she did not mistake the volume of suspicions for their weight. What unsettled her was a different possibility: someone outside the newsroom seemed determined to choose which question she would ask next.

Before bed, a second courier envelope was waiting at her door. The letter bore Claire's name: ‘Stop asking about the scholarships. If you publish anything, you will only hurt people who have already suffered.’ The injunction ran against the first letter's invitation to investigate. Emma preserved the envelope and tracking label, recorded its arrival and sent Sarah a copy. She filed the two originals separately. The signature established what the writer wished her to believe, not who the writer was. Until she could trace it, the warning belonged among her unverified sources.

She entered Fiona Bell and Fiona Kerr separately in her source list: the current records contact and the former external accountant were different women with different knowledge of the trust.

options.text: Emma has now solved Claire’s disappearance.

questions.explanation: A growing number of suspicions does not make them strong evidence.

units.title: The Correction
units.transcript:
Emma opened the trust’s annual report on her laptop. Sarah had sent her a link to the accounts, but Emma was still thinking about the anonymous call.

“Ask who signed the payments,” the man had said.

She found a table of grants paid to students in 2011. It gave totals for the year, but not the names of the students or the people who had approved each payment. She checked another page. There was a note about a student support programme. It did not explain how each student had received the money.

Emma called Sarah.

“These totals don't tell us whether any payment was wrong,” Emma said.

“Can we ask for the detailed records?”

“We can ask. But we shouldn't say the money was stolen just because the report doesn't show every name.”

A reply arrived from Fiona Bell. Fiona confirmed that the foundation had held a board meeting in September 2011. She said there might be paper copies of its minutes in storage, but she had not checked the boxes herself. She also explained that the published accounts showed groups of payments, not every individual transaction.

Fiona offered to ask the records team which boxes were still available. She did not promise that they would find anything.

Emma read the message twice. It was a useful answer, but it did not solve the mystery.

That afternoon, she visited the public library. She wanted to see an old local newspaper that had not been fully copied online. In a report about a fundraising event in 2011, she found a photograph of Claire standing beside several students. Malcolm Vale was at the other end of the group. The caption said the foundation had promised travel grants to help students attend courses outside the village.

Emma photographed the page and recorded its date.

The picture proved that the promise had been made in public. It did not show who had received money.

Sarah rang again. “So what do we have?”

“A promise to students, a yearly total, and a question about the individual payments,” Emma said. “Not an answer.”

Before she left, the librarian brought her a second newspaper from the same month. Emma was about to close it when she noticed a small correction printed near the bottom of the page. It referred to the foundation’s student travel scheme.

The correction said that the number of students named in an earlier article had been wrong.

Emma copied the notice. She would need to find the earlier article before she could understand the difference.

For the first time that day, the next step was clear. She needed to compare what the foundation had promised with what its records could actually confirm.

Money given to help someone study or complete a project.
To officially agree that something may happen.
A place where records or objects are kept.
Words printed beside a photograph.
A published statement fixing an earlier mistake.

units.title: The Correction
units.transcript:
Emma began with the trust’s published accounts. The caller's instruction had sounded specific—find out who authorised the payments—but the annual report offered only aggregated figures. A line for student support showed how much the foundation had spent across the year. It did not identify individual recipients or the people who had approved each transfer.

Sarah joined her on the phone.

“Is the information deliberately missing?” Sarah asked.

“We can't tell. These are summary accounts, not a list of transactions. They're doing a different job.”

They agreed to keep separate notes: what the report stated, what the anonymous caller alleged and what they still needed to request.

Then Fiona Bell replied to Emma's earlier email. According to Fiona, the board had met in September 2011. Some paper minutes might remain in storage, but she had not inspected the boxes and could not guarantee that the relevant records survived. The public index, she confirmed, was not a complete record of every meeting.

Fiona also explained that the annual figures grouped several grants together. She offered to contact the records team and check what material could be located. There was no promise of access, and no suggestion that she had seen evidence of improper payments.

“That's more helpful than it sounds,” Emma told Sarah. “At least we know which questions are still open.”

Emma went to the city library to consult an old local newspaper that had been only partly digitised. In a report about the foundation's 2011 fundraising event, she found a photograph showing Claire Morrison with a group of students. Malcolm Vale stood near the edge of the frame. The caption described a public pledge to help local students pay for travel to courses outside Glenarraidh.

units.title: The Correction
units.transcript:
The annual accounts had the reassuring appearance of precision: totals arranged in columns, notes beneath them, a statement of expenditure that invited the reader to believe every pound had been accounted for. Emma knew better than to mistake financial presentation for a transaction history. The figure for student assistance was an aggregate. It could establish what the Glenarraidh Education Trust reported spending; it could not, by itself, identify beneficiaries, authorising officers or the purpose of individual transfers.

Sarah rang as Emma compared the report with her notes from the withheld call.

“Doesn't the lack of names tell us something?”

“It tells us the report doesn't contain names,” Emma replied. “Whether the underlying records are absent is another question.”

They created three headings: Reported, Alleged and Unverified. Emma placed the caller's instruction in the second category, not the first. Whoever had telephoned might possess inside knowledge, but neither his authority nor his motive had been established.

Fiona Bell's reply arrived before midday. She confirmed that the trust's board had met in September 2011, qualifying the impression left by the incomplete online index. Some historical minutes had been transferred to storage, she wrote, although she had not personally examined the relevant boxes. She would ask the records team to establish whether copies could be located and whether any could be made available for inspection.

As for the accounts, Fiona explained that the published line for educational assistance consolidated multiple grants. It was not intended as a beneficiary-by-beneficiary schedule. Emma noted what Fiona had confirmed and, equally carefully, what she had not: nothing about the authenticity of a particular payment, the existence of a signed authorisation or any deliberate concealment.

Later, at the library, Emma consulted the paper edition of a local newspaper whose early archives were incomplete online. A photograph from a 2011 fundraising evening showed Claire with several prospective students; Malcolm Vale stood at the far side of the group. Beneath it, the caption repeated the trust's pledge to support travel expenses for courses beyond Glenarraidh.

She captured the complete page, including publication date, rather than cropping away its context. A public pledge was relevant to Claire's concerns about promises and outcomes. It was not evidence that any named student had been deprived of support.

The more intriguing discovery appeared almost by accident: a small correction in a subsequent issue. The paper acknowledged that its earlier coverage had misstated the number of students involved in the travel programme. The correction did not supply the revised figure or explain the source of the original mistake.

For several seconds Emma imagined the discrepancy as the first visible crack in an elaborate deception. Then she stopped. A numerical error could arise in reporting, administration or communication without indicating fraud. The proper next step was to retrieve the initial article, establish precisely what had been claimed and compare it with whatever grant schedules the trust might lawfully disclose.

Sarah texted to ask whether the accounts had yielded anything substantial.

Not yet, Emma wrote. We have a public promise, a summary figure and an unresolved correction. No evidence of an improper transfer.

She set the two newspaper references beside Fiona's email. The anonymous voice had attempted to supply a conclusion and a route towards it. Emma would follow the documentary trail instead.

As she closed her notebook, she noticed something else about the correction: it referred not merely to the number of applicants, but specifically to the number of students selected. That distinction had appeared nowhere in the public statement she had just read. She circled the word and wrote one question underneath.

Selected by whom?

units.title: The Selection List
units.transcript:
Emma returned to the library the next morning. She had one clear task: find the newspaper article mentioned in the correction. The small notice had said that an earlier report gave the wrong number of students selected for the foundation's travel scheme.

The librarian brought her a bound collection of newspapers from September 2011. Emma found the article on a page with several photographs of local events. Its title was simple: “Eight Students Chosen for Travel Support.”

Eight, Emma wrote in her notebook.

The article said the Glenarraidh Education Trust had selected eight students to receive help with travel costs. It quoted Malcolm Vale, the chair, who described the scheme as a way to give young people more opportunities. It did not name the eight students or explain how they had been chosen.

Emma checked the date. The article had appeared two days before her interview with Claire, on 16 September 2011. The correction had been published later that month, after Claire disappeared.

She compared the two pages. The correction said the original number was inaccurate, but it did not give a new number. It was impossible to know from these papers whether seven, nine or some other number of students had actually been selected.

She called Sarah.

“There's a number in the original article,” Emma said. “Eight students. But the correction doesn't tell us the right number.”

“Does that prove something went wrong with the money?”

“No. It proves the paper printed a wrong figure. We need the student selection records and the payment records before we can say more.”

Emma asked the librarian whether there were more local reports about the scheme. The librarian suggested checking the letters page and the following week's edition.

There, Emma found a short letter from a parent. The writer complained that families had not been told how students were selected. The newspaper had removed the writer's name, but the date and text were clear.

Emma photographed the page. The parent's complaint was important, but it was only one person's account. It did not prove that any particular student had been treated unfairly.

When Emma opened her notebook again, she made three separate lines: what the trust announced, what the paper corrected, and what one parent had questioned.

She looked at Claire's old interview notes. Claire had spoken about promises made to students. Emma now had a better question for Fiona Bell: did the trust still have the selection rules from 2011?

She wrote the question without mentioning the anonymous caller. The next answer, she decided, should come from a document.

Emma went back to the library to find the article to which the correction referred. The librarian located a bound volume of the local paper, and Emma worked through September 2011 until she found a report headed “Eight Students Chosen for Travel Support.”

The original article, dated 16 September, described a scheme run by the Glenarraidh Education Trust. Malcolm Vale had praised it as an opportunity for young people to attend courses beyond the village. Eight students were said to have been selected. Their names were not printed, and the report offered no explanation of the selection process.

The correction Emma had found the previous day appeared after Claire's disappearance. It acknowledged that the figure in the earlier article was incorrect, but offered neither a replacement number nor a reason for the mistake. She photographed both complete pages, making sure the dates and headings were visible. A corrected newspaper report was useful evidence of what the public had been told; it was not a register of grants awarded or payments made.

“Eight was wrong,” Sarah said when Emma called. “Doesn't that suggest the trust exaggerated its work?”

“Possibly. But it could also mean someone at the newspaper misunderstood a figure. We need to know which number the trust supplied, if any, and how selection worked.”

The librarian suggested looking for readers' letters. A few pages later, Emma found one printed under the heading “Questions About Student Grants.” Its author, described only as a local parent, said families had not been given clear information about the criteria used to select students.

Emma read the letter twice. It was a contemporary complaint, not proof of wrongdoing. The newspaper had withheld the parent's identity, and Emma could not know whether the writer had applied for a grant or had first-hand knowledge of the process. Still, the complaint showed that questions about fairness had been raised at the time, not invented fifteen years later.

Back at her table, Emma divided her notes into three columns: announcement, correction, and complaint. Each source had a different purpose and different limitations. None identified a recipient or an approving officer.

She then reopened her notes from her 18 September interview with Claire. Claire had questioned whether the foundation delivered what it promised. The old remark now suggested a line of enquiry rather than an answer.

Emma drafted a follow-up question for Fiona: could the trust locate its 2011 selection criteria and any record of decisions made under them? She kept the request separate from the anonymous caller's accusation about payments.

It was tempting to jump from a disputed number to a missing payment. Emma closed the notebook before the temptation became a headline.

units.transcript:
The correction had offered Emma an apparently straightforward task: identify the inaccurate figure in the original report and establish what should have stood in its place. At the library, the first half proved easy. The second did not.

A bound volume of the local newspaper yielded an article dated 16 September 2011, two days before Emma interviewed Claire Morrison. Beneath the headline “Eight Students Chosen for Travel Support,” Malcolm Vale was quoted celebrating the Glenarraidh Education Trust's commitment to widening educational opportunities. Eight applicants, the article asserted, had been selected for travel assistance. It named none of them and described neither the eligibility criteria nor the panel responsible for the decision.

The later correction conceded that the number had been wrong. It supplied no substitute and attributed the error to no one. Emma resisted reading that silence as an admission by the trust: the notice was issued by a newspaper, and its omissions established remarkably little about the organisation's underlying records.

She photographed both pages intact, including the masthead and publication dates. A crop of the disputed sentence might be persuasive on a screen; it could also disguise the difference between a reporter's account and a primary administrative record. Emma wanted to preserve precisely that distinction.

Sarah answered on the third ring. “So the announcement was inflated?”

“We don't know whether it was inflated. We know the paper later corrected its figure. The trust might have supplied the number, the journalist might have misheard it, or the circumstances might have changed before publication. None of those explanations is established.”

Further searching produced a letter from a reader, published shortly afterwards under the heading “Questions About Student Grants.” The writer was identified only as a parent from Glenarraidh and complained that families had not been told how candidates were chosen. The editor had withheld the name. Emma could neither contact the writer from the printed record nor assess whether the complaint came from direct experience. Nevertheless, its contemporary date mattered: uncertainty about the selection procedure had been voiced publicly in 2011.

She constructed a source table. The announcement represented a published claim. The correction documented an acknowledged reporting error. The letter registered a complaint whose factual basis remained unknown. Treating the three as interchangeable would manufacture a certainty that no single document possessed.

In her notes from 18 September, Claire had questioned whether the trust gave students what they had been promised. Emma remembered how readily she had interpreted that remark as personal hostility towards the directors. The newly recovered material did not vindicate Claire's suspicions, but it supplied a more disciplined way to examine them.

Before leaving, Emma wrote Fiona Bell a separate, neutral request: were the criteria for selecting recipients in 2011 retained, and did the trust hold any contemporaneous record of decisions? She did not refer to the withheld caller's instruction about authorising payments. That allegation would be tested on its own merits, not smuggled into a question about eligibility.

At the exit she checked the dates once more. The first report preceded her interview with Claire. The correction followed Claire's disappearance. Between those printed facts lay a period in which assumptions had hardened into public stories.

For Emma, the urgent question was no longer whether the figure eight concealed a scandal. It was who had been entitled to choose—and whether the surviving records could show how the choice was made.

units.title: Three Different Numbers
units.transcript:
Emma was making breakfast when Fiona Bell's email arrived. Fiona had spoken to the records team at the Glenarraidh Education Trust. They had found a box marked “Student Travel — 2011”. She had not opened all the folders, and she could not promise that the documents Emma wanted were inside.

But Fiona could confirm one detail. The travel programme had two stages. Students first applied for support. A smaller group was then selected. After that, the trust checked whether the students had started their courses before sending money.

Emma read the explanation again. The old newspaper had reported eight students selected. The correction said that figure was wrong. Neither article said how many people had applied or how many had received money.

She rang Sarah.

“We've been treating three numbers as one,” Emma said. “Applicants, selected students and students who got a payment aren't necessarily the same people.”

“So the corrected figure could refer to only one of those groups?”

“Yes. We need the original records.”

Fiona had attached a blank application form from the programme. It asked for a student's course, the cost of travel and the reason they needed help. There was also a space for an official decision. The form had no student's name on it. It did not show that anyone had actually received an award.

Emma looked at the form and remembered Claire's warning about promises made to students. A clear form did not mean the selection process had been fair. But an unclear newspaper article did not prove it had been unfair either.

Later that day Emma phoned the library. She asked whether the newspaper still kept letters from readers that had not been published. The librarian said the library did not hold the newspaper's private correspondence. Emma thanked her and made a note to contact the newspaper archive instead.

Sarah sent another message. She had found a public statement from the trust, dated October 2011, saying the travel scheme was “continuing”. It did not give any student numbers.

“Does that help?” Sarah asked.

“It tells us what the trust said in October. Nothing more.”

Emma added the statement to her notes. Then a second email from Fiona appeared.

The records team had located a list of application reference numbers. Fiona said some pages were missing, and she was checking what could legally be shared. She had not supplied the list itself.

Emma did not know what the numbers would reveal. But she now knew exactly what to ask next: how many applications had been received, how many students had been chosen, and how many payments had been made.

She wrote those three questions on separate lines.

Fiona Bell's reply arrived as Emma was preparing breakfast. The records team had located a box labelled “Student Travel — 2011”, although nobody had yet established whether it contained the minutes, selection decisions or payment records Emma had asked about. Fiona had been careful not to promise access.

There was, however, one useful explanation. The trust's travel scheme had operated in stages: applications were assessed, candidates were selected, and payments were released only after certain course details had been checked. Those stages could produce three different totals.

Emma called Sarah and returned to the two newspaper cuttings. The article from 16 September described eight students as selected. Its later correction withdrew that figure without giving a replacement. Neither item identified the number of applicants or the number who ultimately received grants.

“We've been asking whether eight payments were made,” Emma said. “But eight was the newspaper's selection figure, not necessarily a payment figure.”

“Then the correction might not concern the accounts at all.”

“Exactly. Or it might. We can't know yet.”

Fiona had attached a blank copy of the 2011 application form. It requested information about the intended course, estimated travel expenses and the applicant's circumstances. It also included a section for an administrative decision. The blank form established what information the trust had asked for; it said nothing about whether the decisions had been consistent or whether money had reached particular students.

Emma made a second enquiry at the library. Could unpublished readers' letters from 2011 still be consulted? The librarian explained that the library held printed issues, not the newspaper's private correspondence. Emma recorded that distinction. The parent's published complaint was a lead, but she had no right to assume that more letters existed or that their authors could be identified.

By early afternoon Sarah had discovered an October 2011 statement on an old version of the trust's website. It said the travel scheme was continuing, but provided no figures. Emma saved the page with its date and web address. She resisted the temptation to read “continuing” as proof that every promised grant had been delivered.

Then Fiona wrote again. The records team had found a partial list of application reference numbers. It appeared that some pages were absent, and she needed to check what could lawfully be disclosed. She did not send the list, and Emma could not infer its total size.

Sarah wondered whether missing pages suggested deliberate removal. Emma would not go that far. Boxes deteriorated, filing systems changed, and incomplete records were not unusual. Deliberate interference remained a possibility, not a finding.

She drew three columns in her notebook: Applied, Selected and Paid. The foundation, the newspaper and the anonymous caller had each pointed towards a different column. Until she could reconcile them, the mystery was one of definitions as much as numbers.

units.title: Three Different Numbers
units.transcript:
Fiona Bell's email interrupted Emma halfway through a comparison of the newspaper correction and the Glenarraidh Education Trust's annual accounts. The records team had located a carton labelled “Student Travel — 2011”. That was a promising archival lead, but Fiona was explicit about its limitations: the contents had not been fully catalogued, and she could not yet confirm the survival of the board minutes, selection schedules or authorisations.

The more revealing detail lay in her description of the programme's administration. Applicants submitted forms; a panel made selection decisions; payments followed only when enrolment and travel arrangements had been checked. Three stages, Emma realised, meant three populations that could overlap without being identical.

She called Sarah and set the September newspaper article beside its later correction. The original had announced eight students selected for travel support. The correction conceded an inaccurate figure yet supplied no replacement. Neither source measured applications received or transfers completed.

“We have treated a selection count as though it were a payment ledger,” Emma said.

“Which is exactly what the anonymous caller wanted us to examine.”

“Perhaps. But that doesn't mean the caller was right—or wrong. It means we have been careless about the category.”

Attached to Fiona's email was an unused application form from 2011. The questions concerned course details, estimated costs and financial circumstances, followed by a panel-decision section. Emma could establish what the formal process was meant to capture, but not how faithfully it had been followed. A blank template was neither proof of procedural fairness nor evidence of its violation.

At the library, she asked whether the institution held correspondence submitted to the local newspaper but never printed. It did not. Its holdings comprised published editions, and any surviving editorial correspondence would have to be pursued through the newspaper's own archive. The parent's letter, therefore, remained a contemporary expression of concern whose author's identity and access to the selection process were unknown.

Sarah later uncovered an archived October 2011 statement declaring that the travel scheme was “continuing”. Emma preserved the page's date and context. The word suggested public reassurance, not a measurable outcome. It did not resolve whether the original announcement, the corrected number and the reported expenditure described the same students.

A second message from Fiona sharpened the problem without solving it. A partial list of application reference numbers had apparently been located. Some pages seemed absent, and the trust was considering which information it could disclose without exposing students' personal details. Fiona had supplied neither the list nor a complete count.

“Missing pages,” Sarah said when Emma forwarded the update. “That sounds convenient.”

“It might be,” Emma answered, “but we don't know whether anything was removed. Partial survival isn't evidence of deliberate concealment.”

She considered the alternative possibilities. The correction could reflect confusion between applicants and successful candidates. An approved grant could have gone unpaid if a student withdrew. Expenditure could be recorded in a later accounting period. Each explanation was testable in principle; none could be selected simply because it made the story more dramatic.

Emma ruled three columns across a clean page: Applied, Selected, Paid. Beneath them she listed the records required to establish each total, marking every gap. The anonymous instructions had offered her a direction. The documents were now giving her a method.

At the bottom she wrote a final reminder: A name on a list is not a payment. A payment is not proof of fair selection.

units.title: Appeals and Reviews
units.transcript:
Emma looked at the three headings in her notebook: Applied, Selected, Paid. The trust had found part of an old list, but Fiona had not sent it. Emma wanted to know more. She did not want to put pressure on Fiona to share private information about students.

The next morning, Fiona called her.

“I can tell you something about the papers,” she said. “The records team has counted the pages we have. The list begins at reference number eleven and ends at number twenty-six. There are gaps between some numbers.”

“Does that mean twenty-six students applied?” Emma asked.

“No. Numbers can be used more than once for different years, and some forms may never have been completed. We cannot use the last number as a total.”

Fiona said she could send a description of the documents, but not the names of students. She was still checking what information could be shared.

“Do you know who made the decisions?” Emma asked.

“The blank form has a space for a panel's decision. I haven't found a complete record of the people on that panel.”

Emma thanked her. She wrote down what Fiona had actually said. She had not seen the pages herself.

Sarah called during lunch.

“We have a list from eleven to twenty-six. That's useful, isn't it?”

“It is a clue. But we don't know how many people applied, who was selected or who was paid.”

Emma went back to the newspaper archive. She searched for another report about the travel scheme. There was a short article published in early October 2011. It said that some students were waiting for information about their travel grants. It did not say which students or whether they had been selected.

This mattered to Emma. Waiting for a reply was not the same as waiting for money. The article did not explain the difference.

She saved a copy and sent Sarah the date and title. They agreed not to publish any conclusion before comparing the original documents.

That evening, Emma received a brief message from Fiona: “One folder contains a covering sheet. Its heading is 'Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011'. I have not checked the contents.”

Emma stared at the words. Someone might have asked the trust to reconsider a decision. Or the sheet might have been prepared for a process that was never used.

She put a question mark beside the heading. This was the first time she had seen a possible way to understand the parent's old complaint. But it was not yet an answer.

She closed her notebook. Tomorrow, she would ask what the trust meant by an appeal.

units.transcript:
Three headings filled the page in front of Emma: Applied, Selected, Paid. They had given her a way to organise the uncertainty, but not yet a reliable figure for any of the stages. Fiona Bell had located a partial list of application references; the trust was still considering what could be disclosed without identifying former students.

The following morning Fiona rang. The records team had completed a preliminary description of the surviving papers. The visible references began at eleven and ran as far as twenty-six, with several gaps. The figures sounded promising until Emma asked whether the final reference indicated the total number of applications.

“Not necessarily,” Fiona said. “A reference could have been reserved for a form that was never submitted. And we haven't established whether the numbering began again at any point.”

Fiona could provide an inventory description, but not the underlying list or names. She had also seen the decision section on the blank form; she had not located a complete membership record for the selection panel.

Emma kept the distinction clear in her notes: a description of records, reported by Fiona, was not the same as examining those records herself.

Sarah was enthusiastic when they spoke at lunchtime. “At least we can say there were twenty-six applicants.”

“We can't. Twenty-six is the highest reference Fiona mentioned, not a confirmed headcount.”

Emma searched the newspaper archive again and located a small report from early October 2011. It said that several students were still waiting for news about travel support. It offered no names, and it failed to distinguish between applicants waiting for a decision and successful candidates waiting for payment.

“That may explain why families were frustrated,” Sarah said.

“Perhaps. But we can't work backwards from a report of delays to a claim of misconduct.”

They saved the item and its publication date, retaining the original wording rather than rewriting it as a stronger allegation. Emma drafted a separate request about the selection process, asking whether a policy had provided for unsuccessful applicants to challenge decisions. She did not send it immediately. Fiona was already trying to identify what records existed, and Emma wanted to avoid confusing a document request with an accusation.

That evening an email arrived from Fiona. A folder in storage had a covering sheet headed “Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011”. Fiona stressed that she had not inspected its contents. The title could refer to actual challenges, standard paperwork or a procedure never used.

Emma read the note twice. The parent's letter from September had complained about a lack of transparency. Now she had a heading that might lead towards the way decisions were reconsidered.

She wrote a new question: Was an appeal possible—and did anyone make one?

This time she had a precise next step, not a suspect.

units.transcriptMarkdown:
Three headings filled the page in front of Emma: Applied, Selected, Paid. They had given her a way to organise the uncertainty, but not yet a reliable figure for any of the stages. Fiona Bell had located a partial list of application references; the trust was still considering what could be disclosed without identifying former students.

The following morning Fiona rang. The records team had completed a preliminary description of the surviving papers. The visible references began at eleven and ran as far as twenty-six, with several gaps. The figures sounded promising until Emma asked whether the final reference indicated the total number of applications.

“Not necessarily,” Fiona said. “A reference could have been reserved for a form that was never submitted. And we haven't established whether the numbering began again at any point.”

Fiona could provide an inventory description, but not the underlying list or names. She had also seen the decision section on the blank form; she had not located a complete membership record for the selection panel.

Emma kept the distinction clear in her notes: a description of records, reported by Fiona, was not the same as examining those records herself.

Sarah was enthusiastic when they spoke at lunchtime. “At least we can say there were twenty-six applicants.”

“We can't. Twenty-six is the highest reference Fiona mentioned, not a confirmed headcount.”

Emma searched the newspaper archive again and located a small report from early October 2011. It said that several students were still waiting for news about travel support. It offered no names, and it failed to distinguish between applicants waiting for a decision and successful candidates waiting for payment.

“That may explain why families were frustrated,” Sarah said.

“Perhaps. But we can't work backwards from a report of delays to a claim of misconduct.”

They saved the item and its publication date, retaining the original wording rather than rewriting it as a stronger allegation. Emma drafted a separate request about the selection process, asking whether a policy had provided for unsuccessful applicants to challenge decisions. She did not send it immediately. Fiona was already trying to identify what records existed, and Emma wanted to avoid confusing a document request with an accusation.

That evening an email arrived from Fiona. A folder in storage had a covering sheet headed “Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011”. Fiona stressed that she had not inspected its contents. The title could refer to actual challenges, standard paperwork or a procedure never used.

Emma read the note twice. The parent's letter from September had complained about a lack of transparency. Now she had a heading that might lead towards the way decisions were reconsidered.

She wrote a new question: *Was an appeal possible—and did anyone make one?*

This time she had a precise next step, not a suspect.

units.title: Appeals and Reviews
units.transcript:
Emma's notebook had become an exercise in refusing false equivalences. Applications were not selections; selections were not payments; and the existence of a file was not proof of what it contained. Three columns offered a useful method, though they provided none of the totals she wanted.

Fiona Bell telephoned the next morning with an update from the records team. The surviving pages of the student travel reference list began at eleven and extended to twenty-six, with discontinuities. Emma asked the obvious question before allowing herself to be impressed: did the highest reference correspond to the number of applicants?

“I'm afraid we can't say that,” Fiona replied. “A number might have been assigned to an abandoned application. We haven't even established whether the sequence was continuous throughout the programme.”

Fiona was willing to share a descriptive inventory once it had been checked for personal information, but she could not release the identifiable list. Nor had the team located a complete record of who sat on the selection panel. The blank form's space for a decision indicated a procedure on paper; it did not identify the people who had exercised it.

Emma recorded the conversation as Fiona's account of a preliminary inspection. The documents themselves remained unavailable to her. She was becoming acutely aware of how easily second-hand descriptions acquired the authority of primary evidence when repeated often enough.

At lunchtime Sarah greeted the news with relief. “So there were at least twenty-six applicants.”

“Not established,” Emma corrected. “Twenty-six is an identifier, not a census. The numbering might include abandoned forms, or it might not begin with one.”

A fresh search of the newspaper archive produced a brief item from early October 2011. Several local students, it reported, were awaiting news of travel assistance. Neither names nor application statuses were given. Someone awaiting an initial selection decision and someone awaiting a promised payment might both have described their position in exactly those words.

Emma filed the article with its date and original wording. It supplied evidence that delays had been publicly discussed, not an explanation of their cause. It might be relevant to the parent's complaint about opaque selection criteria. It could not substantiate the anonymous caller's suggestion that payments had been improperly authorised.

She considered sending Fiona a forceful question about who had benefited. Instead she drafted a narrower enquiry: had the scheme provided for a review or appeal, and did any surviving policy specify how challenges were handled? She left it unsent while Fiona continued her inventory. Documentary requests were more useful when their purpose was clear and their assumptions were not embedded in the questions.

Shortly after six, Fiona sent a final message. One storage folder bore a covering sheet labelled “Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011”. She had not inspected the contents and made no claim that an appeal had actually been lodged. It might be a standard folder assembled in anticipation of challenges, or it might contain records of disputed decisions.

Emma compared the heading with the parent's published letter and felt a familiar temptation to join them into a conclusion. Instead she wrote two possibilities and drew a line beneath both. A process could exist without being used. A complaint could exist without ever becoming a formal appeal.

At the bottom of the page she added a question whose answer might prove more informative than another financial total: Who was entitled to challenge a selection decision, and what happened if they did?

She had not found the missing students. She had found the next document worth asking for.

units.title: The Review Procedure
units.transcript:
Emma opened a new page in her notebook. At the top she wrote: Appeals and reviews. Fiona had found a folder with that title, but she had not read the documents inside. Emma knew that a title was not proof that anybody had complained.

Before lunch Fiona sent another email. The records team had found a separate printed sheet describing the rules for the student travel scheme in 2011. Fiona could share a copy because it did not include anyone's personal information.

The sheet said that students who were not selected could ask for a review. They had to write to the foundation within fourteen days of receiving a decision. The request would be considered by someone who had not made the first decision.

Emma read the rules carefully. There was no name beside the word reviewer. The sheet did not explain how the foundation chose that person.

She called Sarah.

“So students could appeal,” Sarah said.

“The rules say they could. We still don't know if anyone did.”

“Does the folder prove there were appeals?”

“No. Fiona hasn't opened it yet.”

Emma compared the rules with the parent's letter from September 2011. The parent had complained that families did not understand how students were chosen. But the letter did not say that the parent had sent a formal appeal. Emma drew two boxes in her notes: public complaint and formal review. She did not join them.

Then she looked at the old newspaper article again. It had announced eight students selected. A later correction said that this number was wrong, but it never gave the right number. The new rules did not solve that problem. They said how students could challenge a decision, not how many people had been chosen.

In the afternoon Fiona phoned. The records team could see several folders inside the box, but they needed more time to check them. The folder marked Appeals and reviews was still unopened.

“Could you ask whether there is a record of who reviewed decisions?” Emma asked.

“I can ask,” Fiona said. “I can't promise it exists.”

Emma thanked her. She had learnt something important about the official process, but nothing yet about whether it had worked properly.

Sarah sent a message: Do we have a story?

Emma answered: We have rules. We don't yet have evidence of how they were used.

As she put the phone down, she noticed the date printed at the bottom of the sheet: August 2011. The rules had existed before the newspaper announcement and before Claire disappeared.

That made the question more precise. If families had not understood the process, had the foundation actually told them about these rules?

units.title: The Review Procedure
units.transcript:
Fiona Bell's latest email arrived with an attachment rather than another cautious description. The records team had located a printed sheet setting out the 2011 student travel scheme's review procedure. Because the sheet contained no personal information, Fiona was able to send Emma a copy. The folder labelled Appeals and reviews, however, remained unopened.

Emma read the document with the September newspaper cuttings beside her. According to the procedure, an unsuccessful applicant could request a review in writing within fourteen days of receiving a decision. The review was supposed to be handled by someone who had not taken part in the original selection.

That was a more useful detail than the folder's title, but it raised questions of its own. No reviewer was named on the sheet, and it did not explain how an independent person was appointed. Emma noted the difference between a written rule and evidence that the rule had been followed.

“Then an appeal was possible,” Sarah said when Emma called.

“On paper. We have no appeal letters, no completed reviews and no evidence that anyone was told how to request one.”

“Could the parent who wrote to the newspaper have appealed?”

“Perhaps. But a letter to an editor isn't the same as a formal request to the trust.”

Emma examined the parent's published complaint again. It questioned the lack of clear information about selection. It did not identify an application, describe a decision notice or mention a review request. Emma added a separate heading to her notes: Communication of the rules. A procedure could exist without being clearly explained to the people entitled to use it.

She returned to the original newspaper announcement of eight selected students and the later correction. Neither item gave the true selection total. The newly discovered sheet could not repair that gap: it concerned what happened after an unsuccessful decision, not the number of decisions made. Nor did it establish whether any grant had been paid.

Fiona telephoned that afternoon. The records team had identified several folders in the storage box but needed to check their condition and contents before describing them more precisely. No one had yet opened the folder about appeals. Fiona agreed to ask whether the trust held a record of reviewers or evidence that applicants had received the procedure.

Emma thanked her without pressing for names. She did not need a former student's identity to establish whether rules had been communicated consistently.

Later, she checked the date at the bottom of the procedure: August 2011. It therefore predated both the public announcement and Claire's disappearance. That made it relevant to the historical process, although a dated document did not prove it had reached every applicant.

Sarah texted: Can we say students had a right to appeal?

Emma considered the wording before replying: The written scheme offered a review. We can't yet say who knew about it or whether it was used.

For the next stage, she wrote one question in the margin: Where was this procedure given to applicants?

units.title: The Review Procedure
units.transcript:
Fiona Bell's attachment was the first review-procedure sheet Emma had obtained rather than merely heard described. It was a printed guidance sheet for the Glenarraidh Education Trust's 2011 student travel scheme, released because it contained no identifiable applicant information. The separate folder bearing the heading Appeals and reviews had still not been opened.

Emma placed the guidance beside the September press cuttings. Unsuccessful applicants, it stated, could seek reconsideration by writing to the trust within fourteen days of receiving a decision. A reviewer who had not participated in the initial selection was to examine the request. The provisions were clear enough as aspirations. Their implementation was another matter.

The sheet named no reviewer. It specified neither the method of appointment nor what record should be kept of a review outcome. Emma resisted calling the omission evidence of a flawed process. Those details might have appeared in another document. For now, she could establish only that this sheet did not contain them.

“Does that finally tell us there were appeals?” Sarah asked over the telephone.

“It tells us a review mechanism was described. Nothing about whether it was invoked.”

Sarah suggested the parent's published complaint might have been one. Emma looked back at the letter. Its author had objected to the lack of transparency in choosing students, but had mentioned no rejection notice, formal submission or reconsidered decision. A grievance voiced publicly was not necessarily a procedural appeal. Equating the two would convert a possibility into a fact.

Emma opened a fourth column in her notes: Notification. A review right of which eligible applicants had never been informed might exist formally yet be difficult to exercise. Conversely, a dissatisfied parent might know the rules and choose to complain to a newspaper instead. The document could not decide between those scenarios.

Neither could it settle the figures that had brought her here. The article published on 16 September 2011 had reported eight students selected, and the subsequent correction had withdrawn that figure without replacement. The review procedure addressed unsuccessful decisions; it offered no headcount, payment schedule or list of successful beneficiaries. One documentary gap could not be filled by material designed for another purpose.

That afternoon Fiona called. Her colleagues had identified several folders within the student travel box, but the appeals folder remained unopened pending a careful inventory. She could not say whether it contained requests, blank templates or something unrelated. Emma asked instead about records showing who was appointed to consider reviews and whether applicants received the guidance sheet. Fiona promised only to pass on those questions.

Emma checked the document's footer. The sheet was dated August 2011, before the selection announcement, Claire's interview with Emma and the later disappearance. Its date gave the procedure a place in the chronology. It did not show distribution, compliance or awareness.

Sarah sent a short message asking whether the newsroom could describe a right to appeal. Emma revised the proposed wording: The scheme's written guidance provided for reconsideration of rejected applications; the extent to which the procedure was communicated or used has not been established.

She reread it. Restrained language sometimes sounded less dramatic than a mystery deserved. It was also the only language the evidence warranted.

Her next question was not whether a particular student had complained. It was more basic, and potentially more revealing: How, in September 2011, were applicants told that the review procedure existed?

units.title: The Decision Notice
units.transcript:
Emma was checking her notes when Fiona Bell called. The records team had found another sheet in the old student travel files. It explained how the foundation planned to tell students about the result of their applications.

“Can you send it?” Emma asked.

“I can send a blank copy,” Fiona said. “It has no names or addresses.”

The document was a model decision letter. At the top were spaces for a student's name, the course and the date. Under the result was a short paragraph explaining that an unsuccessful student could ask for a review within fourteen days.

Emma compared it with the rules she had received the day before. Both described the same period for requesting a review. But neither proved that the trust had sent the letter to anyone.

“Have you found any completed letters?” she asked.

“Not yet. The records team is still checking. The appeals folder has not been opened.”

Emma thanked her and rang Sarah.

“So the students were told about the review,” Sarah said.

units.title: The Decision Notice
units.transcript:
Fiona Bell had located a second procedural document among the surviving student travel papers. Unlike the still-unopened appeals folder, this was an unused template: a letter intended to notify applicants of the outcome of their applications. As it contained no personal details, Fiona sent Emma a scanned copy.

The letter had spaces for an applicant's name, the course and the date of the decision. Below the outcome, a paragraph told unsuccessful candidates that they could seek a review in writing within fourteen days. Its wording matched the guidance sheet Fiona had supplied the previous day.

“That sounds as though applicants were informed,” Sarah said when Emma described it.

“It sounds as though the trust designed a way to inform them,” Emma replied. “We haven't seen a single completed letter, or proof that it was delivered.”

Emma asked Fiona whether the records team had found any issued notices. Fiona said they had not yet confirmed any, and the appeals folder remained unopened. A blank template did not identify a selection panel, a reviewer or a recipient.

Emma revisited the parent's letter published in September 2011. Its author had questioned the fairness and clarity of the selection process but had not mentioned receiving—or failing to receive—a decision notice. Emma resisted treating that silence as evidence either way. A short letter to a newspaper was not a complete account of the family's correspondence with the trust.

An email from the newspaper archive arrived that afternoon. Staff said they might still hold unpublished correspondence from the period, although the collection had not been checked. Even if material survived, access would depend on privacy considerations and archival rules. Emma recorded this as a possible route for further enquiry, not evidence that other parents had complained.

When she returned to the model notice, a line at the foot of the page caught her attention: Copy to scheme administrator. The role was identified; the individual was not. If copies had been retained, they might help establish which decisions had been communicated and when. Their existence, however, was entirely unconfirmed.

Emma sent Fiona a narrow follow-up: was there a dispatch register, a file of copies or another record showing that decision notices had been issued? She avoided asking for names. A count and a description of the system would already clarify whether the procedure had been put into practice.

Sarah wanted to know whether the newsroom could now say that applicants had enjoyed a working right of appeal.

“Not yet,” Emma said. “We can say the rules and the model notice included a review process. We still can't say who was informed or whether anybody used it.”

The two documents agreed with each other. That made the intended procedure clearer, but it did not fill the space between written policy and lived experience.

units.title: The Decision Notice
units.transcript:
The latest attachment from Fiona Bell was reassuring in exactly the way Emma had learnt to distrust. It was a clean, carefully formatted model decision notice for the Glenarraidh Education Trust's 2011 student travel programme. Blank fields invited an applicant's name, course and decision date. Beneath the proposed outcome, a paragraph advised rejected candidates that they could request reconsideration in writing within fourteen days.

Its language was consistent with the procedural guidance Fiona had sent the previous day. That consistency mattered: the two documents described the same intended mechanism. Yet Emma refused to mistake a coherent paper system for a verified history of its operation.

“A standard letter is evidence that notification was planned,” she told Sarah. “It doesn't establish that notices were issued, delivered or understood.”

Fiona had released the template because it contained no identifying information. She had not found a completed copy, and the folder marked Appeals and reviews remained unopened. Nor had she identified the person responsible for independently reviewing unsuccessful decisions. None of those gaps demonstrated misconduct. They indicated the limits of what the accessible material could substantiate.

Emma reread the contemporary parent's complaint in the local newspaper. Its author had criticised the opacity of the student selection process but had made no claim about the receipt of a formal decision notice. The omission could mean several things, including a simple choice to focus the published letter on another grievance. Inferring that the parent was never notified would be speculation.

A reply from the newspaper's archive complicated matters further. Staff believed that some unpublished correspondence from 2011 might survive, but they had not inventoried the relevant boxes. Access to any personal letters would require a separate assessment. Emma had neither a new witness nor a corroborated account; merely another possible archive to approach responsibly.

Back at the template, a seemingly routine instruction attracted her attention: Copy to scheme administrator. It suggested that the trust had contemplated keeping an internal duplicate. It did not specify who held that office or whether copies had been retained in practice.

Emma drafted a request that deliberately excluded personal details. Was there a register showing how many decision notices were issued, when they were sent and whether copies were routinely filed? She asked for the existence and format of records before requesting access to any of their contents.

Sarah suggested describing the scheme as one in which applicants had been guaranteed a route of appeal. Emma revised the sentence. The documentation provided for a review route; it did not show that the route was communicated to every eligible person, much less that any review had taken place.

The old newspaper's disputed figure of eight selected students remained unresolved. So did the separate questions of applicants, selections and payments. A dispatch register, if one existed, might help establish a decision count, but Emma would still need to distinguish a letter prepared from one actually sent, and a letter sent from one received.

She added those distinctions to her notebook. The deeper the investigation went, the less useful it became to ask what the trust had meant to do. The more precise question was what contemporary records could demonstrate that it had done.

units.title: The Dispatch Register
units.transcript:
Emma received a message from Fiona Bell the next morning. The records team had found a small book labelled “Outgoing letters — Student Travel 2011”. Fiona said it looked like a register used by the scheme administrator.

“Does it tell us which students received a letter?” Emma asked.

“Not exactly. Some lines contain dates and reference numbers. Others are blank. We have not compared the book with the original letters.”

“Can you tell me how many entries there are?”

“Not yet. The team needs to check the pages carefully. And we cannot share students’ personal details.”

Emma thanked her. She wrote register found in her notebook, but refused to write letters delivered. A list of letters prepared for sending was not proof that they reached anyone.

She called Sarah. Sarah wanted to know whether the book solved the mystery of the parent’s complaint.

“No,” Emma said. “We still do not know whether that parent received a decision. We don't even know whether the parent had applied.”

Fiona sent a photograph of the register’s cover and a blank page that showed its headings. There were four columns: reference number, date prepared, date sent and notes. The photograph did not show any student entries.

Emma noticed something useful. The two date columns were different. It seemed possible for a letter to be prepared on one day and sent on another. It was also possible for the second date to remain empty.

Later, the newspaper archive replied to Emma’s earlier enquiry. Staff had not yet checked the private letters from 2011. They reminded her that access might be restricted. Emma decided not to rely on material she had not seen.

In the afternoon Fiona called again. The team had begun making an inventory of the register. They could confirm that some rows contained dates in the sent column, but they could not say whether the letters had arrived. No postal receipts had been identified.

Sarah sighed when Emma told her. “So we finally have proof the letters were delivered?”

“Not delivered. At most, the register says that some were marked as sent.”

Emma thought about Claire. The teacher had worried about promises made to students. Now Emma was investigating the difference between written procedures and what happened in practice. The distinction mattered even if the records eventually showed no misconduct.

Before closing her notebook, Emma drew three short lines:

Prepared. Sent. Received.

She had evidence that the trust used those first two labels. For the third, she had nothing yet.

At the bottom of the page she added a new question: Who was responsible for checking whether a student received a decision?

units.title: The Dispatch Register
units.transcript:
Fiona Bell's latest update seemed at first to answer the question Emma had asked. The records team had located a ledger headed “Outgoing letters — Student Travel 2011”, apparently maintained by the scheme administrator.

Emma was careful about the word outgoing. A dispatch record might tell her that a notice had been processed for sending; it would not necessarily establish that it had reached the intended applicant.

Fiona described entries containing reference numbers and dates. Other spaces were blank. The team had not compared the ledger with completed notices, and Fiona would not disclose information identifying students. She could not yet offer even a reliable total of entries.

“Could you share its layout rather than its contents?” Emma asked.

Fiona agreed. Later she emailed images of the cover and an unused page. The page carried four headings: reference number, date prepared, date sent and notes. Two separate date columns immediately caught Emma's attention. A prepared notice and a dispatched notice were not automatically the same thing.

Sarah listened while Emma explained.

“Then we can finally prove those students were notified.”

“We can establish that the trust kept a system for recording notices. Fiona says some entries have dates marked as sent. We still have no delivery confirmation.”

“Doesn't a sent date count for something?”

“Of course. But the claim has to match the evidence.”

The newspaper archive also replied. Staff had not yet examined its unpublished correspondence from 2011 and warned that any access might be limited by privacy rules. Emma added the message to her research log without treating the possibility of surviving letters as confirmation of further complaints.

That afternoon Fiona clarified the team's preliminary observations. Several lines in the ledger appeared to contain dispatch dates. No matching postal receipts had been located, and the inventory was not complete. Fiona had not established whether the entries represented every decision, or whether the dates were accurate.

Emma returned to the parent's published complaint. It asked why selection decisions had been unclear, but offered no account of a notice arriving or failing to arrive. She could not connect the anonymous author to a particular ledger entry without more evidence.

She divided a page into three stages: Prepared, Sent, Received. The first two now had documentary headings and some reported entries behind them. The third remained an unverified outcome. Even a correctly completed dispatch register might fail to demonstrate delivery.

Sarah asked what Emma would request next.

“Not names,” Emma said. “The administrator's instructions. Was anyone meant to follow up on letters that weren't received?”

The question was narrower than an allegation that students had been deliberately kept uninformed. It was also something a surviving policy might be able to answer.

For the first time, Emma could see a route from the scheme's written promises towards a test of its actual administration—provided she continued to respect the boundaries of what each document could prove.

Fiona's message appeared to offer the bridge Emma had been looking for between the trust's decision-notice template and its actual correspondence. The records team had located a ledger labelled “Outgoing letters — Student Travel 2011”, apparently used by the scheme administrator. Its existence was significant; its evidential reach remained narrow.

Fiona described a mixture of reference numbers, dates and empty fields. There had been no reconciliation with completed notices or any postal documentation, and the inventory was still preliminary. Identifiable student details could not be released. Emma requested images of the ledger's structure rather than its entries, explaining that she wanted to understand what the document was designed to record.

The cover and one blank page arrived later that morning. Four headings appeared above the ruled columns: Reference number, Date prepared, Date sent and Notes. The distinction between preparation and dispatch was explicit. There was no corresponding field for acknowledgement of receipt.

She asked Fiona whether the procedural files contained instructions for checking that notices reached applicants, and how undelivered letters were handled.

units.title: The Missing Decision
units.transcript:
Emma read the final question in her notebook: Who checked that students received their decision letters? The trust's register had spaces for dates prepared and sent, but no place to record delivery.

The next morning, Fiona Bell emailed her a short page from an old office manual. It described what staff should do when a letter came back because the address was wrong. They should check the address, try to contact the student and make a note in the office records.

“Does this mean the trust followed up every letter?” Emma asked when Fiona called.

“No. It shows the instructions. I haven't found completed notes about returned letters.”

“Could the same instructions apply to letters that never came back, but never arrived?”

“I don't know. The page only mentions returned post.”

Emma called Sarah. They agreed that a missing receipt was not proof of a lost letter. The instructions were useful, but they did not show what had happened to any student.

“Can we look for a record of returned letters?” Sarah asked.

“That's the next question,” Emma said.

Emma sent Fiona a written request for a description of any records about returned post. She did not ask for students' names or addresses. While she waited, she checked the newspaper archive again.

The archive had not given her access to private letters. Instead, a member of staff offered to check whether an old index listed correspondence about the travel scheme. They warned that an index could describe a letter without showing what it said.

In the afternoon the archive sent one result. An entry from October 2011 described a letter under the subject “Student Travel — decision not received”. It did not include the writer's name or the letter itself.

Emma read the subject twice.

“That sounds like someone didn't get a decision,” Sarah said.

“It sounds like someone wrote about a missing decision. We haven't read the letter. We don't know what happened.”

“Could it be the parent who complained in September?”

“Possibly. But we have no evidence they're the same person.”

Emma added the entry to her notes, with the date and the archive's description. It was a lead, not a confirmed account.

At the end of the day, Fiona replied. The office manual did not mention sending reminders to students who had not replied. She was still checking for records of returned post.

Emma drew a line between two questions in her notebook. The first was whether the trust had tried to send decisions. The second was whether students could actually use their right to ask for a review.

A date in a register could not answer both.

She closed the laptop. Tomorrow, she would ask what the archive could verify about that October letter.
