units.title: The Missing Decision
units.transcript:
The dispatch register had given Emma a set of dates, but not the confirmation of receipt she needed. If a student had fourteen days from receiving a decision to request a review, a record of posting was only part of the story.

Fiona Bell sent her another document: a page from the trust's 2011 office manual headed “Returned correspondence”. It instructed staff to check an address when a letter came back undelivered, attempt further contact and record what action had been taken.

Emma phoned Fiona.

“Have you found any completed records of those follow-ups?”

“Not yet. And the manual doesn't tell us whether these instructions were always followed.”

“Would it cover letters that were lost without being returned?”

“Nothing on this page explains that.”

Emma wrote the limitations beside the document. A sensible procedure could exist without being used consistently. Equally, a missing record did not establish that staff had ignored a problem.

Sarah suggested asking for a count of returned decision notices, rather than individual names. Emma sent Fiona a narrow request along those lines, making clear that anonymised totals or a description of surviving records would be sufficient.

Meanwhile, a member of the newspaper archive contacted Emma. The private correspondence collection remained closed pending checks, but staff could search an old subject index. The index did not reproduce the letters, and its descriptions could be incomplete.

That afternoon the archivist identified a single entry from October 2011 labelled “Student Travel — decision not received”. No author was named in the material shared with Emma. Nor was the text of the letter available.

Sarah was excited. “We finally have a student saying a decision never arrived.”

“Perhaps,” Emma said, “but we have an index entry. We don't know whether the writer was a student, a parent or someone else. We don't even know exactly what the complaint said.”

“Could it be the September parent?”

“There's no basis for joining them yet.”

Emma recorded the exact wording and the archive reference. She also noted that an October letter could have concerned any stage of the scheme. Its title alone did not establish a missed deadline or an improperly denied appeal.

By evening Fiona had replied again. The manual did not describe reminders to applicants who failed to respond, and the records team had not yet confirmed any returns log. It was a gap worth examining, not grounds for an accusation.

Emma returned to the three headings she had used the previous day: Prepared, Sent, Received. Beneath them she added a fourth: Able to appeal.

The first two might be reconstructed from the ledger. The third required other evidence. And the fourth depended on more than delivery alone: a student had to understand the decision and the review procedure in time to act.

For the first time, the correspondence trail raised a question about access, not merely administration. Emma still needed the original October letter before she could judge what had gone wrong, if anything.

units.title: The Missing Decision
units.transcript:
Emma had been tempted to treat the dispatch ledger as the point where the foundation's procedures met reality. On reflection it marked only an intermediate step. An entry recording dispatch could be accurate while the intended recipient remained unaware of the decision, and the fourteen-day review period made that distinction potentially consequential.

Fiona Bell's next email contained a page from a 2011 office manual headed “Returned correspondence”. It directed staff, when post came back undelivered, to verify the address, attempt renewed contact and document the action taken. The instructions were unremarkable; the uncertainty lay in whether and when they had been applied.

Emma asked Fiona whether any completed returns log or follow-up notes had survived. Fiona could confirm neither. She also cautioned that the manual dealt specifically with mail returned to the office. It did not address the more elusive possibility of a letter going astray without being returned.

“The procedure might have worked perfectly,” Sarah observed when Emma explained.

“It might. But its existence cannot substitute for a record of what actually happened.”

Nor could the absence of such a record demonstrate neglect. Emma requested an inventory-level account of any surviving returns documentation, avoiding names or addresses. A count, if responsibly derived, would be more useful than an intrusive search for a particular applicant.

An unexpected lead came from the newspaper archive. Staff were not prepared to release unpublished correspondence from 2011, but an archivist offered to search a subject index whose entries summarised the material held. The index was not a transcript. Its headings might have been supplied by an editor rather than by the original writers.

In the afternoon a single description emerged: an October 2011 item indexed as “Student Travel — decision not received”. No author was disclosed, and the underlying letter remained unavailable.

Sarah interpreted it immediately as testimony from a student whose appeal rights had been frustrated. Emma disagreed with the certainty, not the possibility. The heading did not identify a student, establish what decision was awaited or reveal whether any review deadline had expired. It could even describe a question about communication rather than an allegation of failed delivery.

The temptation to connect it to the parent's September complaint was equally strong. Yet two documents concerning dissatisfaction with the same scheme were not automatically from the same household. Emma kept their provenance separate.

She entered the October reference in her research log exactly as supplied, including the archivist's warning about the index. Then she checked Fiona's latest reply. No returns log had yet been confirmed, and the manual offered no general reminder system for applicants who did not acknowledge receipt. Both details were potentially relevant, neither decisive.

Emma had previously written three stages across her notebook: Prepared, Dispatched, Received. Now she added Able to seek review. That final condition was not merely administrative. Even confirmed delivery could not by itself show that a recipient understood the decision, the fourteen-day limit or the procedure for challenging it.

The anonymous caller's instructions about payments suddenly seemed remote. The financial questions still mattered, but the documents were directing Emma towards a different uncertainty: whether a formal opportunity to challenge a decision had been meaningful in practice.

She closed the file without drafting a headline. Her next request would be to the archive, asking what could be verified about the October entry without exposing the writer. Only then might she begin to distinguish a communication failure from a misleading label.

units.title: The Index Entry
units.transcript:
Emma received an email from the newspaper archivist. The staff had checked the entry called “Student Travel — decision not received”. They could confirm that it came from the October 2011 correspondence index. They could not give Emma the letter or the writer’s name.

“The words in the index were written by newspaper staff,” the archivist explained. “We don't know whether they are the writer's exact words.”

Emma thanked her. It was important. She had almost treated the title as a sentence from a student. Now she knew it was a description made by someone else.

She called Sarah.

“So we still don't know what happened?” Sarah asked.

“We know a letter was listed under that subject. We don't know who wrote it, what it said, or whether a decision really failed to arrive.”

The archivist offered one more piece of information. The entry was dated 12 October 2011. This was after Claire disappeared, but the date alone did not connect the letter to her case.

Later Fiona Bell sent Emma another message. The trust's records team had not found a confirmed record of returned decision letters. They had, however, found a blank form headed “Contact attempt”. It had spaces for a reference number, a date and a note about the action taken.

“Does that mean the trust called students who did not receive letters?” Emma asked.

“No,” Fiona said. “It tells us what staff could record. We haven't found a completed form.”

Emma placed the blank form beside the office manual. Both explained how staff were supposed to deal with problems. Neither showed that they had used the procedure in a particular case.

Sarah suggested that Emma ask the archive to identify the October writer. Emma disagreed. She wanted to understand the evidence without exposing anyone's private details.

Instead she asked whether the archive could confirm how many entries about the travel scheme appeared in the index, without sharing names or letter contents. The archivist said staff would check, but did not promise a complete count.

That evening Emma looked again at her four headings: Prepared, Sent, Received, Able to appeal. The new date helped her place a document in time, but it did not fill any of the missing columns.

She wrote her next question below them: If a notice was not received, how would anyone know that the fourteen-day review period had begun?

She closed the notebook. It was a fair question. It was not yet an accusation.

“The words in the index were written by newspaper staff,” the archivist explained. “We don't know whether they are the writer's exact words.”

Emma thanked her. It was important. She had almost treated the title as a sentence from a student. Now she knew it was a description made by someone else.

She called Sarah.

“So we still don't know what happened?” Sarah asked.

“We know a letter was listed under that subject. We don't know who wrote it, what it said, or whether a decision really failed to arrive.”

The archivist offered one more piece of information. The entry was dated 12 October 2011. This was after Claire disappeared, but the date alone did not connect the letter to her case.

Later Fiona Bell sent Emma another message. The trust's records team had not found a confirmed record of returned decision letters. They had, however, found a blank form headed “Contact attempt”. It had spaces for a reference number, a date and a note about the action taken.

“Does that mean the trust called students who did not receive letters?” Emma asked.

“No,” Fiona said. “It tells us what staff could record. We haven't found a completed form.”

Emma placed the blank form beside the office manual. Both explained how staff were supposed to deal with problems. Neither showed that they had used the procedure in a particular case.

Sarah suggested that Emma ask the archive to identify the October writer. Emma disagreed. She wanted to understand the evidence without exposing anyone's private details.

Instead she asked whether the archive could confirm how many entries about the travel scheme appeared in the index, without sharing names or letter contents. The archivist said staff would check, but did not promise a complete count.

That evening Emma looked again at her four headings: Prepared, Sent, Received, Able to appeal. The new date helped her place a document in time, but it did not fill any of the missing columns.

She wrote her next question below them: If a notice was not received, how would anyone know that the fourteen-day review period had begun?

She closed the notebook. It was a fair question. It was not yet an accusation.

units.title: The Index Entry
units.transcript:
The newspaper archivist's reply was useful chiefly because it narrowed what Emma could legitimately claim. Staff had checked the October 2011 subject-index entry headed “Student Travel — decision not received”, but access to the original correspondence remained restricted. The archivist could confirm its index date—12 October—and explained that newspaper employees had written the heading. It was not necessarily a quotation from the person who submitted the letter.

Emma realised how easily she had nearly mistaken an archive label for a witness statement. She forwarded the clarification to Sarah, who called immediately.

“Doesn't the heading still suggest somebody was waiting for a decision?”

“It suggests the archive classified a letter that way. We haven't seen its wording, and we don't know whether the writer was an applicant, a parent or someone else.”

The date placed the indexed item after Claire's disappearance, but Emma had no basis for linking the two events. Chronological proximity did not establish a connection.

Fiona Bell supplied a separate update from the trust. The records team had not identified a verified register of returned decision notices. They had located an unused “Contact attempt” form with fields for a reference number, a date and the action taken. Fiona stressed that no completed example had yet been found.

The form fitted the office manual's instructions for dealing with returned post. Even together, however, the two documents described a possible administrative process rather than proving that staff followed it. Emma recorded the distinction beside her notes on the dispatch ledger.

Sarah suggested trying to identify the October letter's author. Emma was reluctant to turn an archival question into a search for a private individual's identity. She asked the archivist a narrower question instead: could staff establish how many entries concerning the student travel scheme appeared in the surviving index, without releasing correspondence or names? The archivist agreed to investigate but warned that any count might be incomplete.

Emma returned to the procedure governing reviews. Students were supposed to request reconsideration within fourteen days of receiving their decision. A dispatch date did not establish receipt, and the blank contact form could not show what happened when delivery was uncertain.

“Then the deadline might have been impossible to use,” Sarah said.

“Might have been,” Emma replied. “We still lack a real case and any evidence about how the trust applied the rule.”

She drew a careful distinction in her notebook between a weakness that could exist in a system and a failure shown to have occurred. The former justified questions. Only evidence of the latter could support a factual allegation.

By evening, two institutions had promised to check their records. Neither had confirmed a missed notification or an unfair refusal of appeal. Emma ended the day not with a revelation, but with a sharper test: what would have counted as proof that an applicant had received the decision from which the fourteen days ran?

units.title: The Index Entry
units.transcript:
The archivist's response did not open the private correspondence file. Instead, it exposed a weakness in the story Emma had almost begun to tell herself. The entry catalogued as “Student Travel — decision not received” was dated 12 October 2011, but its heading had been supplied by newspaper staff. It might summarise the letter accurately; it could not safely be treated as the writer's own testimony.

Emma entered the date and provenance separately. The item postdated Claire's disappearance, although that sequence furnished no causal link. A temporal coincidence could make a lead worth examining without making it evidence of a connection.

Sarah called as soon as Emma forwarded the archivist's explanation.

“Somebody must have complained about not receiving a decision.”

“Possibly. What we actually possess is a description in an index. We don't know whether the writer was an applicant, whether the decision was delayed or whether the phrase even reflects the complaint's exact wording.”

At the trust, Fiona Bell's records team had made another modest discovery. No verified log of returned decision notices had been identified, but a blank form headed “Contact attempt” survived. Its fields provided for an application reference, a date and the action taken. Fiona had found no completed example and cautioned against assuming that every return, or indeed any particular return, had been followed up.

Placed beside the office manual, the form supplied a plausible mechanism for documenting renewed contact after undelivered post. It did not demonstrate the mechanism's operation. Emma was struck by how many pieces of paperwork described desirable administrative behaviour while leaving the underlying events inaccessible.

Sarah proposed locating the author of the October letter. Emma preferred a less intrusive question. She asked whether the archivist could count the surviving subject-index entries connected with the student travel scheme while keeping names and original correspondence confidential. Even a count would require qualification: a partial index could neither exclude additional letters nor establish that its entries represented different people.

The archivist undertook to check what could be established. Fiona likewise offered to continue searching for records explaining how uncertain delivery had been handled. Neither promised a conclusive result.

Emma reopened the review guidance. It made receipt of a decision the starting point for a fourteen-day period in which an unsuccessful applicant could seek reconsideration. A record of dispatch fell short of that event; an unused contact form fell shorter still. If the trust had applied the deadline from the posting date, fairness questions might arise. But Emma had no evidence that it had done so, nor that any applicant had been prevented from appealing.

She wrote two headings on a clean page: Potential procedural vulnerability and Documented individual failure. The first column contained a question about proof of receipt. The second remained empty. That absence was not a verdict in the trust's favour or against it; it was a boundary around what she could responsibly publish.

Her next request would therefore concern the rule itself, not an imagined victim: what evidence, if any, had the trust required before treating a decision as received and starting the review clock?

At last she had a question that could be answered without first deciding who was guilty.

units.title: The Three Entries
units.transcript:
Emma was working at home when the newspaper archivist called. Staff had checked the old index again. They had found three entries about the student travel scheme in October 2011, including the one dated 12 October. The archivist warned that the index might be incomplete.

“Can you tell me what the other letters say?” Emma asked.

“Not yet. We can share the dates and general subjects, but not the private letters.”

One entry concerned questions about selection. Another was marked as a request for information. The third had the heading about a decision not received. The headings had been written by newspaper staff, not necessarily by the writers.

Emma copied the details into her notebook. Three entries did not mean three different families. One person could have written more than once, and some letters might never have been listed.

Sarah called while Emma was checking the dates.

“Three complaints,” Sarah said.

“Three index entries,” Emma corrected her. “We don't know whether all of them were complaints.”

Later Fiona Bell sent a short reply about the foundation's contact records. The records team had still not found any completed contact-attempt forms. They had found a page from an office guide explaining that staff should record letters returned by the post. Fiona could not confirm that every returned letter had been recorded.

“So we still don't know if any student missed a decision?” Emma asked.

“That's right. And I can't tell you whether the appeals folder contains any real appeals. It has not been checked.”

Emma thanked Fiona. She was disappointed, but she understood the limits of the evidence.

That afternoon she opened her notes from the interview with Claire in September 2011. Claire had worried about what the foundation promised and what students actually received. Emma remembered her own quick conclusion at the time. She had thought Claire simply disliked the foundation's directors.

Now she saw how much she had missed by not asking a better question.

Emma wrote four words across the page: Prepared. Sent. Received. Understood. A form could show the first stage. A register might show the second. But the last two needed information that the trust and the newspaper had not yet supplied.

Sarah sent a message: Can we publish something?

Emma replied: We can report what the documents say, but not a story about students losing their right to appeal. We don't have that evidence.

At the bottom of the archivist's email was one more detail: the three entries had been filed in different sections of the old index. Emma had assumed they were connected because they were about the same scheme. She decided to ask how those sections had been organised.

The answer might explain the entries—or show that she had put unrelated letters together.

units.title: The Three Entries
units.transcript:
The newspaper archivist's next message brought a modest development. A fresh check of the surviving October 2011 subject index had identified three entries concerning the trust's student travel programme, including the item dated 12 October and labelled “decision not received”. Staff could provide dates and general headings, but access to the original correspondence remained restricted.

Emma copied the descriptions exactly. The other two entries concerned selection questions and a request for information. All three titles had been assigned by newspaper staff. They could not be treated as quotations from the authors, or even as proof that the writers had complained.

Sarah rang almost immediately.

“Three letters from unhappy families.”

“Possibly,” Emma said. “But three entries aren't necessarily three letters from three families. One writer might appear twice, and the index may not be complete.”

Sarah accepted the correction. Emma added a note beside each entry: Author unknown; content unavailable; classification editorial.

Fiona Bell's reply arrived in the afternoon. The trust's records team had not located a completed contact-attempt form. A further page from the office guidance instructed staff to record post returned as undeliverable. Yet Fiona could not verify that the rule had been followed in every case. She also confirmed that the appeals folder had not been inspected.

Emma considered what the paperwork allowed her to say. The trust had designed a process for recording outgoing notices and handling returned letters. The index suggested that correspondence about the travel scheme had reached the newspaper. Neither fact established that an unsuccessful applicant had been denied an effective opportunity to request a review.

She returned to her notes from the 18 September 2011 interview with Claire. Claire's concern had been about promises to students and what actually happened to them. Emma now wondered whether her younger self had reduced that concern to a personal dispute because it made a simpler article. Her past mistake did not make the present allegations true. It merely gave her a reason to be more exacting.

She drew four columns: Prepared, Sent, Received and Understood. A model letter addressed the first; a ledger entry could support the second. Evidence of the last two was still missing. Even proof that a decision arrived would not necessarily show that the applicant knew how to challenge it within fourteen days.

When Sarah asked whether they had enough to publish, Emma distinguished a report on the documented procedures from an accusation about individual harm. The former might be possible with proper context. The latter was not supported.

Then she noticed something in the archive's reply: the three subject entries came from different sections of the index. She had mentally grouped them because they concerned the same programme, but the filing scheme itself might explain why their headings differed.

She wrote to the archivist asking how the sections had been organised. Before drawing connections among three uncertain entries, she wanted to know whether the archive had intended them to be connected at all.

units.title: The Three Entries
units.transcript:
The archivist's second response provided an instructive test of Emma's discipline. Three October 2011 subject-index entries appeared to concern the Glenarraidh Education Trust's travel scheme, one of them the item dated 12 October and labelled “decision not received”. The archive could release their dates and general classifications, not the original correspondence or identifying details. It also cautioned that the surviving index might be incomplete.

The other two headings referred broadly to selection questions and an information request. Emma transcribed them without attempting to reconstruct the letters underneath. The classifications had been supplied by newspaper staff: they were editorial descriptions, not authenticated statements from the people who had written in.

“Three complainants,” Sarah announced over the telephone.

“Three entries,” Emma corrected. “Not necessarily three authors, still less three established grievances. We can't even assume the index captured every letter.”

She annotated each record with the limits of its provenance. A shared subject did not prove common authorship, nor did a repeated label establish that any recipient had failed to receive a decision notice. She was wary of manufacturing a pattern merely by placing fragments side by side.

Fiona Bell's reply arrived later that day. The trust had still found no completed contact-attempt forms. Another page of the office guidance directed staff to document correspondence returned as undeliverable, but Fiona could not confirm consistent compliance. The appeals folder remained unopened. Emma recorded the procedural expectation separately from any claim about what had happened in practice.

The documentary trail was becoming more detailed without becoming conclusive. A model letter demonstrated intended notification; a dispatch ledger could contain entries marked as sent; a returned-post policy explained a response to one kind of failed delivery. None by itself established receipt or comprehension. And the ability to seek reconsideration within fourteen days of receiving a decision was not identical to merely being sent the relevant information.

Emma reopened the notes she had made during her 18 September 2011 interview with Claire. The teacher had questioned the difference between what the trust promised and what students received. Emma had once treated her unease as resentment towards its management, a reading that had suited a hurried newspaper story. Recognising that error now offered no retrospective proof of wrongdoing. It did, however, make the temptation to compress uncertainty into a dramatic account particularly uncomfortable.

She revised the labels in her notebook: Prepared, Dispatched, Received, Understood. These were successive propositions requiring different evidence. The archive's three entries might eventually illuminate one of them, but their wording did not yet do so.

Sarah asked whether Emma intended to publish. She could envisage a carefully qualified account of the procedures documented by the trust and the limits of their surviving records. She could not responsibly allege that particular students had been deprived of a review, or that the foundation had deliberately withheld decisions.

Before answering, she noticed a subtlety in the archivist's email. The three entries were drawn from different sections of the index, whose categories had not been explained. Emma had treated their common subject as grounds for comparison; the archive's internal arrangement might instead reflect different types of correspondence or different cataloguing practices.

She sent a final, narrowly framed question: how had those sections been organised in 2011, and were their headings intended to identify the writers' concerns or merely facilitate filing?

Emma closed her notebook with an uncomfortable but necessary recognition: assembling more clues did not remove the obligation to understand what each clue actually was.

Three October 2011 subject-index entries appeared to concern the Glenarraidh Education Trust's travel scheme, one of them the item dated 12 October and labelled “decision not received”. units.transcript:
Emma received a reply from the newspaper archive on Monday morning. The archivist had checked the old filing guide. In 2011, the newspaper used separate sections for letters from readers, questions for the editor, and documents sent only for information. The three entries about student travel came from different sections.

“Does that mean they were written by different people?” Emma asked.

“No,” the archivist said. “A person could write more than once. The sections tell us why the newspaper filed something, not who wrote it.”

Emma made three notes. One entry was in the readers' letters section. Another was among questions sent to the editor. The entry dated 12 October was in the information section. The title about a decision not received had been created by newspaper staff.

She called Sarah.

“We shouldn't call them three complaints,” Emma said. “Now we know the index was organised by type of correspondence.”

“Can we read any of the letters?”

“Not yet. The archive is still checking its rules about private information.”

Emma looked at the date of the October entry again. Claire had disappeared weeks earlier. But the index gave no reason to connect the letter to Claire. Emma refused to turn a date into a story.

At lunchtime, Fiona Bell emailed her from the foundation. The team had found a list of records stored in boxes. It included the appeals folder, the outgoing letters book and some general office instructions. It did not say what was inside the appeals folder. Fiona had not opened it.

“Can you confirm whether students were told about the review rules?” Emma wrote back.

“Not from this list,” Fiona replied. “It only tells us that some records were stored.”

Emma spent the afternoon comparing the two organisations' information. The newspaper index explained how letters had been classified. The foundation's list explained how papers had been stored. Neither showed what had happened to an individual student.

Sarah called again. “We've found lots of documents, but very few answers.”

“Then we need better questions,” Emma said.

She wrote one for the archive: could staff describe the October document without revealing the writer's identity? She wrote another for Fiona: was there any general instruction about when students should receive decision letters?

Before sending them, Emma read Claire's old interview notes. Claire had said that people sometimes asked the wrong questions. Emma had once thought she meant something dramatic. Now the words seemed much simpler.

If she wanted to understand what had happened, she had to know the difference between a label, a document and a fact.

She sent the two questions and closed her notebook.

The archivist's response arrived with a copy of the newspaper's 2011 filing guide. It was not the missing correspondence Emma had hoped to inspect, but it corrected an assumption she had almost allowed into her reporting.

The newspaper had kept readers' letters, editorial enquiries and material supplied for information in separate index sections. The three October entries about the Glenarraidh Education Trust's student travel programme came from different categories. The headings were created by staff to help them retrieve documents; they were not reliable quotations from their authors.

“So they're three different people?” Sarah asked when Emma rang.

“There's no reason to assume that. The categories describe how the newspaper handled the material, not who sent it. One person might have contacted the paper several times.”

The entry dated 12 October 2011, bearing the phrase “decision not received”, appeared in the information section. That placement was interesting but inconclusive. It did not establish that the author had been an applicant, that a notice had failed to arrive or that a review deadline had been missed. Even the description might reflect an editor's interpretation rather than the original wording.

Emma recorded the section names and the archivist's explanation alongside the dates. Access to the letters themselves remained restricted while the archive considered privacy requirements.

Later Fiona Bell sent an inventory of boxes held by the foundation. It listed the outgoing correspondence ledger, some office guidance and the folder headed “Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011”. The document was an inventory, not an examination of the contents. Fiona repeated that the appeals folder had not been opened and no complete set of completed decision notices had been verified.

Emma asked whether the inventory showed that students had been told about the fourteen-day review procedure.

“No,” Fiona replied. “It tells us what was filed, not what was communicated.”

The answer brought Emma back to a distinction that had become central to her investigation. The newspaper recorded what its staff had received and classified. The trust recorded—or had intended to record—what its staff prepared and sent. Neither institution's surviving summary could establish what any particular student had understood.

Sarah sounded frustrated. “We keep getting descriptions of documents instead of the documents.”

“Descriptions are useful when we know their limits,” Emma said. “They're dangerous when we forget them.”

She drafted two precise requests. To the archivist she asked for a non-identifying description of the October item, if the rules allowed it. To Fiona she asked whether any general guidance explained when decision notices should reach applicants. She sought procedures, not private names.

Before pressing send, Emma glanced at her notes from the 18 September 2011 interview. Claire had warned her about asking the wrong questions. Emma could not know exactly what Claire had intended by those words. But she finally understood what a wrong question could do: it could force uncertain evidence to produce an answer it had never contained.

She sent both requests, leaving the identity of the writer—and the contents of the appeals folder—unresolved.

units.title: The Filing Guide
units.transcript:
The archivist's reply provided a small lesson in how documentary patterns could be manufactured by careless reading. Attached was the newspaper's 2011 indexing guide, which divided incoming material into readers' letters, editorial enquiries and documents supplied for information. The three October entries concerning the Glenarraidh Education Trust's travel scheme had not been drawn from a single correspondence series. They had been retrieved from separate categories whose purpose was administrative classification.

Emma had been tempted to read their shared subject as evidence of a common complaint. The guide undermined that shortcut. An index heading reflected a newspaper employee's description, not necessarily an author's chosen words. Nor did three entries establish three correspondents: one writer might submit several items, while other material might never appear in the surviving index.

Sarah asked whether the different categories at least proved the documents were unrelated.

“No,” Emma said. “They prove how the newspaper filed them. Relationship and authorship are separate questions.”

The 12 October 2011 entry, labelled “decision not received”, belonged to the material-for-information section. Its position neither confirmed nor contradicted a claim of failed notification. Without the underlying letter, Emma could not establish whether the phrase described an applicant's experience, a parent's enquiry or an editor's shorthand for a different issue entirely. Its proximity to Claire's disappearance in the calendar conferred no causal connection.

The archivist continued to withhold the private correspondence pending an access review. Emma noted the restriction without implying concealment. A repository could preserve an item responsibly while declining to expose its writer.

Fiona Bell, meanwhile, supplied a preliminary inventory of the trust's storage boxes. It named the outgoing correspondence ledger, general office guidance and the folder entitled “Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011”. The inventory described holdings, not their contents. Fiona again confirmed that the appeals folder had not been opened and that complete issued notices had not been located.

“Does the list tell us whether applicants were made aware of the fourteen-day review period?” Emma asked.

“It can't,” Fiona replied. “A file's presence doesn't prove a letter reached anyone.”

Emma placed the newspaper and foundation records side by side. Both were secondary layers of description created for legitimate institutional purposes. Yet a filing label was not a witness statement; a box inventory was not a case file; and a dispatch ledger was not an acknowledgement of receipt. Each distinction narrowed what could responsibly be inferred.

“We have become collectors of labels,” Sarah complained.

“Only if we treat the labels as answers,” Emma said. “Properly understood, they tell us which questions can be tested.”

She prepared two requests that respected those limits. Could the newspaper provide a non-identifying account of the 12 October item within its access policy? Could the trust locate a general instruction specifying when, and by what means, decision notices were expected to reach applicants? Neither request depended on identifying a vulnerable former student.

Before sending them, Emma revisited the transcript of her 18 September 2011 conversation with Claire. The teacher's warning about the wrong questions had once struck a young journalist as evasive. Emma still could not claim to know precisely what Claire meant. Her own experience, however, had supplied an interpretation: a question built on an untested premise could turn archival silence into a false certainty.

She pressed send. Somewhere behind the records lay human decisions. She would have to reach them without pretending that the labels were the people.

units.title: An Invitation to Speak
units.transcript:
Emma checked her email after breakfast. The newspaper archivist had replied to her latest question. Staff could provide a short description of the document filed on 12 October 2011, but not the letter itself or the writer’s name.

The old index described it as a request for information about the student travel scheme. The archivist explained that staff had added the words “decision not received” when they created the entry. They could not say exactly what the writer had asked.

Emma read the message again. A request for information was not necessarily a complaint. It did not prove that a decision letter had been lost.

She called Sarah.

“So what do we know?” Sarah asked.

“That the newspaper received something about the scheme and placed it in its information section. We don't know who sent it or why.”

“Could it still be important?”

“Of course. But we need the original before making stronger claims.”

A few minutes later Fiona Bell called from the trust. She had asked the records team about the instructions for sending decision letters. They had found a page saying that staff should prepare notices soon after the selection panel met. It did not give a fixed number of days.

“Does it say when the letters were actually sent?” Emma asked.

“No. It describes what staff should do. We would need completed records to know what happened.”

Fiona had not checked the contents of the appeals folder. She could not confirm that any student had asked for a review.

Emma wrote two headings in her notebook: What was planned and What happened. She put the office instructions under the first heading. The newspaper's index description went under a third heading: Needs checking.

That afternoon Sarah suggested speaking to someone who had applied for a travel grant in 2011. Emma agreed that a person's experience might help, but she would not ask Fiona to reveal private names from the files. They could publish a general invitation through the newspaper and allow people to contact them if they wished.

Emma drafted a short notice. It asked anyone with direct knowledge of the travel scheme to get in touch privately. It did not claim that money was missing or that students had been treated unfairly.

Before sending it to Sarah, she read the wording twice. She remembered how her old article had hurt Claire's family.

This time, Emma wanted people to tell their own stories before she decided what the story was.

units.title: An Invitation to Speak
units.transcript:
The newspaper archive had managed to clarify the classification of the 12 October 2011 item without releasing the correspondence itself. Its surviving catalogue description placed the document among requests or material provided for information about the student travel scheme. The phrase “decision not received” was a staff-generated label, the archivist confirmed; its relationship to the sender's exact language could not be established without examining the underlying document.

Emma relayed the update to Sarah, who initially treated it as disappointing.

“Perhaps it wasn't even a complaint.”

“Perhaps not,” Emma replied. “But a catalogue category isn't a reliable substitute for the writer's intention. It tells us how the newspaper filed the material.”

The temptation was to turn the ambiguous label into an anonymous allegation. Emma resisted. Whatever the item contained, no evidence yet established its author, the status of any application or an actual failure to deliver a decision.

Fiona Bell's subsequent call added a procedural detail from the trust's 2011 office instructions. Staff were expected to prepare decision notices promptly after the selection panel met. The instructions did not define a dispatch deadline, and Fiona could not match the rule to particular completed letters. The appeals folder still awaited inspection; its title disclosed nothing conclusive about whether formal reviews had occurred.

Emma assembled a matrix distinguishing prescribed action, recorded action and verified outcome. The notice template and office guidance belonged in the first category. Fiona's preliminary description of dispatch entries offered limited evidence for the second. Nothing she had received yet established that any named applicant had obtained, understood or been denied the opportunity to request review.

Sarah proposed contacting former applicants directly. The suggestion was sensible in principle, but the route mattered. Requesting personal details from the trust's historical files would be intrusive, and a journalist's interest in a case did not erase the privacy of people who had once applied for financial support.

They decided instead to invite voluntary contact through the newspaper. Emma drafted an appeal to readers asking for first-hand experiences of the 2011 travel programme. On rereading it, she found a sentence that asked whether applicants had been wrongly refused assistance. It presumed a conclusion that her documents did not justify.

She replaced it with neutral questions: had readers applied, assisted someone with an application, received a decision notice or been informed about the review procedure? She made clear that contacting the newsroom would not automatically lead to publication. The newsroom would need to explain any confidentiality limits and obtain permission before sharing identifying material.

It was an unglamorous intervention, and one that carried risks of its own. People might misremember events from fifteen years earlier; a former applicant might confuse selection with payment; someone with an unrelated grievance might find the wording suggestive. Emma added a verification plan: record when an account was given, distinguish recollection from contemporaneous documents and seek independent corroboration where possible.

She thought briefly of Claire's warning that journalists sometimes asked the wrong questions. In 2011 Emma had allowed a tidy interpretation to replace a careful inquiry. This time she was trying to design a question that could be answered without first accepting her assumptions.

She sent the draft to Sarah for editorial approval. No witness had yet come forward, and no publication had been authorised. Still, the next stage of the investigation was taking shape: not the revelation of a culprit, but the creation of a way for the people affected to speak on their own terms.

units.title: The First Reply
units.transcript:
Sarah called Emma the next morning. “The editor has approved your invitation,” she said. “We can publish it on the newspaper's website this afternoon.”

Emma read the final text once more. It asked people who knew the Glenarraidh student travel scheme in 2011 to contact the newsroom. It did not say that the foundation had stolen money or treated students unfairly. It also explained that sending a message did not mean a person's name would appear in the newspaper.

“Good,” Emma said. “Please keep the contact details private.”

The invitation went online at two o'clock. Emma saved a copy with the publication date. Then she returned to her notes. She did not expect an answer immediately.

At four, the newsroom received a short email. The writer said they had helped a student apply for travel support in 2011. They offered to speak, but did not want their name published.

Sarah forwarded the message to Emma. “A witness?” she asked.

“Maybe. We don't know who this person is yet.”

Emma replied politely. She asked whether the writer would agree to a private conversation and whether they had any documents from the time. She promised only to discuss confidentiality before using any identifying details. She did not promise complete anonymity.

The writer answered an hour later. They had kept a copy of an application form and a letter, but they wanted to check what they could share. They did not say whether the student had been accepted, rejected or paid.

Emma felt excited. A document completed by a real applicant might help her compare the foundation's instructions with what had actually happened. But she had not seen the documents. An email was not proof that the writer's account was correct.

She called Sarah again. “We must not call this a rejected application,” she said. “They haven't told us the result.”

Sarah agreed. They would arrange a conversation only if the writer wanted one. They would check any evidence carefully and protect private details.

Before leaving work, Emma looked at Claire's old photograph. For weeks, she had studied registers and empty forms. Now someone might be able to explain what those papers had meant to a real person.

Her phone showed a new message: “I can speak tomorrow. Please don't record me until we have discussed it.”

Emma wrote one word in her notebook: Consent. She would begin there.

units.title: The First Reply
units.transcript:
Sarah rang with the news shortly after breakfast: the editor had approved Emma's carefully worded invitation to anyone with first-hand knowledge of the Glenarraidh student travel scheme in 2011. It would appear on the newspaper's website that afternoon.

Emma checked the final copy. The notice asked former applicants and people who had helped them to contact the newsroom voluntarily. It made no allegation of fraud or unfair treatment, and explained that correspondence would not automatically be published. Contact details would be handled privately, although the newsroom would need to discuss the limits of confidentiality with anyone who replied.

At two o'clock the invitation appeared online. Emma kept a dated copy and returned to the records she had been comparing: an unused decision-letter template, an outgoing-mail ledger and a policy for dealing with returned post. None showed whether a particular applicant had received or understood a decision.

Late that afternoon Sarah forwarded a reply. Its author claimed to have helped a student complete an application in 2011 and was willing to talk, provided their identity was not made public.

“Is that our first witness?” Sarah asked.

“It's a possible source. We haven't established who wrote the message or what they actually know.”

Emma sent a measured response. She offered a private conversation, asked whether the person possessed any contemporary records and explained that publication and confidentiality would need to be agreed separately. She avoided guaranteeing absolute anonymity before understanding what it could mean in practice.

The response came an hour later. The writer said they had kept a completed application form and a letter, but wanted to check what could be shared. They did not identify the student, describe the decision or state whether a grant had been paid.

Sarah wondered whether the saved letter was a rejection. Emma stopped her. “It could be an acknowledgement, a request for more information or a decision. Until we see it, we cannot know.”

They agreed not to seek private identities from Fiona Bell's records and not to connect the correspondent with the September parent's complaint or the October archive entry. Similar subjects did not establish a shared source.

In the evening another message arrived: the writer could speak the following day, but asked that no recording begin until they had discussed the conditions. Emma accepted.

She made a list for the conversation: establish the person's connection to the application, distinguish memory from documents, ask permission before recording and verify dates independently. For the first time in days, the investigation might move beyond descriptions of records. It still had not acquired a verified witness statement.

Emma closed her notebook at the heading Consent. That, rather than an accusation, would be her first question.

units.title: The First Reply
units.transcript:
Sarah's call brought the first tangible consequence of Emma's decision to invite voluntary testimony. The editor had approved a restrained public notice seeking first-hand knowledge of the Glenarraidh Education Trust's 2011 student travel scheme. It would be published that afternoon, without implying that selection had been unfair, funds misappropriated or appeals deliberately obstructed.

Emma examined the approved copy for unintended assumptions. Readers were invited to describe applications they had made or assisted with, notices they had received and any information they had been given about the review procedure. Contacting the newspaper did not constitute consent to publication. Nor could the newsroom responsibly promise anonymity without first explaining its practical and legal limits.

When the notice appeared at two o'clock, Emma preserved the text and timestamp. She resisted checking for responses every few minutes. The archive still held only restricted descriptions of correspondence; Fiona's inventory had not established the contents of the unopened appeals folder. A public invitation was a method of finding evidence, not evidence in itself.

Shortly after four, Sarah forwarded a brief email from someone claiming to have assisted a student with an application in 2011. The correspondent was prepared to speak but asked not to be identified publicly. No name or supporting record in the message had yet been independently verified.

“Finally,” Sarah said. “Someone who knows what happened.”

“Someone who says they were involved,” Emma corrected. “That may prove invaluable. It isn't yet a verified account.”

Emma replied without leading questions. She proposed a confidential preliminary conversation and invited the person, if comfortable, to describe the nature of their involvement and any contemporaneous documents they retained. She distinguished a private discussion from an agreement to use quotations or identifying details in print. She also declined to offer an unconditional guarantee that no circumstances could require disclosure.

An hour later, the correspondent said they still possessed a completed application form and a letter, although they needed to decide what could appropriately be shared. Their reply gave no outcome: it did not say whether the student was selected, received money or requested reconsideration.

Emma could feel the old narrative machinery beginning to work. A preserved letter sounded like the document she had been seeking. Yet its content might be an acknowledgement, an enquiry or a final decision. Nor was there any reason to equate this person with the anonymous September parent or the author of the October item indexed by the newspaper. These were separate evidential strands until a connection could be corroborated.

The correspondent's next message proposed a conversation the following day, on the condition that recording would not begin before they had discussed consent. Emma agreed and prepared a careful interview plan: verify the person's relationship to the application, distinguish recalled events from surviving documents, agree the terms of any recording and check significant dates against independent sources.

She put the plan beside the dispatch register and the blank appeal template. The possible witness might illuminate what an administrative process felt like to someone subject to it. That perspective mattered, but it would not by itself settle every question about the trust's practices.

Emma wrote Consent at the top of a fresh page. Tomorrow she would hear a person rather than an index entry. Tonight she would make no claim about what the person was going to say.

A willingness to speak did not imply consent to recording, identification or publication. Emma checked with Sarah that a quiet meeting room was available.

The visitor introduced herself as Helen Ward. She said she had helped her younger cousin apply for travel support in 2011. Before saying anything about the application, she asked what the newspaper would do with her name.

Emma proposed a preliminary conversation without recording, explained the distinction between internal notes and publishable attribution, and asked Helen to decide which details could be retained. She would not publish identifying information without a further agreement. She also said she could not promise protection in every possible legal circumstance. Helen considered the limits, requested that her cousin remain unidentified, and agreed to proceed on those terms.

“I kept some of the papers,” Helen said. She opened a folder containing a photocopy of a completed application and a letter bearing the foundation's name. Emma distinguished the date printed on the photocopied letter from its unknown delivery date. Even an apparently official document required provenance checks before it could establish an event.

Her knowledge of receipt, however, was second-hand or uncertain; she could not remember witnessing the decision letter arrive.

“I don't want to guess. We should read the letter properly. I haven't looked at it in years.”

Emma resisted the urge to capture either page. Permission to inspect a document was not permission to reproduce its personal details. She asked whether Helen would allow a later examination of copies with private details covered. Helen said she wanted to speak to her cousin first.

units.title: The Folded Letter
units.transcript:
Two days after meeting Emma, Helen Ward called the newsroom. She had spoken to her cousin, who did not want to meet a journalist. However, the cousin had agreed that Helen could show Emma a copy of the old letter, with the name and address covered. Emma asked whether that permission included taking a copy. Helen said it did not. For now, Emma could read it during another private meeting.

They met in the same quiet room. Sarah stayed outside until Helen agreed that she could join them. Helen took a folded sheet from an envelope and placed it on the table. The foundation's name appeared at the top. Below it was a date in September 2011.

Emma read the letter slowly. It said that the student's application had been selected for travel support. But it also said that payment would depend on proof of enrolment and the final travel costs. The letter was not a promise that money had already been sent.

“So your cousin received a grant?” Sarah asked.

“The letter says selected,” Helen answered. “I don't know when money was paid, or whether it was paid at all.”

Emma pointed to a paragraph at the bottom. It explained that unsuccessful applicants could request a review within fourteen days. The same paragraph appeared in the blank model letter Fiona had sent earlier. But Helen's cousin had been selected, according to this copy. The review paragraph did not tell Emma anything about people who were rejected.

“Do you remember when your cousin got this?” Emma asked.

“No. I remember helping with the application. I found the letter years later among our family papers.”

Emma wrote down the printed date, but not a date of delivery. She also noted that she had seen a copy, not the original. She did not take a photograph or record Helen's words.

When the meeting ended, Helen agreed to ask her cousin whether a copy with personal information removed could be shared for checking. She made no promise. Emma thanked her for asking.

Back at her desk, Emma compared what she had read with the newspaper announcement of eight selected students. One letter described one selection; it could not confirm the newspaper's total. Nor could it establish a payment.

She opened her notebook and wrote: Selected — supported by one unverified copy. Paid — unknown.

A small piece of the story had become clearer. The larger question had not.

units.title: The Folded Letter
units.transcript:
Helen Ward contacted Emma two days after their first conversation. She had consulted her cousin, who preferred not to speak to a journalist but was willing for Helen to show a redacted copy of the foundation's 2011 letter. The permission was limited to reading it in a private meeting. It did not include photographing, copying or publishing the document.

Emma repeated those conditions when Helen arrived. Sarah joined them only after Helen agreed. The paper was folded and bore the Glenarraidh Education Trust's name and a date in September 2011. Emma treated those features as details to verify, not proof that the document was genuine.

The wording was significant. It described the cousin's application as selected for travel support, then explained that payment was conditional on evidence of course enrolment and confirmed travel costs. It did not state that funds had been transferred.

“Then the student was a beneficiary,” Sarah suggested.

“A selected applicant,” Emma corrected. “We don't yet know whether the conditions were met or any payment followed.”

The letter also contained a paragraph on the fourteen-day review procedure for unsuccessful applicants. Its wording resembled the blank template that Fiona Bell had previously supplied. That similarity suggested a possible connection between the template and an issued notice, but did not authenticate either copy or show how consistently the wording had been used.

Emma asked Helen when her cousin had received the decision. Helen could not remember. She recalled helping to complete the application, but had found the letter much later with family paperwork. The date printed at its head was not evidence of delivery on that day.

She also asked whether Helen knew of any appeal. Helen shook her head. Her cousin had apparently been selected, and Helen knew nothing about other applicants. Emma deliberately avoided inviting guesses about students whose details Helen had never seen.

Throughout the meeting, Emma took brief notes within the limits Helen had agreed. No recording was made, and she did not retain an image of the paper. Before leaving, Helen offered to ask her cousin whether a redacted copy could later be provided for examination. That decision remained the cousin's.

Emma returned to the original newspaper report: eight students reportedly selected, followed by a correction that gave no replacement figure. Even if the letter proved authentic, it would establish at most one case of selection. A total could not be reconstructed from a single example, and selection still did not equal payment.

In her notebook, she drew two boxes: What the letter says and What has been verified. They did not yet contain the same information. It was progress, but of the careful kind.

Helen Ward's second call arrived forty-eight hours after her first meeting with Emma. She had spoken to the cousin whose 2011 travel application she had helped prepare. The cousin declined an interview, but had authorised Helen to show a copy of a decision letter with identifying details obscured. The permission was explicitly limited to inspection: no reproduction, recording or publication had been agreed.

Emma confirmed the terms before examining anything. Sarah entered the meeting room only with Helen's consent. Helen unfolded a photocopy bearing the Glenarraidh Education Trust's letterhead and a printed date in September 2011. Its appearance was consistent with the material Emma had seen elsewhere, but consistency of presentation was not authentication. Provenance and completeness remained unresolved.

The central sentence described the application as having been selected for travel support. A subsequent paragraph made any payment contingent upon documentary confirmation of enrolment and final travel expenditure. That distinction mattered. It identified an administrative decision in the language of the scheme, not evidence that an award had been disbursed.

“So we can add a beneficiary to our list,” Sarah said.

“Only if by beneficiary you mean someone described as selected in a copy we have not authenticated,” Emma replied. “It tells us nothing conclusive about payment.”

The same page included the fourteen-day review wording for unsuccessful applicants. Emma recognised its resemblance to the unused model notice Fiona Bell had obtained. units.title: The Payment Exceptions
units.transcript:
Emma did not sleep well after seeing Helen's folded letter. It showed that one application had been selected, but it did not prove that money had been paid. She had seen only a copy, and Helen's cousin had not allowed her to keep it.

The next morning Helen sent a message. Her cousin was willing for the newspaper to examine a copy with the name, address and course details hidden. They did not agree to publication. Emma replied that she understood and would explain how the document would be checked.

When the redacted scan arrived, Emma saved it in a private folder. She did not send it to anyone outside the small investigation team. She compared its printed layout with the blank decision-letter template Fiona had supplied. The headings and review paragraph were similar, but that did not prove the scan was genuine.

Sarah noticed a line near the bottom: “Payment subject to final verification.” There was no amount marked as paid.

“So we still can't say the student got the money,” Sarah said.

“Exactly. We need a payment record, or another reliable source.”

Emma asked Helen one question: did her cousin have any bank record or letter confirming a transfer? Helen did not know. She would ask, but she made no promise.

Meanwhile Fiona Bell responded to Emma's request about the trust's records. The team had located an old list of payment authorisations. Fiona said an authorisation was permission for staff to make a payment, not proof that a bank had sent it. The list had not been fully checked, and Fiona could not provide personal details.

Emma remembered the hidden caller who had told her to ask who approved the payments. She had nearly forgotten those words while studying letters and review rules. Now they seemed important again. But the caller's identity was still unknown, and Emma had no reason to trust the caller without documents.

She wrote three questions in her notebook. Who selected the students? Who approved each payment? Which payments actually reached students?

Sarah asked if the two lists would finally match.

“We haven't seen them,” Emma replied. “We must not decide that they match—or that they don't.”

In the evening Emma looked at the scan one last time. The word selected was clear. The word paid was not there.

Then she received another message from Fiona: the records team had found a separate heading in the accounts index, “Payment exceptions — 2011”. Fiona had not examined those records yet.

Emma closed her laptop. A heading was only a heading. But this one gave her a question she could no longer ignore.

units.title: The Payment Exceptions
units.transcript:
After the meeting with Helen Ward, Emma kept returning to the distinction that had shaped the investigation: a selection decision was not a completed payment. The copy Helen had shown her named a successful application, subject to confirmation of enrolment and travel costs. Yet Emma had neither authenticated the copy nor established whether the conditions were met.

The following morning Helen wrote that her cousin would allow a redacted scan to be examined privately by the newsroom. Names, addresses and course details were concealed; publication was not authorised. Emma acknowledged the restrictions before receiving the file and stored it in a limited-access folder.

She compared its formatting with the blank notice previously supplied by Fiona Bell. The headings and the paragraph about reviews appeared consistent. That gave her a useful point of comparison, not independent authentication: a convincing reproduction could still be incomplete or altered.

Sarah pointed to the final line. “Payment subject to final verification.”

“Which means this isn't a receipt,” Emma said.

Nor did the document contain a completed transfer date. Emma asked Helen whether her cousin possessed an account statement or subsequent notice showing that money had arrived. Helen did not know and would enquire without committing her cousin to further contact.

Fiona's latest update introduced another kind of record. The trust's team had identified a list of payment authorisations, although it remained incompletely catalogued and was not available to Emma. Fiona stressed that approving a payment was an administrative step distinct from executing a bank transfer. Individual records might also contain protected personal information.

The phrase brought Emma back to the anonymous telephone warning: ask who approved the payments. She had no evidence that the caller knew the answer or had acted in good faith. Still, the existence of an authorisation list made the question testable.

She divided her notebook into Selected, Authorised and Transferred. Each stage would require separate documentary support. She would not treat a mismatch as evidence of wrongdoing without checking explanations such as withdrawn courses, delayed paperwork or different accounting dates.

Sarah wondered whether Helen's cousin might appear in the payment records. Emma would not try to identify a private student through Fiona's files. If Helen's cousin chose to provide evidence of a transfer, the newsroom could compare the dates and descriptions without publishing personal details.

That evening another message arrived from Fiona. The records inventory included a separate heading, “Payment exceptions — 2011”. The team had not inspected the documents beneath it.

“Exceptions,” Sarah repeated when Emma told her. “That sounds suspicious.”

“It may refer to routine delays or corrections,” Emma said. “We need to know what the trust meant by the word.”

The new label did not prove that money was missing. It did, however, bring the investigation back to the boundary between approval and payment—and to a question the anonymous caller had raised before Emma had the evidence to understand it.

units.title: The Payment Exceptions
units.transcript:
Emma regarded the redacted copy of Helen Ward's family letter as a modest but important advance: for the first time, she could examine a document linked by a potential witness to an actual application, rather than another uncompleted template. Its evidential value, however, depended on restrictions she had agreed to respect and checks she had yet to perform.

Helen's cousin had authorised confidential examination of a scanned copy, not publication. Personal identifiers and course details had been obscured. Emma confirmed those terms in writing, limited access within the newsroom and avoided treating the possession of a scan as a licence to disclose its contents indiscriminately.

Comparison with Fiona Bell's unused decision-notice template produced encouraging similarities in layout and wording, particularly the paragraph about the fourteen-day review procedure. Such consistency was relevant to provenance, but hardly dispositive. The template might have been widely available; the scan might omit later pages; neither possibility had been tested.

A final sentence proved more instructive than the matching typography: “Payment subject to final verification.” Selection was stated; a transfer was not. There was no remittance confirmation, banking reference or evidence that the student had satisfied the outstanding conditions.

Sarah asked whether Helen could find a bank statement or subsequent correspondence. Emma sent a restrained enquiry. Helen replied that she would consult her cousin, without promising more information or access. The relative's decision would govern any additional disclosure.

Fiona's parallel investigation of the trust's archive yielded a new category of material: a list of payment authorisations. Fiona cautioned that the list had not been reconciled with banking records or examined in full. An authorisation could permit expenditure without establishing that funds had left an account, much less reached the intended beneficiary. Privacy constraints also ruled out releasing identifiable applicants' details.

The development returned Emma to a line she had recorded weeks earlier. An unidentified caller had urged her to ask who signed off payments rather than concentrate solely on missing minutes. The caller's motives and knowledge remained unknown. Yet the newly located records gave that instruction a possible documentary route. Emma refused to elevate the anonymous warning into corroboration of itself.

She revised her working categories: Selected, Authorised, Transferred. A difference among those populations would not, by itself, demonstrate fraud. Applications could be withdrawn, conditions remain unmet, transfers be reversed or entries fall in different reporting periods. The task was to establish both what had occurred and which explanation best accounted for it.

Sarah asked whether the selected student described in Helen's letter could be traced through the authorisation list. Emma ruled out using restricted foundation records to identify the cousin. A voluntarily shared, appropriately redacted payment record might permit a narrower comparison, but no such permission or record yet existed.

Near the end of the day Fiona sent one more inventory detail: a heading reading “Payment exceptions — 2011”. She had not inspected the contents and could not say what an exception represented. Sarah's immediate suspicion was understandable, but an administrative exception might be an ordinary delay, correction or reversal rather than an irregular transfer.

Emma wrote the heading beside the caller's words, leaving a space between them. Their apparent connection was a hypothesis, not a finding. The next question was no longer simply who had been selected. It was what the trust meant by an exception—and whether any independently verified bank transaction lay behind it.

units.title: Manual Approval
units.transcript:
Emma opened Fiona's email before breakfast. The records team had finally examined the first sheet inside the folder marked “Payment exceptions — 2011”. It was a guide to the words used in the trust's accounts, not a list of students.

The guide described three reasons for marking a payment as an exception: missing documents, a changed travel plan, or a payment returned by the bank. It did not say how often these things had happened. Fiona warned Emma that the team had not checked the individual records.

“Does a returned payment mean a student lost their grant?” Emma asked.

“Not necessarily,” Fiona said. “The money might have been sent again after the problem was fixed. We don't know.”

Emma called Sarah. They had spent weeks trying to understand why selected students and payments might not match. Now they had a possible explanation, but no figures.

“So the foundation did have problems with payments,” Sarah said.

“It had a way to record problems,” Emma corrected her. “That's different from proving any particular payment failed.”

They made a list of the evidence they still needed: how many exceptions had been recorded, what happened afterwards, and whether any transfer had finally reached a student.

Later Helen Ward replied to Emma's question about her cousin's grant. Her cousin had found no bank statement from 2011 and did not remember the exact date of any payment. Helen asked Emma not to treat this as proof that the money had never arrived.

Emma agreed. An old statement might have been lost. A forgotten date was not a missing payment.

In the afternoon Fiona sent one more detail. The guide told staff to write a second reference beside any exception that had been resolved. Fiona did not yet know whether the surviving records included those second references.

“Then we should ask for totals of open and resolved cases,” Sarah suggested.

“Yes, if the records allow a reliable count,” Emma said.

Emma remembered the anonymous caller's warning about the people who signed the payments. She still could not identify the caller, and she refused to assume the warning was true.

Before closing her notebook, she drew two columns: Exception recorded and Exception resolved. Between them she left a space for documents she had not seen.

Then a new email arrived from Fiona. The records team had noticed that some entries used the words “manual approval”. Fiona had not checked who approved them or what they were for.

Emma stared at the phrase. It might describe an ordinary office task. But now she knew exactly which question to ask next.

Fiona Bell's email arrived with the first account of what was actually inside the folder labelled “Payment exceptions — 2011”. The records team had examined an introductory sheet defining the category. It was a guide to recordkeeping rather than a ledger of individual cases, and Fiona was careful about the distinction.

According to the sheet, a payment could be marked as an exception when supporting documents were missing, travel arrangements changed or a bank transfer was returned. The guide gave no totals. Nor had the team reconciled any entries with evidence of transfers eventually reaching students.

“A returned payment sounds serious,” Sarah said when Emma called.

“It could be,” Emma replied. “But a returned transfer might have been corrected and sent again. We need the later record, not just the first problem.”

They mapped the new information against Helen Ward's redacted decision letter. Helen's cousin had apparently been selected, subject to enrolment and travel checks. That notice still did not establish that an authorisation had been made, or that any money had been transferred.

Helen later responded to Emma's enquiry. Her cousin had not located a bank statement from 2011 and could not remember when, or even with confidence whether, a payment had arrived. Helen specifically asked the newsroom not to treat the missing paperwork as proof of non-payment. Emma recorded that limitation without trying to persuade the family to release more private records.

Another paragraph in the trust's guidance caught Emma's attention. When an exception was settled, administrators were instructed to enter a follow-up reference. In principle, a sequence of original and follow-up entries might establish whether a problem had been resolved. But Fiona had not yet determined whether those references survived or could be matched reliably.

Sarah proposed counting the outstanding cases. Emma agreed only conditionally: they would need to distinguish cases still unresolved in 2011 from files that were merely incomplete today. A missing follow-up document was not necessarily an unresolved transfer.

Then Fiona sent a brief update. In the preliminary material, staff had seen entries marked “manual approval”. No signatory, reason or associated bank transaction had yet been checked. The phrase might simply refer to a standard exception-handling process.

Emma thought again about the caller who had urged her to ask who approved the payments. The wording was suggestive, but anonymous instructions could not authenticate an accounting entry.

She wrote three questions: What required manual approval? Who was authorised to give it? What happened to the payment afterwards? Unlike the newspaper's disputed selection total, these questions could eventually be answered by records of a particular process.

For the moment, the trust had supplied definitions, not findings. Still, it had given Emma a sharper route through the numbers.
