units.title: Manual Approval
units.transcript:
The first material Fiona Bell could describe from the folder marked “Payment exceptions — 2011” was not a scandalous ledger but an administrative glossary. Emma felt a flicker of disappointment before recognising its value. A category could not be interpreted fairly until she understood the institution's rules for assigning it.

The introductory sheet listed several circumstances in which an expected payment might be classified as an exception: incomplete supporting evidence, changes in travel arrangements and transfers returned by a bank. None of those descriptions implied misconduct. Equally, their routine appearance in a manual could not establish that every subsequent case had been handled properly.

Fiona had no verified case count and had not reconciled the relevant entries with remittance or banking records. She cautioned that an exception might be resolved through a later transaction, but that this had not been confirmed for any particular student.

Sarah suggested they might finally have evidence of unpaid grants. Emma rejected the inference. What they had was evidence that the trust anticipated circumstances in which an authorised payment might not proceed normally. The real questions were frequency, cause and eventual outcome.

She revisited Helen Ward's redacted copy of the selection notice. It supplied a limited account of one successful decision, subject to further documentation. Helen had now asked her cousin about historical banking records. None had been located, and the cousin's recollection of any payment was uncertain. Crucially, the absence of an old statement did not establish that the account had never been credited. Emma accepted the family's reluctance to undertake a broader search.

One feature of the exception guidance offered a method. Administrators were instructed to enter a follow-up reference when a problem was resolved. If the surviving records permitted the initial and subsequent entries to be matched, Emma might be able to distinguish a temporarily interrupted transfer from a permanently outstanding one. Yet the failure to locate such a link in an incomplete archive would not itself prove that a payment remained unsettled.

Sarah proposed requesting aggregate figures for unresolved exceptions. Emma refined the proposal. They needed totals defined by the scheme's own categories and dates, alongside an explanation of missing or damaged records. Otherwise an apparent discrepancy might result from surviving paperwork rather than from anything that happened to students.

Late in the afternoon Fiona reported an additional notation in the preliminary register: “manual approval”. Neither the reasons for the notation nor the authorised signatories had been checked. Emma recognised the phrase as a possible route back to the anonymous caller's insistence that she examine payment approvals, not merely meeting minutes. But the caller's knowledge and intentions remained unverified. Two suggestive details did not automatically corroborate one another.

Emma placed three questions beside the notation: What circumstances required manual approval? Who had authority to provide it? Was the subsequent transfer completed?

A form could establish a procedure; a signed authorisation, if genuine, could establish a decision; a bank record might establish a transaction. Those were different kinds of proof. For the first time, though, she could see how all three might be brought together without exposing a former student's identity.

She closed the file on the phrase “manual approval”, treating it not as an accusation but as the next testable question.

units.title: Delegated Authority
units.transcript:
Emma found an email from Fiona Bell when she reached her desk. The records team had looked at another page from the trust's 2011 accounts guide. It explained what staff should do when a payment needed manual approval.

The guide said that a member of staff could request an exception, but a second authorised person had to approve it. Both steps were meant to be recorded with dates and reference numbers. The page did not name any particular person.

“Does this tell us who signed the payments?” Emma asked Fiona on the phone.

“No. It tells us how approval was supposed to work. We haven't checked the individual entries.”

Emma wrote down the difference. A rule about two people did not prove that two people had approved every exception.

Sarah came into the office with two cups of tea. “At least we can say the trust needed two signatures.”

“The guide says two separate roles,” Emma corrected her. “We haven't found two signed documents.”

Fiona had one more detail. The records team had seen a few entries with the words “approved manually”, but some of the neighbouring fields were difficult to read. Staff were making clearer copies before trying to count them. Fiona could not say how many entries were involved, who had approved them or whether any bank transfer followed.

Emma thought of Helen Ward's cousin. The family had a letter saying a grant was selected, but no confirmed record of payment. Emma would not try to connect that student to an exception without evidence.

In the afternoon Helen emailed. Her cousin had agreed that Emma could ask general questions about the payment process, but did not want to share more bank details. Emma thanked Helen and did not press further.

Sarah pointed at the notebook. “Selected, authorised, paid. And now requested?”

“Yes,” Emma said. “A request for approval is another step. We must keep each one separate.”

She drew four boxes and put an arrow between them. Beside the final box she wrote a question mark.

Later Fiona forwarded the title of a second office sheet: “Delegated authority — September 2011”. The team had not checked its contents, and she did not know whether it listed names or just job titles.

Emma read the words carefully. The anonymous caller had asked who approved the payments. Now there was a possible document about who had authority to approve them. It was a lead, not yet an answer.

She sent Fiona a simple question: “Can you confirm what the sheet describes, without identifying students?”

Then she closed her notebook. Tomorrow's work would begin with the rules, not with an accusation.

units.title: Delegated Authority
units.transcript:
Fiona Bell's latest message contained a second extract from the trust's 2011 accounting guidance. Emma opened it beside her notes on the words “manual approval”, which had appeared in the preliminary records without any confirmed signatory or linked transfer.

The guidance described a two-stage arrangement. A member of staff could request an exceptional payment decision; a person with delegated authority was then supposed to authorise it. Both actions should be recorded, together with dates and reference numbers. The passage supplied roles, not individual names, and did not establish that the procedure had been followed in every case.

“So it required two signatures?” Sarah asked.

“Not necessarily signatures,” Emma replied. “The document says the request and authorisation should be recorded separately. We still need to see how that happened.”

When Emma spoke to Fiona, she asked whether the team had identified actual authorisers. Fiona said they had not. Several entries apparently bore a manual-approval notation, but adjacent fields were unclear on the surviving copies. Staff were preparing better images before attempting a reliable count or matching the entries to later transactions.

Emma resisted interpreting illegible fields as missing signatures. A poor copy was not evidence that the original record had been left blank. Equally, the existence of a policy did not verify compliance.

She turned back to Helen Ward's redacted letter. Its selection decision was conditional on further checks, and the family had not established that a grant was ultimately paid. Nothing linked that application to the exceptional-payment material. Helen subsequently confirmed that her cousin was happy for general questions about procedure to be asked but did not wish to disclose further banking information. Emma accepted the boundary.

By afternoon, her notebook contained four headings: Requested, Authorised, Transferred and Received. A payment request might never be approved; an authorisation might not lead to a transfer; a transfer might be returned. She could not collapse any of the stages into another.

Fiona's final email introduced a further lead. The inventory included a sheet labelled “Delegated authority — September 2011”, but its contents had not been examined. It might explain who was entitled to approve exceptions, though it could just as easily list positions rather than named individuals.

Sarah remembered the anonymous caller's advice to ask who approved payments. Emma remembered it too, without assuming the caller was trustworthy. The new title made the question investigable; it did not answer it.

She asked Fiona for a non-identifying description of the sheet once it had been examined. Until then, the strongest finding was a procedural distinction, not a scandal.

units.title: Delegated Authority
units.transcript:
The notation “manual approval” had seemed tantalising when Fiona Bell first reported it, but Emma knew that an unexplained label acquired meaning only when placed within the system that produced it. Fiona's next attachment provided part of that system: an extract from the Glenarraidh Education Trust's 2011 accounting guidance.

The document distinguished the initiation of an exceptional-payment request from its authorisation. An administrator could flag a case; a person exercising delegated authority was then expected to approve or refuse the proposed action. Separate dates and reference identifiers were to be recorded. No individual officer was named in the extract, and nothing in it established that staff had complied consistently.

Sarah read Emma's summary and asked whether two signatures were compulsory.

“Two recorded functions,” Emma replied. “That's what the guidance describes. It doesn't tell us whether approval was handwritten, entered in a system or documented on another sheet.”

The distinction mattered. Treating a procedural requirement as proof of its implementation was precisely the error Emma had tried to avoid with the selection notices and appeal rules. The absence of a legible name on a preliminary copy, meanwhile, did not prove that the original lacked an authorisation.

Fiona confirmed that the records team had observed manual-approval notations in some entries. However, adjacent fields were difficult to decipher, and the surviving pages had not been reconciled with subsequent accounting or banking evidence. The team was preparing clearer images before making any claim about quantities, signatories or outcomes.

Emma considered whether Helen Ward's cousin could help. The family possessed a redacted selection notice but no verified transfer record, and there was no documentary bridge to these accounting exceptions. Helen later relayed that her cousin permitted general enquiries about procedure but declined to disclose more personal banking material. Emma accepted that decision without trying to infer that withheld information concealed anything significant.

She revised her working model yet again. Requested did not mean authorised. Authorised did not mean transferred. Even a transfer recorded by the trust might not demonstrate receipt by the intended beneficiary. A returned transfer, a later correction or a change in course arrangements could explain divergent totals without implying impropriety. Each proposition demanded an appropriate source.

Then Fiona mentioned an unexamined inventory item headed “Delegated authority — September 2011”. It might describe the limits attached to particular posts, identify individuals who could authorise exceptional expenditure, or merely reproduce generic governance language. Fiona was unwilling to speculate before reading it.

The timing caught Emma's attention. A September document could be relevant to the period of the original selection announcement and Claire's disappearance. Yet a document bearing that month was not necessarily operative on the exact dates of either event. Its effective period would have to be established independently.

The anonymous caller's instruction—ask who approved the payments—now had an intelligible documentary direction. But the caller remained unidentified, and the guide did not corroborate any allegation of misconduct. It simply showed that authorisation and payment were administratively distinguishable.

Emma drafted a precise request to Fiona: could the records team identify the document's date, scope and named or role-based authority, while excluding students' personal details? She sent it without mentioning the caller.

For once, a potentially revealing clue was also a test of her patience. She would have to discover who could approve a payment before claiming to know who did.

A returned transfer, a later correction or a change in course arrangements could explain divergent totals without implying impropriety. Each proposition demanded an appropriate source.

Then Fiona mentioned an unexamined inventory item headed “Delegated authority — September 2011”. It might describe the limits attached to particular posts, identify individuals who could authorise exceptional expenditure, or merely reproduce generic governance language. Fiona was unwilling to speculate before reading it.

The timing caught Emma's attention. A September document could be relevant to the period of the original selection announcement and Claire's disappearance. Yet a document bearing that month was not necessarily operative on the exact dates of either event. Its effective period would have to be established independently.

The anonymous caller's instruction—ask who approved the payments—now had an intelligible documentary direction. But the caller remained unidentified, and the guide did not corroborate any allegation of misconduct. It simply showed that authorisation and payment were administratively distinguishable.

Emma drafted a precise request to Fiona: could the records team identify the document's date, scope and named or role-based authority, while excluding students' personal details? She sent it without mentioning the caller.

units.title: Who Could Approve?
units.transcript:
Fiona's next email arrived while Emma was reading her notes about manual approval. The records team had finally opened the sheet marked 'Delegated authority — September 2011'. Emma hoped it would give her the name of a person who had approved payments.

Instead, Fiona sent a description. The sheet listed three job roles: scheme administrator, finance manager and trust chair. It explained which role could ask for an exception and which role could authorise one. It did not contain a list of payments.

'Are there names?' Emma asked.

'There are initials beside two roles,' Fiona replied. 'The copy is faint. We can't read them with confidence, and we don't know whether they were names or an internal checking mark.'

Emma wrote down exactly what Fiona had said. She had no reason to put a person's name beside any payment.

Sarah looked at the description. 'But Malcolm Vale chaired the trust. Doesn't that mean he approved the exceptions?'

'No,' Emma answered. 'A chair might have authority under a rule without using it in a particular case. We need an actual approval record.'

Fiona had found one more detail. The sheet said that an exception above a specified limit should be referred to the trust chair. Fiona could not yet read the amount on the old copy. Emma did not know whether any of the 2011 exceptions had reached that limit.

They returned to Helen Ward's family letter. The student had been selected for travel support, but Helen had not confirmed a transfer and did not want to share bank details. Nothing connected the family to the manual-approval records.

Emma phoned Fiona again. 'Could you ask for a clearer copy of the limit and a count of entries that needed approval? No student names.'

'I can ask,' Fiona said. 'But we must check the records before saying there is a count.'

By evening Sarah had prepared a page for their investigation file. It had four headings: request, authorisation, transfer and receipt. They could explain the first two as rules. They could not fill the last two with facts about a particular student.

Then Fiona sent a final note. The records team had discovered a reference to a separate authorisation register. They had not located the register itself.

Emma stared at the message. The sheet told her who could approve. The missing register might tell her who did.

That was the question she would take into the next day.

units.title: Who Could Approve?
units.transcript:
Fiona Bell's latest update concerned the document that had ended Emma's previous day's work: 'Delegated authority — September 2011'. The team had now inspected the sheet, although parts of the surviving copy were difficult to read.

Rather than naming people responsible for particular payments, the document described three positions: scheme administrator, finance manager and trust chair. It distinguished the authority to request an exceptional decision from the authority to approve it. The distinction mattered, but the document remained a statement of responsibilities rather than a record of their exercise.

'Does it identify the approvers?' Emma asked.

'Not reliably,' Fiona replied. 'There are faint initials beside two roles, but we can't establish what those marks mean.'

Emma recorded the uncertainty without attempting to decipher the marks herself. A partly legible initial was not sufficient grounds for naming an individual.

Sarah suggested that Malcolm Vale's role as chair might explain the approvals. Emma disagreed. Even if a chair possessed delegated authority, that did not establish that Malcolm had signed any particular entry. A policy assigning power and a dated authorisation were different kinds of evidence.

One paragraph specified that exceptions above a financial limit should be referred to the chair. Unfortunately, the threshold was not legible in the available copy. Nor had Fiona established whether any surviving case exceeded it. The paragraph therefore supplied a conditional rule, not a finding about the trust's transactions.

Emma returned to the document Helen Ward had shown her. It described a student's selection and made payment dependent on further checks. Helen's cousin had not authorised further disclosure of bank details. Emma would not try to match that private application to a trust entry on the basis of guesswork.

She sent Fiona a carefully limited request: could the records team obtain a clearer reproduction of the threshold, describe the categories of authorisation and determine whether a reliable count of entries existed? She did not request student names.

In the newsroom Sarah drafted a simple sequence: Request → Authorisation → Transfer → Receipt. The first two stages could be described from the rules. The latter stages still required transactional evidence. Emma added a warning that an approval might never have resulted in money leaving the account.

Shortly before closing time Fiona emailed again. An inventory note referred to a separate authorisation register, but the records team had not located it. Its existence, completeness and contents remained unknown.

'At last, a register that might have names,' Sarah said.

'Might,' Emma replied. 'And the question isn't merely who had power. It's who exercised it in a recorded case.'

Emma ended the day facing an absence precise enough to investigate: the rules identified possible authority, but the primary record of actual approvals was still missing.

units.title: Who Could Approve?
units.transcript:
When Fiona Bell confirmed that the trust's records team had inspected the sheet headed 'Delegated authority — September 2011', Emma expected her investigation to move from institutional procedure towards named decision-makers. The document delivered a more limited, though genuinely useful, distinction.

It assigned responsibilities among a scheme administrator, finance manager and trust chair. A member of staff could initiate a request for exceptional treatment; another role could authorise that departure from ordinary procedure. The sheet described competences attached to offices. It was not an authorisation register and did not identify the approver of any individual transaction.

Two faint sets of initials appeared beside the descriptions, Fiona reported. Their interpretation remained uncertain: the marks could signify initials, an internal check or something else. Neither Emma nor the records team had a reliable basis for attributing them to a named person. Emma declined to convert imperfect legibility into a speculative allegation.

Sarah nevertheless raised Malcolm Vale. As chair of the Glenarraidh Education Trust, he might have possessed the higher level of delegated authority described by the document. Emma accepted the possibility and rejected the inference. Possessing authority is not evidence of exercising it; still less does it establish a payment, an improper decision or a motive connected with Claire Morrison's disappearance.

A paragraph on the sheet required exceptions above a specified financial threshold to be referred to the chair. The amount was unreadable on the copy currently available. Fiona also lacked a reliable count of cases, let alone evidence identifying any exception above the threshold. The referral rule therefore remained conditional. Emma could not claim it had actually been triggered.

The resemblance between this administrative trail and the anonymous caller's warning about payment approvals was striking. Yet a caller whose identity and sources were unverified could not authenticate the newly inspected guidance. The same caution applied to Helen Ward's redacted copy of her cousin's selection notice. It described a conditional award but demonstrated neither authorisation nor transfer. Helen's family had declined further banking disclosure, a boundary Emma would respect.

Emma formulated a narrower request. Could the team obtain a legible reproduction of the threshold, establish what sort of marks appeared by the office titles and report whether the surviving exceptions could be counted without identifying students? Each task concerned the quality and structure of evidence rather than the exposure of a private beneficiary.

Sarah created a diagram with four successive claims: Requested, Authorised, Transferred, Received. The first two appeared in the trust's procedural language. Transaction records would be needed for the third, and reliable evidence of arrival for the fourth. A discrepancy between stages could have routine explanations; its mere existence would not prove misconduct.

Fiona's final message supplied another archival lead. A storage inventory mentioned an 'authorisation register', but no one had yet found the register. Its condition, scope and very survival were uncertain. Emma added the reference to her notes without calling it recovered evidence.

In the silence of her office, the distinction became clear. The delegated-authority sheet could tell her who was entitled to approve an exceptional request. A completed authorisation entry might tell her who actually approved one. Only subsequent records could establish whether money moved.

She underlined the unresolved question: Where is the record of decisions made under this authority?

units.title: The Missing Carton
units.transcript:
Emma stared at Fiona's last email. The trust's old papers mentioned an authorisation register, but nobody had found it. The document about delegated authority explained which jobs could approve unusual payments. It did not show who had approved anything in 2011.

The following morning Fiona rang with news. The records team had found an old storage list from 2012. One line referred to a book of approvals for the travel scheme. Beside it was a box number. But that box was not among the boxes now held in the trust's main store.

“Does that mean the book was destroyed?” Emma asked.

“No. It may have been moved or put in another store. We have no record of its destruction.”

Emma noted the box number. She could not visit the store or see private student records, but Fiona agreed to ask whether other storage lists mentioned the same box.

Sarah came into the room carrying coffee. “At least we know the register existed.”

“We know it was listed in 2012,” Emma said. “We don't know whether the list was correct, or where the book went.”

They checked the information they already had. The September 2011 rules described an administrator, a finance manager and the trust chair. Certain exceptions had to be sent to the chair when they were above a limit. The amount of that limit was still unreadable.

“Malcolm Vale was the chair,” Sarah said quietly.

“That tells us his position. Not that he signed any particular approval.”

Emma remembered Helen Ward's cousin. A letter said one application had been selected. There was no verified record that money had reached the student. Emma would not link the family to an exception without evidence.

That afternoon Fiona found a second reference to the missing box, in a list of papers transferred to an outside storage company. The list did not say whether the box had arrived safely, and the company's name was difficult to read.

“So our next step is the storage company?” Sarah asked.

“First we need the correct company and a record of the transfer.”

Emma opened a fresh page. She wrote three questions: Was the box transferred? Was it received? Does it still exist?

The strange thing was that she was now asking about the journey of a book, not a journey made by a student. But until she could follow the records, she could not follow the money.

At the bottom of the page, she wrote: A missing record is not proof of a missing payment.

units.title: The Missing Carton
units.transcript:
The reference to an authorisation register had looked promising when Fiona first mentioned it. By morning it had become another problem of incomplete records. The September 2011 delegated-authority sheet named roles and responsibilities, but no verified approver; the register that might contain actual decisions had not been located.

Fiona called with the results of a further search. A storage inventory prepared in 2012 referred to an approvals book for the student travel scheme and assigned it a box number. That numbered box was not among those currently kept in the trust's principal store.

“Then it was removed,” Sarah said when Emma told her.

“Possibly moved, yes. But removed deliberately? We have no evidence of that.”

Fiona was equally cautious. The box might have been transferred, reorganised or recorded incorrectly. No destruction notice had been found, which did not guarantee that the material survived. She offered to check other inventories without revealing applicants' personal information.

Emma compared the new reference with the delegated-authority procedure. It distinguished requests for exceptions from approvals and required cases above a threshold to be referred to the trust chair. The threshold figure remained illegible. Malcolm Vale's position as chair did not establish that he had signed any particular authorisation, still less that a payment had been executed.

Sarah wanted to connect the book with Helen Ward's cousin, whose redacted letter described a selected application. Emma refused. There was still no verified transfer, and nothing tied that application to an exception, an approval or the missing register.

In the afternoon Fiona forwarded a further description, this time from a transfer list for an external storage provider. It contained the same box reference. The provider's name was faint, and the paperwork did not confirm receipt of the box.

“Now we have a chain,” Sarah said.

“A possible chain,” Emma replied. “A line on a transfer list is not a signed delivery record.”

The distinction mattered. If a box had reached an outside warehouse, it might still be retrievable. If it had been mislabelled or never collected, looking there could lead nowhere. Neither scenario, on its own, suggested interference with the trust's accounts.

Emma wrote three questions for Fiona: could the provider be identified, was there a receipt or tracking number, and did a later inventory mention the box? She asked for descriptions, not the names of students or recipients.

As she saved the notes, she heard the anonymous caller's instruction again: ask who approved the payments. That question was unchanged. The route to answering it had become unexpectedly physical: a possible book, a numbered carton and an uncertain journey into storage.

For the moment, she could report only that a historical inventory referred to a register whose whereabouts were unknown.

Sarah wanted to connect the book with Helen Ward's cousin, whose redacted letter described a selected application. Emma refused. There was still no verified transfer, and nothing tied that application to an exception, an approval or the missing register.

“Now we have a chain,” Sarah said.

“A possible chain,” Emma replied. “A line on a transfer list is not a signed delivery record.”

The distinction mattered. If a box had reached an outside warehouse, it might still be retrievable. If it had been mislabelled or never collected, looking there could lead nowhere. Neither scenario, on its own, suggested interference with the trust's accounts.

Emma wrote three questions for Fiona: could the provider be identified, was there a receipt or tracking number, and did a later inventory mention the box? She asked for descriptions, not the names of students or recipients.

units.title: The Missing Carton
units.transcript:
Fiona's reference to a missing authorisation register had raised the possibility of evidence more substantial than the delegated-authority sheet. The latter described who was permitted to approve exceptional payments; the former, if it existed and could be authenticated, might identify decisions actually taken. Emma understood the attraction of that possibility. She also understood how little the archive had yet established.

A further inventory search produced a dated reference from 2012. It described an approvals book associated with the student travel programme and assigned it a carton number. The carton was not among those catalogued in the trust's present main store. No verified disposal record had been located.

Sarah interpreted the absence as grounds for suspicion. Emma disagreed with the inference, not with the need to investigate. A box omitted from one location could have been transferred, renumbered, misfiled or mistakenly entered in the first place. Conversely, the absence of a destruction notice did not prove survival. The central question was one of custody, not culpability.

Emma reconsidered the September 2011 delegated-authority document. Its division between requesting an exception and authorising one was clear. It also directed cases above a threshold to the trust chair, although the threshold itself was illegible on the surviving copy. Malcolm Vale had occupied that office. The procedural power to approve, however, remained distinct from evidence that he had exercised it in any identified transaction.

The redacted selection letter shown by Helen Ward offered no shortcut. Its wording indicated conditional selection of one applicant; it could not establish authorisation, bank transfer or receipt. Moreover, nothing linked that application to the exceptional-payment process. Emma would not manufacture a connection merely because two gaps in the evidence seemed to fit together.

Later that afternoon Fiona discovered a second historical listing. The same carton reference appeared on a form describing records intended for an external storage provider. The company name was partly illegible. Crucially, there was no signature or delivery confirmation on the copy Fiona had inspected.

“So the book went to an outside warehouse,” Sarah said.

“The paperwork suggests that transfer was contemplated,” Emma corrected. “Whether it happened is still open.”

A chain of custody, she explained, required more than successive references. The investigators needed evidence that the item was collected, received and retained under a traceable identifier. Even then, the register itself would have to be examined, its dates checked and its entries reconciled against any available payment documentation. A signature, if found, would not automatically establish that the corresponding money had reached a student.

Emma drafted a narrow enquiry for Fiona: identify the storage provider if possible; look for a signed receipt or tracking reference; check later inventories for the carton number or a renumbered equivalent. No private beneficiary information was needed to establish whether the archive had a recoverable book.

The anonymous caller's earlier insistence on identifying payment approvers now had a testable documentary target. That did not make the caller credible by association. The caller's identity, motives and access to the trust's financial records remained wholly unverified.

As evening drew in, Emma drew three successive boxes in her notebook: Listed for transfer, Received in storage, Register examined. Only the first had documentary support, and even that support rested on preliminary descriptions rather than originals inspected by her.

Her final note read: Before asking what the register proves, establish where the register is.

units.title: Location Changed
units.transcript:
Emma had three questions about the missing box. Had it left the trust? Had the storage company received it? Was it still there?

Fiona called on Tuesday morning. The records team had found a clearer copy of the 2012 transfer list. It showed the name of a storage company and a number for the box. There was also a date beside the line.

“Does that mean the company received it?” Emma asked.

“No,” Fiona replied. “This is the trust's list of boxes prepared for collection. We haven't found the company's receipt.”

Emma wrote prepared for collection in her notebook. It was a useful fact, but not the answer she wanted.

Sarah suggested calling the company. Emma agreed, but first she asked Fiona whether the trust could make the enquiry. The papers might contain private information about former students.

Later Fiona reported that the company had changed its name some years earlier. An old public notice confirmed the change, but it said nothing about the missing box.

“So we have the right company?” Sarah asked.

“We have a possible link between two names. We still need its records.”

Emma looked again at the 2012 list. There were small marks in a column headed Collected. The line for the authorisation book had a mark too.

“Then it was collected,” Sarah said.

“The trust marked it as collected. We need to know who made the mark and whether the company agreed.”

That afternoon Fiona sent an update. The company had agreed to search its historical records, but had not confirmed receiving the box. It would answer the trust, not Emma, because the trust was the customer.

Helen Ward also wrote. Her cousin could not find any papers showing that a grant payment had arrived. Helen reminded Emma that an old document might simply have been lost. Emma thanked her and made no further request.

As evening fell, Emma placed the transfer list beside her notes about payments. The two problems looked similar. In both cases a record described an action, but did not prove that it had been completed.

She drew three boxes across the page: Prepared, Collected, Received.

Then Fiona's final message arrived. The storage company had located an old index entry under the box number. The entry gave no contents, only the words Location changed.

Emma stared at the screen. The box might not have vanished at all. But she still had no idea where it had gone.

units.title: Location Changed
units.transcript:
Fiona's next update finally made the 2012 storage paperwork legible. The trust had located a clearer transfer schedule showing a box number, a collection date and the name of an external records company. None of those details, Fiona warned, amounted to proof that the company had accepted custody of the box.

Emma kept that warning in mind as she read the schedule. The document had been prepared by the trust, apparently to arrange a collection. Its column headings included Prepared and Collected, but there was no corresponding confirmation from the destination.

Sarah thought the question could now be settled with a phone call. Emma suggested that Fiona contact the company instead. The box might contain personal details of former students, and the trust was the organisation entitled to enquire about its own records.

The company named on the schedule no longer traded under that name. A public notice showed it had been renamed, which provided a plausible corporate link without establishing anything about the box itself.

Emma noticed a small mark beside the relevant entry in the Collected column.

“At least that shows the driver picked it up,” Sarah said.

“It shows someone marked the trust's schedule. We don't know who made the mark, or whether the box reached the warehouse.”

Fiona contacted the successor company. Its staff agreed to look through historical location records but had not yet confirmed receipt. For privacy reasons, they would respond to their former client rather than release details to a journalist.

Meanwhile Helen Ward said her cousin had found no surviving confirmation of a grant payment. Emma resisted connecting that absence to the authorisation book. Missing family paperwork was not evidence of an unpaid grant, and nothing associated the cousin with a manual exception.

By late afternoon Fiona had obtained one more detail from the storage company. A historic index contained the box number, accompanied by the phrase Location changed. It offered neither a location nor a description of the contents. The entry could indicate an internal move after receipt, a corrected reference or some other administrative change.

Sarah saw a breakthrough. Emma saw a lead that required checking.

“If the company had a location entry, perhaps it once held the box,” Sarah said.

“Perhaps. But we can't claim it held this particular register until the references and custody records agree.”

Emma drew a timeline with three separate events: preparation by the trust, collection recorded on the trust's schedule, and receipt at the storage site. Only the first was supported by a clear originating document; the second was a mark requiring explanation; the third remained unverified.

The new index entry gave her a precise question for Fiona: what location had been changed, when, and by whom?

units.title: Location Changed
units.transcript:
The clearer 2012 transfer schedule appeared at first to resolve the uncertainty surrounding the missing authorisation register. It identified an external records company, a box reference and a date designated for collection. Fiona Bell nevertheless cautioned that the document was the trust's own schedule, not a receipt issued by a storage provider.

Emma examined the distinction before discussing the news with Sarah. An organisation might prepare a box for transfer, record its departure and then assume that it had arrived safely. Each proposition required a different evidential basis. The schedule substantiated preparation; its remaining marks needed interpretation.

The named storage contractor had since changed its trading name. A public notice supported continuity between the old and new names, but established neither the custody of this particular box nor its survival.

“Surely we can ask them directly,” Sarah said.

“Fiona should,” Emma replied. “The trust is the customer, and the records may contain former applicants' personal information. We're not entitled to their contents simply because they might be relevant.”

A tick appeared in the schedule's Collected column beside the box reference. Sarah treated it as evidence that a driver had taken possession. Emma regarded it more cautiously. The mark had no visible signature; the person who made it and the event it represented were unknown. It could have been added before collection, during a stock check or afterwards.

Fiona contacted the successor storage company. Staff agreed to review its historic indexing records, but initially found no signed acknowledgement of receipt. They undertook to communicate with the trust rather than disclose client material directly to Emma.

Helen Ward's reply arrived while Emma was comparing the two records systems. Her cousin had not located any surviving bank paperwork confirming payment of the selected grant. The absence was unsurprising after fifteen years and supplied no reason to associate the family's application with the missing authorisation register. Emma noted the limitation and did not press Helen for another disclosure.

Later Fiona forwarded a brief description from the storage company's internal index. The box number appeared beside the words Location changed. There was no contents list, no explanation of the previous location and no indication of who had amended the entry.

Sarah thought the notation meant the box must once have been in the warehouse. That was plausible, Emma conceded, but not established. The same reference might have been transferred from a predecessor system, corrected during data migration or linked to a physical box that could not yet be identified. She would not convert the mere existence of a catalogue entry into an uninterrupted chain of custody.

On a fresh page she separated the stages: Prepared for collection, Marked collected, Received by contractor, Moved internally. She placed the available document beside each and left the unverified stages blank.

There was an irony in the investigation. Emma had been trying to determine whether authorisation entries corresponded to completed financial transfers. Now she was asking whether an administrative transfer entry corresponded to the physical movement of a box. In both cases, a record of intention or approval was not interchangeable with a verified outcome.

She asked Fiona to enquire what the index had meant by Location changed: the former location, the destination and the date of amendment. A detailed answer might lead to the register. It might equally reveal a clerical correction.

Either result would be better than an accusation built on an unexplained tick.

units.title: The Sealed Box
units.transcript:
On Wednesday morning Fiona called Emma with an update from the storage company. Staff had checked the old note marked “Location changed”. It had been entered during a warehouse reorganisation in 2013. The company had moved records from one building to another and changed the codes used to describe their places.

“Does that mean you have found the authorisation register?” Emma asked.

“Not yet,” Fiona said. “The index connects the old box number to a newer location code. It doesn't describe what is inside.”

The company had also found a stock-check sheet from 2014. Beside the new code was a tick and a date. Fiona warned that a tick in a stock list did not prove every document in a box had survived.

Sarah was excited when Emma explained the news. “They must have the register, then.”

“They may have the box,” Emma answered. “Even that needs a physical check. We can't say the register is there.”

Fiona had asked the company to search its current shelves. Because the records belonged to the trust and could contain private student information, Emma could not visit the warehouse or inspect the box herself.

While she waited, she looked again at the four headings in her notebook: request, authorisation, transfer and receipt. If the missing book existed, it might show who had approved unusual payments. It would not, on its own, prove that the bank had sent the money.

Helen Ward sent a short message. Her cousin had nothing more to share at present. Emma thanked her. She would not treat an absent bank statement as evidence of a missing grant.

In the afternoon Fiona called again. The warehouse team had found a box carrying the newer location code. Its label included the old reference from the trust's transfer list. The seal was dusty but unbroken, according to the warehouse worker.

“So it is the right box?” Emma asked.

“It may be. We need to compare the references and check the contents properly. The company hasn't opened it.”

A physical box was more than a catalogue entry, but the identification was still provisional. Emma asked Fiona to ensure that anyone opening it recorded what was found, including any pages missing or damaged. She also asked that student details remain private.

Late that evening Fiona sent a final email. The trust and the storage company had agreed to arrange a supervised examination. They would first verify the box label, then record the contents before deciding what information could lawfully be shared.

Sarah read the message and smiled. “Tomorrow we might finally learn who signed.”

“Maybe,” Emma said. “First we find out whether the book is inside.”

She closed her notebook, then opened it once more and wrote: Found a possible box. Not yet found the truth.

On Wednesday morning Fiona called Emma with an update from the storage company. Staff had checked the old note marked “Location changed”. It had been entered during a warehouse reorganisation in 2013. The company had moved records from one building to another and changed the codes used to describe their places.

“Does that mean you have found the authorisation register?” Emma asked.

“Not yet,” Fiona said. “The index connects the old box number to a newer location code. It doesn't describe what is inside.”

The company had also found a stock-check sheet from 2014. Beside the new code was a tick and a date. Fiona warned that a tick in a stock list did not prove every document in a box had survived.

Sarah was excited when Emma explained the news. “They must have the register, then.”

“They may have the box,” Emma answered. “Even that needs a physical check. We can't say the register is there.”

Fiona had asked the company to search its current shelves. Because the records belonged to the trust and could contain private student information, Emma could not visit the warehouse or inspect the box herself.

While she waited, she looked again at the four headings in her notebook: request, authorisation, transfer and receipt. If the missing book existed, it might show who had approved unusual payments. It would not, on its own, prove that the bank had sent the money.

Helen Ward sent a short message. Her cousin had nothing more to share at present. Emma thanked her. She would not treat an absent bank statement as evidence of a missing grant.

In the afternoon Fiona called again. The warehouse team had found a box carrying the newer location code. Its label included the old reference from the trust's transfer list. The seal was dusty but unbroken, according to the warehouse worker.

“So it is the right box?” Emma asked.

“It may be. We need to compare the references and check the contents properly. The company hasn't opened it.”

A physical box was more than a catalogue entry, but the identification was still provisional. Emma asked Fiona to ensure that anyone opening it recorded what was found, including any pages missing or damaged. She also asked that student details remain private.

Late that evening Fiona sent a final email. The trust and the storage company had agreed to arrange a supervised examination. They would first verify the box label, then record the contents before deciding what information could lawfully be shared.

Sarah read the message and smiled. “Tomorrow we might finally learn who signed.”

“Maybe,” Emma said. “First we find out whether the book is inside.”

She closed her notebook, then opened it once more and wrote: *Found a possible box. Not yet found the truth.*

units.title: The Book Inside
units.transcript:
Emma was reading the morning news when Fiona Bell called. The trust and the storage company had opened the box under supervision. Two people had checked its labels and written down what they found. The box was not empty.

“Was the approval register inside?” Emma asked.

“There was a book with that title,” Fiona said. “But we must check whether it is the book mentioned in the 2012 list. Some pages are difficult to read.”

Emma put down her coffee. For weeks she had followed the journey of a missing box. Now somebody had finally looked inside it.

Fiona explained that the book contained dates, reference numbers and spaces for approval. Some spaces had initials. Others were empty. The records team had not connected the initials to particular people, and Fiona would not share student names.

“Does it show payments?” Emma asked.

“Approvals, perhaps. We haven't found bank transfers in the book.”

Emma called Sarah. “They found a register. It could help us understand the decisions, but it doesn't tell us who received money.”

“Is Malcolm Vale's name in it?” Sarah asked.

“We don't know. Initials aren't enough to identify anyone.”

In the afternoon Fiona sent a description of the inspection, with no private details. The records team had found a page explaining how entries should be made. It told staff to write a second reference when an exception was resolved. Emma remembered the earlier guide with the same rule.

“That sounds like a match,” Sarah said.

“It makes the book more interesting. We still need to compare the documents.”

One detail caught Emma's attention. The inspection note said that a page near the middle of the book was loose. The paper had not been examined closely, and nobody knew whether any pages were missing. Emma refused to describe it as a page that somebody had removed.

She opened her notebook and wrote three questions. Did the references match the exception records? Could the approvals be linked to real people without guessing? Did any approved payment become a bank transfer?

Before dinner Fiona called again. The team had found a reference in the register that also appeared in the exception guide's sample format. It was not yet linked to a specific payment.

Emma looked towards the window. The investigation had finally reached the book. But finding a book and finding the truth were still two different things.

Before ending the call, Emma asked Fiona to pass on a request if she could reach Claire through a trusted contact. She wanted to hear Claire's own account, not find her address. Fiona promised only to ask whether a private conversation was possible.

units.title: The Book Inside
units.transcript:
Fiona Bell called before Emma had finished breakfast. The supervised inspection at the storage company had taken place. Staff from the trust and the warehouse had compared the old box reference with its newer label, recorded the condition of the seal and made an inventory before examining the contents.

Inside was a bound volume titled “Student Travel — Authorisations 2011”. Fiona would not yet call it the missing register. Its title fitted the 2012 inventory, but the team still needed to confirm that the references and dates matched.

“Does it name the people who approved payments?” Emma asked.

“Some entries have initials. Others are incomplete. We haven't established who wrote them, and we are not releasing identifiable student information.”

Nor did the volume appear to contain bank statements. Fiona said its columns related to requests and approvals, not proof that money had been transferred to students.

Emma called Sarah immediately.

“So we've found the evidence that Malcolm signed?” Sarah asked.

“We've found what may be an approval register. We have no confirmed signature, and even a valid approval wouldn't prove a payment reached anybody.”

Later Fiona supplied a description of the first inspection rather than images of individual records. A page at the front contained instructions for recording follow-up references when exceptional cases were resolved. The language resembled the guide previously found in the exceptions folder. That resemblance made the volume relevant, although the team had not completed a full comparison.

There was also a physical problem. One page near the centre was loose. The inspectors noted its condition without claiming it had been removed or that anything was missing. Emma had learnt not to turn damage into a story before the evidence warranted one.

She considered Helen Ward's cousin, whose letter recorded selection for support but no confirmed transfer. Nothing yet linked that application to any entry in the recovered volume. Emma had no intention of trying to identify the student through the trust's confidential records.

She drew a sequence across her notebook: exception recorded, approval granted, payment attempted, payment received. Only the first two could potentially be investigated using the book itself. The last two would require separate financial evidence.

By early evening Fiona reported a modest further detail. At least one entry used a reference format resembling the examples in the exception guidance, but its significance had not been verified. She was asking the records team to compare the relevant dates and codes before reaching any conclusion.

Sarah wanted to know if they were finally close to the answer. Emma hesitated.

“We're closer to a record that can be tested,” she said. “That's different from having proved what happened.”

Before the call ended, Emma asked whether Fiona could pass a request through a trusted contact: would Claire consider a private conversation? She wanted neither an address nor a forced reunion. Fiona agreed to ask, without promising that Claire would answer.

units.title: The Book Inside
units.transcript:
The call from Fiona Bell came with the kind of news Emma had spent weeks trying not to anticipate. The trust's representatives and the storage contractor had conducted a supervised opening of the carton identified through the 2013 relocation index. They had reconciled the visible box labels as far as possible, documented the seal and prepared a preliminary contents inventory before examining the papers.

Among them was a bound volume headed “Student Travel — Authorisations 2011”. The title corresponded closely to the missing item on the trust's 2012 storage list, though Fiona insisted that its identity had yet to be established by comparing internal references. A plausible match was not an authenticated chain of custody.

Emma asked first about what the book recorded, not who might be implicated. Fiona described dated entries with reference fields and spaces for approval. Some contained initials or marks that could not yet be attributed reliably. Other fields were blank. The volume did not itself comprise bank-transfer confirmations, and the trust would not disclose information capable of identifying former applicants.

Sarah's reaction was immediate. “If Malcolm was the chair, perhaps those are his approvals.”

“Perhaps,” Emma answered, “but authority under a scheme and authorship of a particular mark are separate questions. And neither one establishes that money reached a beneficiary.”

Fiona subsequently provided a non-identifying inspection summary. At the front of the volume, a procedural note instructed administrators to cross-reference a later action when an exceptional case was resolved. The wording resembled the guidance already identified in the exceptions folder. This strengthened the case for comparing the two records, without demonstrating that the procedures had always been followed.

A loose leaf near the volume's centre required conservation advice before further handling. The inspectors had not established whether any page was absent, and Emma rejected Sarah's tentative suggestion that it had been deliberately removed. Physical deterioration, binding damage and interference were different explanations requiring different evidence.

Emma thought of Helen Ward's cousin. The privately examined letter had indicated selection conditional on further checks. It had neither established a completed transfer nor authorised the newsroom to search confidential foundation files for the applicant's identity. Nothing about the newly recovered book changed those limits.

She revised her evidence map into four propositions: an exception was recorded; approval was given; funds were transmitted; funds were received. The volume might clarify the first two, subject to authentication. The latter stages required independent accounting or banking evidence. The anonymous caller's earlier insistence on identifying approvers remained a lead, not proof of the caller's knowledge or motives.

By evening Fiona had reported one preliminary overlap: an entry in the volume used the same reference convention as the examples in the exceptions guidance. No particular payment, signatory or student had yet been matched. The team would compare dates and complete references before deciding what could be stated.

Emma closed her notes with an unfamiliar feeling. The investigation had at last produced a tangible object that might answer a precise question. But the difference between locating a book and verifying an allegation was exactly the difference she could no longer afford to ignore.

units.transcript:
The next morning, Fiona sent Emma a report from the records team. They had compared several reference numbers in the recovered book with the list of payment exceptions. Some matched. This made the book more likely to belong to the student travel scheme, but it did not prove that every entry was correct.

Fiona had also found a clearer copy of the instructions about manual approvals. A finance manager could authorise some exceptions. Larger requests had to go to the trust chair. The amount of the limit was still difficult to read.

“Have you worked out whose initials are in the book?” Emma asked.

“Not safely. We are checking staff records from 2011. We cannot guess from two letters.”

Emma told Sarah. Sarah immediately thought of Malcolm Vale, who had chaired the trust.

“Could he have signed one of them?”

“He could have had the authority,” Emma said. “That doesn't tell us whether he used it.”

In the afternoon the trust's accountants found one more useful document: a summary of payments sent to the bank. It contained totals for a month, but no student names in the version Fiona could describe. The accountants had not yet compared it with individual approval entries.

“So at last we have proof every approved grant was paid?” Sarah asked.

“No. We have another type of record. We need to match the dates and references.”

Emma opened Helen Ward's redacted letter again. It showed one selected application, with payment depending on further checks. Helen's cousin had not provided bank evidence. Emma could not connect that letter to any line in the recovered book.

Then Fiona called. The loose page in the middle of the book had been examined. It was still attached by a thin strip of paper. The team had not established that any sheet was missing.

“That matters,” Emma told Sarah. “We shouldn't describe the book as damaged deliberately.”

Before leaving, Emma asked Fiona whether the trust would make a separate check of the signatures and bank records. Fiona said the team was arranging it. She could not promise what it would show.

That evening Emma wrote three statements in her notebook: Some references match. Some initials remain unidentified. No payment to a particular student is yet verified.

Sarah read them and sighed. “After all this work, we still can't name anyone.”

“Not responsibly,” Emma said.

A final message from Fiona arrived. One approval entry had a follow-up reference, and staff had found the same code in a separate banking index. The records behind that code were still being checked.

Emma stared at the number. This time, there was a specific transaction to trace. It might connect an approval to an actual transfer—or show why they had never been the same thing.

units.title: The Matching Reference
units.transcript:
Fiona's first message of the day contained a cautious but meaningful result. Several reference numbers in the recovered authorisations book corresponded to numbers in the payment-exceptions records. That supported the possibility that the volume belonged to the 2011 travel scheme, although it did not authenticate every page or establish that the approvals had been acted upon.

A clearer copy of the delegated-authority guidance had also been examined. It assigned certain exceptions to the finance manager and required requests above a threshold to go to the trust chair. The threshold figure was still partly unreadable, and the initials entered in the book had not been matched reliably to the people who held those posts.

“Malcolm Vale was chair,” Sarah pointed out.

“Which may tell us what he was authorised to approve,” Emma replied, “not which entries he actually signed.”

Fiona said her colleagues were checking contemporaneous staffing records rather than interpreting faint initials by guesswork. Emma welcomed the distinction. A plausible name was not the same as an identified signatory.

Later, an accounting summary offered a second route towards the money. It recorded monthly bank-payment totals but did not provide a list of identifiable recipients in the version that Fiona could discuss. No reconciliation with the individual approval references had yet been completed.

Sarah wanted to know whether the monthly total proved the grants were paid.

“It shows a reported banking total,” Emma said. “It doesn't connect a particular approved exception to money reaching a particular student.”

Emma reviewed Helen Ward's redacted letter. It said the cousin had been selected subject to further conditions; the family had not verified whether a transfer followed. Emma refused to search restricted records for a name to fill that gap.

The inspection report also resolved one source of suspicion. The loose leaf inside the authorisations book was still attached along one edge. The examiners had identified no missing sheet at that position. Emma crossed out the question removed page? in her notebook. Damage might be accidental, and the physical finding did not justify suggesting tampering.

Fiona agreed to request an independent comparison of staff authorisations and bank evidence, while warning that the surviving records might not support a complete reconstruction.

Towards evening she contacted Emma again. One exception entry bore a follow-up reference which also appeared in a banking index. The underlying transaction documentation had not yet been reviewed, and the code might indicate a correction, a returned payment or a completed transfer.

“Finally, one line we can follow,” Sarah said.

“One line we can test,” Emma corrected.

She wrote the reference in her notebook, without copying any student's identifying details. The prospect of a verifiable financial trail was more useful than the speculation that had surrounded the initials. But until the bank record was examined, the distinction between approval and payment remained intact.

units.title: The Matching Reference
units.transcript:
The first comparison of the recovered authorisations book produced a result that was promising precisely because it was limited. Several reference numbers corresponded to entries in the trust's surviving payment-exceptions material. The overlap supported the volume's connection to the 2011 student travel scheme; it could not certify the authenticity of every page or establish the execution of any particular authorisation.

Fiona Bell described a clearer copy of the delegated-authority rules. Certain exceptions fell within a finance manager's remit, while requests above a specified threshold required referral to the trust chair. The amount defining that threshold remained partly illegible. Moreover, the initials beside several entries in the recovered book had not been matched to verified staff signatures.

“Malcolm Vale held the chair's position,” Sarah observed. “Surely that narrows it down.”

“It narrows down who might have had authority,” Emma replied. “It tells us nothing reliable about who wrote those initials.”

The trust was consulting contemporaneous personnel records before attributing an entry to an individual. Emma knew how seductive a familiar name could become when placed beside an unexplained mark. She was determined not to turn a hypothesis into an allegation.

Another document introduced a different kind of evidence: a monthly summary of payments submitted to the bank. It contained aggregate figures, but Fiona could not yet provide verified links between those totals and the authorisations in the book. An instruction to pay, an accounting summary and proof that an intended recipient received funds were related propositions, not interchangeable ones.

Emma returned briefly to the letter shown by Helen Ward. Its selection language and conditions were clear, but the copy had not been fully authenticated and no corresponding transfer had been established. She would not use confidential student data to manufacture a link between an unnamed family and an unidentified entry.

The physical examination offered a smaller, corrective discovery. The leaf previously described as loose remained attached along a narrow edge. Inspectors found no evidence of a sheet missing at that point. It would have been misleading to continue speaking of a page that had been removed. Emma amended her notes rather than preserving the more dramatic possibility.

Fiona agreed to ask for a separate review of the authorisation entries against staffing information and available banking material. She made no promise of complete reconciliation. A decade and a half of fragmented recordkeeping might prevent any definitive account of some transactions.

At the end of the afternoon Fiona reported a possible bridge between two sets of records. A follow-up reference attached to one exception entry appeared again in a banking index. The underlying entry had not been inspected. The code might refer to an attempted transfer, an adjustment, a reversal or a successfully completed payment. Its repetition established a traceable lead, not its meaning.

Sarah was eager to describe the first confirmed irregularity. Emma stopped her.

“A matching code is not an irregularity. We don't know what the bank did.”

She recorded three findings: selected reference numbers matched; the initials remained unattributed; and the bank index contained one potentially related reference whose transaction status was unknown.

As dusk settled over Edinburgh, she looked again at the final code. Unlike the vague warnings and incomplete figures that had occupied so much of the investigation, it posed a question that a specific document might answer. Its answer, however, belonged to the final stage of the inquiry, not to Emma's imagination.

units.title: The Last Word
units.transcript:
The next morning, Fiona Bell called Emma with news about the matching reference. An independent accountant had examined the banking record behind it. The first transfer had been returned by the bank. A later transfer had gone into an account controlled by the Glenarraidh Education Trust, not directly to a student. The trust's exception book marked the case as resolved.

“Does that mean the student never got the money?” Emma asked.

“We cannot say that,” Fiona replied. “The records we have do not show what happened after the money reached the trust's account.”

There was a second finding. A signed approval sheet linked to the same reference carried Malcolm Vale's full name. The accountant had checked it against signed trust documents from 2011.

“So Malcolm approved that transfer?”

“The evidence supports that one approval. It does not tell us what he intended, or what happened to every other grant.”

Emma told Sarah. At last they could report a real difference between an approval, a bank transfer and a payment received by a student. They still could not call it theft.

Then Fiona sent another document, this time from 2026. It was an email from Malcolm's work account, with the exact words of the second letter Emma had received. The message instructed a colleague to send it in Claire's name. Courier records matched the delivery. Emma and Sarah checked the dates and the wording independently.

“The warning letter wasn't from Claire,” Sarah said.

“Now we have evidence of who arranged it,” Emma replied.

They contacted Malcolm and gave him an opportunity to answer. He admitted arranging the second letter. He said he had wanted Emma to stop upsetting people connected with the trust. He denied taking student money and said the finances would be explained. Emma recorded both his admission and his denial.

That evening Fiona asked whether Emma would accept a private call. Claire Morrison wanted to speak.

Emma sat very still as the screen lit up. The woman looked older than in the 2011 photograph, but Emma knew her voice. Claire showed her the original draft and courier details of the first letter, written on 14 October 2026. They also checked private details with James Morrison, without asking him to reveal Claire's location.

“I sent the first letter,” Claire said. “Not the second.”

“Why did you leave?” Emma asked.

“I was frightened. I thought the trust was calling some grants paid before the students had received them. I asked questions, and I felt that my brother and the students might suffer if I stayed. Daniel Reid helped me leave on 21 September 2011. He didn't take me against my will, and he doesn't know where I live now.”

Emma remembered Nora seeing Claire enter a car. Claire had chosen to get in, but that did not mean she had felt safe staying in the village.

“I wrote that you left after a personal argument,” Emma said quietly. “I was wrong. I didn't check enough.”

“You can correct it now,” Claire answered. “But please don't tell people where I am. And let me speak to James myself.”

Emma promised to respect that choice.

The following day the newspaper published a carefully checked report. It explained the one documented transfer into the trust's account, Malcolm's signed authorisation and the forged warning letter. It also published a correction to Emma's old story. The newspaper asked for an independent review of the remaining grants. It did not claim that every student had lost money or reveal Claire's address.

James read the correction. He did not forgive Emma immediately, but he thanked her for finally changing the headline.

In the investigation file, Emma left the early anonymous calls and message marked ‘sender unknown’. Reid's admission still needed an official response. The students' remaining payment questions belonged in the wider review, not in a guessed ending.

That night Emma put Claire's first letter beside the new article. The mystery had not ended with every bank account explained. It had ended with a false story corrected, a real woman heard, and questions that could finally be investigated openly.

Emma folded the letter carefully. She no longer needed to guess what it meant.

Emma sat very still as the screen lit up. The woman looked older than in the 2011 photograph, but Emma knew her voice. units.title: The Last Word
units.transcript:
Fiona Bell's call the following morning began with a sentence Emma had spent weeks hoping to hear: the bank had located the transaction behind the matching follow-up reference. An independent accountant had compared its surviving record with the recovered authorisations book and the trust's exception register.

The original transfer had been returned. A subsequent payment, carrying the same follow-up reference, had gone into an account controlled by the Glenarraidh Education Trust. The exception was nevertheless marked resolved. There was no verified onward transfer to the intended student among the records examined.

“Then we have proof the grant was stolen,” Sarah said.

“We have proof that the recorded destination was the trust's account,” Emma replied. “That's serious enough to investigate. It isn't proof of what happened afterwards, or of anyone's criminal intention.”

The independent review had also identified a signed authorisation sheet attached to that exception. Malcolm Vale's full name appeared beneath the approval, and the signature had been checked against contemporaneous signed trust documents. Unlike the blurred initials that had tempted them earlier, this was evidence supporting attribution of one specific decision. It did not transform every other manual entry into Malcolm's act, nor establish that he had received the money personally.

Emma could already see the report she would write: an exception closed administratively without evidence, in the material examined, that the intended recipient had received the grant. The discrepancy demanded an explanation and a wider audit. It did not entitle her to invent one.

Then Fiona disclosed the evidence that changed Emma's understanding of the letters. Among the trust's 2026 correspondence was an email from Malcolm's work account containing the complete wording of the later warning sent in Claire Morrison's name. It instructed a colleague to arrange delivery as though Claire were its author. Emma and Sarah checked the original electronic record against courier documentation and the letter Emma had kept. Both the wording and the delivery trail matched.

They contacted Malcolm before publication. Confronted with the records, he acknowledged arranging the second letter and said his intention had been to stop a distressing investigation. He maintained that the travel scheme's accounts had innocent explanations and denied taking students' money. Emma preserved his response in full. A documented act of impersonation was not, by itself, a finding of financial fraud.

That evening Fiona offered something the registers never could: contact with the woman whose disappearance had begun the story. Claire had agreed to a private video conversation, provided her present location remained confidential.

At first Emma saw only the reflection of a lamp in the screen. Then Claire appeared, older, tired around the eyes, unmistakably herself and yet a person Emma could no longer pretend to know. The two women checked the draft and courier booking for the first letter, written on 14 October 2026 and delivered the following day. James Morrison privately confirmed details of their shared past. Emma would neither disclose those details nor turn them into a trail towards Claire's home.

“I sent the first letter,” Claire said. “I didn't send the warning.”

She described the days after their interview on 18 September 2011. She had questioned the way the trust reported support for students, concerned that approval and actual payment were being spoken of as though they were identical. She said she had felt threatened, not because she possessed proof of wholesale theft, but because her questions made powerful people angry and seemed to put her brother and the students at risk. Her fears were part of her testimony, not independently established facts about every person she suspected.

On 21 September, Daniel Reid had helped her leave Glenarraidh. He had driven her away from the village; he had not abducted her, and he did not know where she lived now. Nora's old account of Claire entering a car voluntarily was therefore compatible with Claire's own description of the pressure she had felt.

“People kept asking whether I chose to leave,” Claire told Emma. “I did. Nobody asked what I thought would happen if I stayed.”

Emma remembered the headline she had written after the disappearance, suggesting that Claire had left over a personal dispute. She had been young and ambitious; neither fact excused presenting a poorly sourced interpretation as an answer. James had been right to resent it.

“I published the wrong story,” Emma said. “And I made your family live with it.”

“Then publish what you can prove,” Claire replied. “Keep my address out of it. I'll decide when and how to speak to James.”

Emma agreed. She did not ask where Claire lived. Having finally heard from her, she understood that access was not ownership.

The article appeared the following day. It documented the returned transfer, the subsequent payment into the trust-controlled account, Malcolm's signed approval and the evidence behind the forged letter. It included his denial of financial wrongdoing and called for an independent review of the remaining awards. A separate, conspicuous correction withdrew the old suggestion that a personal quarrel explained Claire's disappearance. The newsroom protected the identities of applicants and did not describe Claire's private testimony as a court finding.

James read the correction. He told Emma that it could not restore the years the family had lost, but that withdrawing the headline mattered. He was not offering forgiveness, and she did not ask for it.

In the research log, the early anonymous contacts remained unattributed; Reid's acknowledged omission still called for an official response. The unresolved student cases, review procedures and missing totals belonged to the wider audit. Emma would not let a corrected headline imply that those separate questions had also been settled.

That night, back in her Edinburgh flat, Emma took Claire's first letter from the drawer where she had kept it. For fifteen years she had wanted a final sentence that explained everything: why Claire vanished, who benefited, where the money went. The surviving evidence could not honestly provide one.

But it had established something more enduring than a neat accusation. The second letter had been a deliberate attempt to silence questions. The first had asked Emma to ask better ones. And Claire, still alive, had chosen to answer in her own voice, without surrendering the right to remain out of sight.

Emma folded the paper along its original crease. This time, she had not made the last word hers.
